title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
authors: Arpit Bahety,Skand Peri,Sriniket Ambatipudi,Chen Xu,Haruki Nishimura,Masha Itkina,Roberto Martín-Martín
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment.
Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data:
existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to our Project Page for videos.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) provide broad manipulation capabilities [1, 2, 3], but can still exhibit systematic failures during deployment [4], such as collisions, dropping objects, etc.
Human interventions offer a natural source of corrective data [5, 6, 7, 8], yet existing interactive imitation methods generally treat corrections as additional state-action supervision [5, 6], making generalization depend on collecting enough corrections in similar states.
Humans can instead infer a reusable principle from only a few corrections.
We ask whether a robot can likewise infer what prompted an intervention, how its behavior should be steered to avoid it, and when the same correction should apply again.

An intervention provides only partial evidence about this principle.
Before takeover, the robot executes the VLA actions; afterward, the human provides a preferred continuation.
Instead, the takeover time localizes the context that prompted the intervention and that generalizes to other similar situations, while the subsequent human-controlled segment provides a preferred continuation from the reached state towards a more optimal situation.
A description such as “keep the mug upright when placing it on the plate” identifies the semantic property motivating the takeover, which may remain valid despite changes in object(s) poses, robot configuration, background, or even task.
Trajectories alone leave ambiguous which property mattered; language alone lacks the sensorimotor grounding needed for visuomotor control.
Together, they constrain a reusable correction.

This ambiguity motivates OopsieRecover, which formulates correction inference as abduction [9]: finding a simple explanation consistent with the observed interventions despite missing or imperfect information.
A vision-language model (VLM) leverages its visual-language priors, together with the scene, robot-controlled initial demonstration, human intervention, and language annotation, to propose candidate explanations.
Since several explanations may fit one intervention, OopsieRecover evaluates each hypothesis across all available interventions and selects explanations that capture the underlying corrective behavior without being overly narrow or permissive.
In this formal-methods inspired procedure, the VLM proposes plausible semantic hypotheses, and the corrective evidence determines whether they are retained or refined.

We represent the selected explanation as one or more gated costs.
Each combines a logical predicate specifying when the correction applies with a continuous cost specifying how the behavior should optimize/change.
E.g., a gate may activate during placement, while its cost penalizes tilting the mug away from upright.
This separation keeps corrections local rather globally biasing the policy.
To execute these costs, OopsieRecover grounds task-relevant robot parts, object parts, and spatial locations and regions as semantic point sets.
At test time, the VLA samples candidate action chunks, and OopsieRecover predicts how each candidate would move these point sets, how they evaluate on the gated costs, and which candidate would lead to the lowest cost overall.
The frozen VLA supplies plausible behaviors, while the inferred correction steers its choices whenever the same semantic situation reappears.

We evaluate OopsieRecover on 3 tasks in both sim and real using pi0 in RoboCasa and DROID, with only 5-8 corrections per task.
OopsieRecover improves real-world task-progress from 35.1% to 61.0%, a 74% relative improvement over the next-best baseline, and transfers corrections to unseen poses, objects and scenes. We show that our gated costs generalize to novel variations in object poses and scenes zero-shot, and successfully steer the base policy.
Our contributions are: i) a semantic, abductive formulation of few-shot VLA correction from human-in-the-loop interventions; ii) a generate-and-test procedure that synthesizes and verifies gated costs; and iii) a test-time steering mechanism that applies and generalizes them without retraining the VLA.

title: Latent RL Priors for Data-Efficient Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Yixiao Wang,Peiyi Chen,Mustafa Mukadam,Shreekant Gayaka,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Son Tran
abstract:
Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. We introduce Latent RL Prior, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using 10×10\times and 5×5\times fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge.
Project website: https://yixiaowang7.github.io/latent-rl-prior-page/.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation requires coordinated arm and finger motion under
changing contacts and object dynamics. Learning these behaviors from limited
visual demonstrations is challenging because the policy must acquire both
perceptual grounding and precise action generation
(Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023). Pretrained vision-language-action
(VLA) models offer transferable priors from broad visual, language, and robot
datasets (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). We investigate
a complementary source of prior knowledge for dexterous control: behaviors
acquired through large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation.

Simulated interaction enables RL policies to acquire manipulation strategies
across diverse object geometries and physical properties
(Andrychowicz et al., 2020; Singla et al., 2024; Kedia et al., 2026).
However, these policies often rely on privileged information, such as object
and goal states, that is not directly available at deployment. Reusing their
control capabilities requires an interface that connects visual observations
to the pretrained controller. Our premise is that preserving pretrained
proprioceptive processing and action generation can reduce the visual
demonstrations needed to adapt these capabilities to downstream tasks.

We introduce Latent RL Prior, a simple yet effective framework for this transfer.
We distill rollouts from an RL teacher trained on procedural pose alignment
into a flow-matching action decoder (Lipman et al., 2023). The decoder
receives proprioceptive history through a dedicated pathway and latent context
encoding privileged task information. During visual adaptation, we freeze the
decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images directly to this context.
This latent transfer uses only the action objective on
image–proprioception–action demonstrations, without requiring
corresponding privileged information, pretrained latent targets, or paired
trajectories between the pretraining and adaptation datasets.

The same design extends a single-arm RL prior to multiple arms. We share the
frozen decoder across arms and learn coordinated visual contexts, each paired
with the corresponding arm’s proprioceptive history. Bimanual adaptation thus
reuses the pretrained control prior while learning inter-arm coordination
through the visual interface.

We evaluate the shared prior on target pose alignment, door lifting, and
bimanual assembly in simulation. With limited visual demonstrations, our
method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of π0.5\pi_{0.5}
(Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) and GR00T N1.7
(NVIDIA, 2026). On door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses
both baselines trained on the full task datasets with 10×10\times and
5×5\times fewer demonstrations, respectively. Comparisons with the same visual
policy architecture trained from scratch further support the value of the
pretrained action prior.

Further investigations examine how to access and adapt this prior. Latent
transfer improves performance and training stability over explicit transfer
through the pretrained state encoder. Separate adaptation studies favor
conservative updates to the image encoder and a frozen action decoder,
particularly for precise alignment. We also investigate the control behaviors
and physical information accessible after transfer. The adapted policies
exhibit robustness to mass variation absent from the visual demonstrations,
and their decoder representations make contact-force information more linearly
accessible than those learned from scratch. These observations are consistent
with retained control knowledge from large-scale RL pretraining.

Our contributions are:

a framework for adapting a frozen RL action prior through latent
visual conditioning with action supervision alone, including reuse of
a single-arm decoder for multi-arm manipulation;

empirical evidence of improved visual-demonstration efficiency
across three dexterous tasks, together with evaluations of the transfer
interface and adaptation choices; and

behavioral and representational analyses of mass robustness and
contact-force accessibility after visual adaptation.

1. a framework for adapting a frozen RL action prior through latent
visual conditioning with action supervision alone, including reuse of
a single-arm decoder for multi-arm manipulation;

2. empirical evidence of improved visual-demonstration efficiency
across three dexterous tasks, together with evaluations of the transfer
interface and adaptation choices; and

3. behavioral and representational analyses of mass robustness and
contact-force accessibility after visual adaptation.

title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
authors: Yu-Cheng Chou,Shihao Wang,Jin Huang,Chi-Pin Huang,Chiao-An Yang,Xianzhe Fan,Jing Wang,Zhiqi Li,Yuanguo Kuang,Ruijie Zheng,Johan Bjorck,Sifei Liu,Hang Su,Abhishek Badki,Lei Zhang,Alan Yuille,Linxi "Jim'' Fan,Jan Kautz,Zhiding Yu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans—points, bounding boxes, and trajectories—to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive’s type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model’s exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25×25\times faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level brains for physical AI systems, interpreting visual observations and task instructions to guide behavior in robotics and autonomous driving (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025; Tian et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025). Their reasoning need not be expressed solely in language. VLMs can formulate intermediate predictions as visual plans: points and bounding boxes identify relevant locations or
objects (Yuan et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025), while trajectories describe intended motion or forecast how a scene will evolve (Gu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a). Recent work uses spatial traces and visual primitives to guide action generation (Li et al., 2025a; Lee et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026).
These plans make spatial goals and anticipated motion explicit before action.
Each visual primitive has identifiable boundaries and an organized
coordinate layout.

Generating such plans efficiently becomes increasingly important as their spatial detail grows.
Longer trajectories, additional objects, and joint 2D image and 3D
predictions require more coordinate tokens, which autoregressive VLMs
decode sequentially (Chen et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025).
For physical agents that update their plans as new observations arrive, sequential decoding limits spatial detail and update frequency under a fixed latency budget. This motivates decoding methods that can generate complete visual plans with fewer sequential forward passes while preserving their spatial accuracy.

Parallel decoding offers a promising route to reducing this sequential cost, particularly for latency-sensitive physical AI systems operating at batch size one. Existing approaches include speculative decoding with parallel
verification (Leviathan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025b) and diffusion language models (dLLMs) with parallel denoising (Nie et al., 2025; Arriola et al., 2025). However, dLLMs often exhibit a speed–quality trade-off relative to autoregressive models (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). DFlash combines these approaches using a lightweight block diffusion draft model to predict draft tokens in a single forward pass, followed by target verification that preserves the autoregressive model’s output
distribution (Chen et al., 2026). For visual outputs, LocateAnything exploits spatial structure through parallel box decoding (Wang et al., 2026).

In this work, we introduce VFlash, a generalist decoding framework for physical AI (Figure 1) that accommodates both text (e.g., sub-task plans) and diverse visual primitives, such as bounding boxes, variable-length trajectories, and dense 3D motion predictions. Our study reveals an interesting observation: a lightweight diffusion drafter can even surpass its autoregressive target in spatial accuracy of the visual plans while decoding much faster. The structure of visual primitives helps explain this finding: once a primitive’s type, dimensionality, and length are specified, its boundaries and coordinate layout are known. Aligning draft blocks with these boundaries allows an entire geometric object to be predicted jointly, with tens to hundreds of tokens decoded in a single forward pass. These observations motivate aligning training and decoding with complete primitive boundaries and directly accepting structurally valid drafts without requiring token-level agreement with the target, while retaining verified decoding for text.

At the center of VFlash is Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD), which uses the requested output structure to organize both drafter training and inference. A tool call specifies the size of a variable-length prediction, while the primitive type determines its coordinate layout. Conditioned on features from a frozen target VLM, a lightweight diffusion drafter learns to predict complete primitives from annotated spatial data. At inference, the decoder applies layout-specific constraints (Willard and Louf, 2023; Geng et al., 2023) and accepts valid primitives in full. The target VLM supplies context for subsequent predictions, and ordinary text retains speculative decoding with target verification.

We evaluate VFlash on 2D and 3D robot trajectories, bounding boxes, and dense 3D point motion forecasting, and study its use in downstream manipulation and driving. VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to its autoregressive target across the evaluated robot trajectory tasks. In the downstream robot manipulation pipeline shown in Figure 1, it reduces inference latency by about 80% on both Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. These visual plans also provide useful conditioning for action models: on MolmoSpaces (Kim et al., 2026b), a world action model (Ye et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2026c) conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

Beyond acceleration, our work suggests a broader role for parallel decoding in multimodal systems. Lossless speculative decoding preserves the autoregressive target’s output distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a), whereas structured visual planning instead permits predictions to be judged by their spatial accuracy and usefulness for action, in the spirit of relaxed acceptance criteria (Bachmann et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c). VFlash enables a System-1 mode (Kahneman, 2011) of visual planning in VLMs, producing fast, structured spatial predictions through joint coordinate decoding. This perspective interestingly connects to recent System-1 models such as Jev, which emphasize fast, typed decisions (Almeida, 2026; Yu and Yao, 2026). VFlash brings this perspective to complete geometric predictions, exploiting structure within each primitive. The resulting gains in both speed and spatial accuracy suggest that autoregressive decoding need not define the quality ceiling for visual outputs.

title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
authors: Michal P. Podolinsky,Yunhao Yang,Daniel Little,Hong Lu,Rohan Siva,Olin Goudey,Neel P. Bhatt,Matthias Scheutz,Ufuk Topcu
comment: Code, videos, and dataset available atthis https URL
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30%30\% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86%86\% of runs, versus at most 21%21\% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44%44\% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,1803{,}180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at vla-tug.github.io.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) Physical Intelligence et al. (2025); Physical Intelligence et al. (2026); NVIDIA et al. (2025) are strong candidates for general-purpose embodied intelligence. By pairing a VLM backbone pre-trained on internet-scale data with an action expert fine-tuned on demonstration trajectories, they excel at complex dexterous tasks such as tightening screws or assembling cardboard boxes. Yet their performance is brittle and can degrade significantly under distribution shift, such as changes in lighting, novel textures, or rare object combinations Wang et al. (2026); Fei et al. (2025). A VLA can therefore fail unexpectedly, especially as task and environment novelty increases, and such failures can be costly, damaging materials and robots, or outright dangerous to humans. This brittleness has slowed the adoption of VLAs in factories, homes, and public spaces.

Among multiple solutions, one solution that the robotics community is exploring is VLA steering. The idea of steering comes from research on LLMs, where activations are selectively modified to nudge a model towards a desired output Turner et al. (2024). Steering VLAs is particularly interesting because it can unlock behaviors that cannot be reached through prompting alone Buurmeijer et al. (2026); Swann et al. (2026). Various steering methods have recently been proposed (Li et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Tan et al., 2026; Swann et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026; Jeong et al., 2026; Li, 2025), but they rarely use a calibrated probe to decide when to steer. Some steer continuously Li et al. (2026b); Liu et al. (2026a); Cui et al. (2026), some rely on human-specified offline triggers Swann et al. (2026); Li (2025), and others are gated by a one-sided calibrated trigger Tan et al. (2026); Jeong et al. (2026). Overall, they lack an efficient and principled trigger that would make them deployable in real-world systems.

Research on failure detection for VLAs is becoming increasingly mainstream Gu et al. (2025); Agia et al. (2024); Ma et al. (2026); Huang et al. (2026). In a nutshell, these methods compute a failure score from signals available in the VLA, often its latent variables Gu et al. (2025) or predicted actions Agia et al. (2024); Huang et al. (2026); Ma et al. (2026), that encode how likely the policy is to fail at the current task. A detection threshold is then calibrated to give probabilistic guarantees on the detector’s performance Gu et al. (2025). However, these guarantees often cover only the false-positive rate (FPR), i.e. the rate of successes misclassified as failures, and not a target true-positive rate (TPR), i.e. the rate of correctly classified failures, which is arguably even more important in safety-critical settings where a single failure could harm a person or damage costly equipment. These methods are also seldom evaluated systematically against ground-truth failure times, which we argue is crucial to assess whether they can prevent failures before they happen and thus enable VLA steering. Finally, they cannot predict failure modes (grasping, pushing, opening), so steering cannot be targeted towards the root cause and would require human interventions.

We argue that steering would be best supported by a probe that is (T.) timely, detecting failures before they occur; (I.) informative, outputting semantic information beyond a numerical score; (C.) calibrated, achieving the desired error rates; and (E.) efficient to train, calibrate, and deploy.

We address this with VLA-Tug11
1
Like a tugboat beside the vessel it guides, the probe is small next to the policy it monitors and acts only when needed., a well-behaved probe designed to support VLA steering in the real world. We train VLA-Tug on the latent layers of two VLAs Physical Intelligence et al. (2025); NVIDIA et al. (2025) using 228 distinct tasks in two simulation environments and 8 real-world tasks, and evaluate it against ground-truth failure times. We show that supervision should focus on the pre-failure part of the trajectory to improve early failure detection, and that calibrating the detection threshold to guarantee both TPR and FPR simultaneously yields guarantees that hold far more often, including on unseen tasks. Building on these findings, we propose a real-time architecture that incorporates VLA-Tug to autonomously support the detection and prevention of VLA failures. Our contributions are as follows:

VLA-Tug: A timely, informative, and efficient probe for early failure detection. On unseen tasks, our probe improves the area under the early-detection curve by up to 30%30\% over the strongest learned baseline. VLA-Tug also predicts the failure mode, raising the top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44%44\% over a majority baseline, at under 11 ms per step.

On unseen tasks, our probe improves the area under the early-detection curve by up to 30%30\% over the strongest learned baseline. VLA-Tug also predicts the failure mode, raising the top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44%44\% over a majority baseline, at under 11 ms per step.

Guarantees on false alarms and missed detections. title: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
authors: Mohammed Hassan,Zhenyang Chen,Zheng Wang,Zhixin Zhu,Tianlong Chen,Yingyan(Celine)Lin,Chaojian Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive: each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3×3.3\times speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Brohan et al., 2023a; Black et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024) provide a unified
interface from pixels and language to robot actions, but this generality carries
a substantial inference burden. At every decision step, the model propagates a
long visual sequence through a large language backbone. In a typical
OpenVLA-style setup, a 224×224224\times 224 image produces 256256 visual
patches (Zhai et al., 2023), and multi-camera inputs multiply this token load before
any action token is predicted. Attending over such long sequences at every
control step is expensive and increases latency, which is detrimental to
real-time control and can further induce observation–action distribution shift
through stale observations and delayed actuation (Arachchige et al., 2025).

Many visual tokens are weakly coupled to the language
instruction (Chen et al., 2024; Shang et al., 2024). These tokens can diffuse attention and distract
action prediction, especially under viewpoint or object-placement shifts.
Effective refinement must both remove irrelevant tokens and reinforce
instruction-relevant evidence among those retained.

Redundancy acts at two coupled stages: token-set construction and
attention allocation. Pruning can discard critical cues, while attention
steering retains the full token cost and noisy input. We therefore prune first
and refine attention only over the retained sequence.

Building on this view, we introduce T3R, a training-free two-stage token
refinement framework. Stage 1 performs segmentation-guided token pruning with
position preservation, so compression happens before the VLA decoder and
every transformer layer benefits from a shorter input. Stage 2 compensates for
pruning-induced information loss by injecting task relevance into the retained
sequence: saliency-guided attention biasing in intermediate layers steers
action-token queries toward instruction-salient words and retained task-relevant
regions.

We evaluate T3R on OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025), CogACT (Li et al., 2024b),
and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) across LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), SIMPLER (Li et al., 2024a),
and RoboTwin (Mu et al., 2025). Across these systems, multi-camera settings show
greater pruning headroom than the single-camera zero-shot setting. This trend
suggests that overlapping visual evidence creates opportunities for token reduction.

Contributions.

We propose T3R, a training-free two-stage framework that couples
segmentation-guided, position-preserving token pruning with saliency-guided
attention biasing, jointly optimizing token selection and attention allocation
in a single inference pass.

On LIBERO-Spatial with OpenVLA-OFT, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera
tokens while retaining 96% success, reduces VLA inference latency by 14%,
and improves OOD success by up to 7 pp. Resolution-scaling profiling shows
up to a 3.3×3.3\times LLM-forward speedup over the unpruned baseline.

We evaluate T3R across VLA backbones and camera setups. The observed
accuracy-efficiency trends are consistent with greater sensor redundancy
providing more headroom for token pruning.

title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
authors: Vongani H. Maluleke,James Ni,Kie Horiuchi,Lea Wilken,Jiahui Lei,Evonne Ng,Roei Herzig,Jitendra Malik,Trevor Darrell,Angjoo Kanazawa
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: CoRL 2026, Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another.
To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner’s motion.
Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner’s motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot.
To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale.
We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions.
Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world.
introduction:
Human interaction is the art of attunement, a continuous interplay of perception, anticipation, and response that enables seamless coordination. Whether synchronizing a high-five or collaborating on a shared task, people adjust effortlessly through gaze, posture, and timing, without words. This ability is a hallmark of social intelligence [56, 18, 21], allowing humans to simultaneously anticipate and align with others in real time. In contrast, existing works train humanoids as solitary agents, leaving them unable to perceive social cues or respond to the people around them.
As humanoids move out of labs and into homes, workplaces, and shared public spaces, they will need the same capacity to operate alongside and with people.

To address this, we formulate the problem of human-humanoid interaction, in which a humanoid must continuously generate and execute coordinated, socially responsive whole-body motion given observations of a human partner.
We present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system with a high-level and a low-level policy. The high-level policy generates reactive humanoid motion from the observed partner’s motion and anticipates the partner’s motion, even when they are occluded or human input is missing, enabling continuous interaction. The low-level policy then executes the generated motion on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.

While recent advances in human motion generation [42, 19, 8, 41] can synthesize realistic dyadic interactions offline, deploying this capability on physical humanoids introduces three challenges:
First, a data gap: human-human interaction is captured at scale, but no dataset captures natural human-humanoid interaction and naively retargeting each partner independently destroys the contact, reach, and spatial structure that defines the interaction.
Second, a representation gap: human and humanoid motion live in different spaces, which forces the generative model to learn the differences between the two embodiments instead of focusing on the interaction itself. This gap has been largely overlooked in prior work.
Third, a generation gap: a natural approach is to generate the interaction with a human motion model and retarget to humanoid through optimization, but optimization-based retargeting is designed for clean, offline data and is brittle to noisy, discontinuous partner observations. A socially responsive humanoid needs a feed-forward model to generate humanoid motion directly.

Social Humanoid addresses these challenges with three contributions that build on one another. (i) For the data gap, we introduce a two-phase Adaptive-HHI Retargeting procedure that retargets one partner to the 29-DoF Unitree G1 and morphs the other’s body pose to preserve contact, reach, and relative scale. Applied to Chi3D [15], Hi4D [62], Harmony4D [33], Inter-X [59], and Embody3D [44], it yields the HHI Benchmark, comprising 260 hours of dyadic and polyadic interactions paired with the G1. (ii) For the representation gap, our key insight is that a shared motion representation lets a single generative model reason jointly about both embodiments, which we instantiate with a shared-codebook VQ-VAE that tokenizes human and humanoid motion into a single discrete vocabulary. This vocabulary also supports real-time shadow teleoperation of the G1 without optimization-based retargeting (Sec. 5.2).. (iii) For the generation gap, our high-level policy is a Diffusion Forcing Transformer that autoregressively generates humanoid responses over this shared vocabulary; its diffusion-forcing objective is well-suited to imperfect, real-world input and supports fluid, long-horizon interaction. Paired with NVIDIA SONIC [39] as the low-level whole-body tracking controller, Social Humanoid demonstrates coordinated, interactive, and human-aligned behaviors in both simulation and real-world hardware experiments. Generation and execution run asynchronously, with a median end-to-end latency of 308 ms from camera frame to humanoid command.

title: A Multimodal Haptic Interface for Simultaneous Softness and Thermal Modulation
authors: Joshua Brown,Fernando Bello,Lynette Jones
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: Published at EuroHaptics 2026
abstract: Haptic interactions, such as touching an object in virtual reality, involve detecting a plethora of sensations through the skin. Whilst tactile displays exist to simulate and manipulate all of these cues individually, little progress has been made constructing devices that can control multiple cues simultaneously. This paper presents a tactile display technology that offers both softness and temperature change.
introduction:
Softness-changing surfaces are becoming increasingly important for creating realistic haptic interactions in VR and medical simulation. Rapid technical advances in this area have been enabled by soft robotics techniques. Softness changing haptic devices have wide-ranging applications, from wearable haptic suits for enhancing entertainment experiences [14, 2], to simulation-based training for medical procedures and examinations with realistic soft tissues [4]. Softness may be approximated via impedance control of haptic robots, emulating force-deformation properties of compliant materials [19], by directly altering the properties of a surface or device to change its compliance [25], or a combination of the two [18].

Particle jamming is an increasingly popular technology for creating tactile displays that can alter their softness. In a jamming system, granular media, which are normally highly malleable, may be stiffened by compressing their volume, causing the individual particles to brace against each other, or ‘jam’, thereby creating the appearance of a solid mass [11]. Jamming has been applied to haptic surfaces that can change their softness to influence user interaction [8], retain their shape after being moulded by a user [20], or simulate palpation in medical training [16]. It has been applied to gloves [21] and exosuits [2], to restrict movement by stiffening the joints in these wearable devices. Particle jamming has also been proposed as a mechanism for creating ‘remote touch’ - perceiving solid objects buried in granular media [7], as well as a basis for multimodal cutaneous interfaces that can leverage the adaptability of jamming technology as a medium for generating other cutaneous sensations [5]. This has become possible with the advent of fully mechanical jamming technologies that do not rely on airtight containers or pneumatic systems [4].

Whilst softness has many important applications in haptics, it is just one of several cutaneous sensations that enable humans to perceive the world via touch [13]. Thermal sensations resulting from changes in skin temperature also play an important and varied role, from warning of danger due to the skin burning or freezing, to playing a more nuanced role in multisensory cutaneous experiences, such as perceiving wetness [3], or discriminating between physical materials based on the rate with which skin temperature changes [12]. Such cues can even influence the ‘pleasantness’ of different tactile experiences [1]. Thermal sensations have also been shown to influence the other senses via crossmodal correspondences, such as the associations between colour and temperature (red-hot, blue-cold) [24]. Thermal cues can be generated in a number of ways, including directly using thermoelectric Peltier modules [22], via convection using heated and cooled air [23] or water [17], or through radiation via infrared light [15].

With these applications in mind, there is a strong motivation for creating tactile display technology capable of producing both softness and thermal sensations simultaneously. Such a device could be used to simulate thermal properties of vascular disease in medical training, or the varying stiffness and thermal emissivity of different materials in a VR simulation. This paper presents a novel multimodal surface that integrates constrictive particle jamming with a fluidic thermal skin. Key contributions are: a demonstration of how pump-free jamming can mediate otherwise incompatible technologies; a mechanical design that optimizes thermal transfer without compromising jamming compliance; and an experimental characterisation of the device’s performance.

title: SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
authors: Shanghao Shi,Jian Xiao,Ching-Hsiang Chan,Sanjoy Baruah,Sastry Kompella,Yevgeniy Vorobeychik,William Yeoh,Ning Zhang
abstract: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose Scale, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, Scale matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, Scale employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate Scale across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that Scale significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/.
introduction:
Communication is fundamental to cyber-physical agents. Individual agents often possess only partial observations or complementary capabilities, and therefore must exchange information with one another to accomplish diverse cyber-physical tasks (Patel et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022). However, transmitting raw sensor observations incurs substantial communication overhead, while natural-language communication introduces additional computational overhead from generating text at the sender and interpreting it at the receiver. These limitations make conventional communication inefficient for real-time multi-agent systems.

Latent communication has emerged as a potential “AI language”, allowing agents to directly exchange hidden states or intermediate representations to improve efficiency (Du et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025). However, existing methods are primarily designed for LLM-based agents and focus on reducing model-side computation, with limited consideration of communication bandwidth and task deadlines. Meanwhile, communication-efficient collaborative-perception methods consider bandwidth and delay (Liu et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024), but primarily focus on task-specific perception rather than multiple concurrent CPS tasks sharing a bandwidth-constrained link. Thus, latent communication for CPS agents under practical network constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines remains largely underexplored.

We propose Scale, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Scale exploits the spatiotemporal continuity of the physical world to reuse latent information already available at the receiver, reducing redundant transmission. It employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send based on semantic gain, available bandwidth, and task deadlines, thereby improving both task utility and message on-time delivery. In addition, Scale is lightweight and operates on latent tokens produced by existing modality encoders without modifying the underlying models, supporting different sensory modalities and downstream CPS tasks.

Designing Scale addresses three technical challenges. First, spatiotemporal variation makes it difficult to determine what information has actually changed.
Physical observations often evolve continuously, but object, agent, or viewpoint motion can make fixed-position latent comparisons overestimate motion for semantic change. Scale therefore performs semantic change evaluation by matching current latent tokens against the receiver’s acknowledged latent state and measuring change relative to their best correspondences.
Second, the amount of latent information to transmit must adapt to each message.
The semantic gain from transmitting additional latent tokens varies across messages, making a fixed transmission size inefficient. Scale therefore performs utility–cost profiling for each message, ranking latent tokens by semantic change and characterizing the cumulative semantic gain and communication cost at different transmission sizes to guide real-time scheduling.
Third, limited and time-varying bandwidth must be allocated across messages with heterogeneous deadlines.
Allocating more latent tokens to one message increases its semantic gain but may delay other messages beyond their deadlines. Scale therefore employs a real-time scheduler that greedily allocates latent tokens based on marginal semantic gain per communication cost, while maintaining deadline feasibility for all selected messages under earliest-deadline-first (EDF) ordering.

We implement and evaluate Scale on CooperScene Wu et al. (2026), OPV2V Xu et al. (2022c), and LIBERO Liu et al. (2023a), covering autonomous driving and robotic manipulation benchmarks. We further conduct a physical spider robot case study. Our evaluation considers constrained bandwidth, time-varying link capacity, and background traffic, with heterogeneous task deadlines. We compare Scale against full latent transmission, uniform compression, and four state-of-the-art methods Xu et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2022b); Hu et al. (2022); Mukhopadhyay et al. (2026). Our results show that Scale achieves the highest task performance in almost all settings while significantly improving on-time delivery rates (see Fig. 1 for an example).

We make the following contributions:

We identify and formulate the problem of real-time latent communication for CPS agents, where latent messages from multiple downstream tasks with heterogeneous deadlines share a bandwidth-constrained communication link, a setting not adequately addressed by existing methods.

We identify and formulate the problem of real-time latent communication for CPS agents, where latent messages from multiple downstream tasks with heterogeneous deadlines share a bandwidth-constrained communication link, a setting not adequately addressed by existing methods.

We propose Scale, a real-time latent communication method that combines spatiotemporal latent reuse, utility–cost profiling, and deadline-aware scheduling to improve both task utility and message on-time delivery under bandwidth constraints.

We implement and evaluate Scale across three CPS benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions, demonstrating its effectiveness in both benchmark evaluations and a physical robotic system.

2. We propose Scale, a real-time latent communication method that combines spatiotemporal latent reuse, utility–cost profiling, and deadline-aware scheduling to improve both task utility and message on-time delivery under bandwidth constraints.

title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
authors: Fuhao Li,Wenxuan Song,Qizhou Huang,Ziyang Zhou,Jingbo Wang,Junwu E,Pengwei Wang,Yan Wang,Shunbo Zhou,Haoang Li

abstract:
Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
Extensive evaluations demonstrate that SLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboDojo-Real, RoboTwin 2.0 under the Clean2Random setting, RoboCasa-Panda, and LIBERO-Plus, highlighting its strong generalization and downstream data efficiency. Across eight real-world deployment conditions, SLA further improves the average success rate over π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 24.0 percentage points.
introduction:
The development of robotic manipulation hinges on integrating semantic reasoning with accurate physical control in the 3D real world.
Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models (Black et al., 2025; Intelligence, 2025; Yuan et al., 2026a; Team et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026b; Bu et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026), capable of instruction following and robotic action execution, have attracted significant attention.
By combining the pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with action experts learning on diverse robot demonstrations, these models offer a promising foundation for general-purpose manipulation.
However, successful manipulation requires not only recognizing objects and understanding instructions but also executing precise actions in the 3D physical world.
Typical 2D VLA foundation models inherit knowledge from VLMs pretrained on 2D image–text pairs and learn robot control without explicitly incorporating 3D physical knowledge during pre-training.
This limits their reliability in scenes that demand fine-grained spatial reasoning.

A direct approach to improving spatial understanding is to introduce 3D modalities during post-training on top of a pretrained 2D VLA foundation model.
Several approaches (Li et al., 2026a; Sun et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026c) use depth maps or point clouds obtained from depth cameras or other 3D sensors, encode their geometric information, and feed it into the VLM backbone or action head.
However, some limitations make it difficult to develop a universal and scalable 3D strategy for this paradigm:
(1) Reliable 3D sensor data is hard to acquire, as measured depth maps and point clouds can be noisy or incomplete.
(2) Robotic sensors vary in types, positions, and calibration status, which introduces substantial heterogeneity into the data.
(3) Portions of existing large-scale robot datasets (O’Neill et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b; Lee et al., 2026; Walke et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2022) do not include depth information, which limits the potential of scaling.

To address these questions, Spatial Forcing (Li et al., 2025a) has propose a implicit 3D representation alignment strategy to enbow 2D VLA with spatial intelligence without explicit demand of depth information.
However, Spatial Forcing still concentrate on post-training, leaving spatial competence as a task-specific add-on and limiting the development of scalable 3D VLA foundation models with transferable spatial understanding.

Recently, continual pre-training has been widely adopted as a means of developing specific capabilities at scale while preserving the knowledge acquired during foundation model pre-training (Yu et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026b). Motivated by this approach, we propose to build on the strong 2D foundation model and develop spatial understanding through continual pre-training, laying the foundation for subsequent adaptation.
We therefore propose SLA,
a robotic foundation model with generalized spatial understanding capabilities developed through implicit representation alignment during both continual pre-training and post-training.
Intuitively, action generation is conditioned on visual and linguistic representations, making the spatial content of visual tokens directly relevant to action. Higher-quality visual tokens that contain richer spatial information can facilitate generating more precise manipulation actions.
Inspired by this, we align the intermediate visual embeddings of the VLA with external spatial representations extracted from a frozen 3D perception foundation model.
This spatial alignment objective complements the standard action-learning objective, encouraging the policy to internalize geometric information in the representations used for action prediction.
Crucially, this supervision requires no changes to the pretrained VLA architecture or the action-generation head.
We can therefore initialize the policy directly from the pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} foundation (Intelligence, 2025) and continue training from its learned robotic knowledges.
This architectural compatibility allows spatial supervision to shape the foundation model while retaining access to the general knowledge encoded in its pretrained weights.

Technically, to support continual pre-training across heterogeneous robot data, we combines a unified training corpus.
We curate multiple large-scale public datasets covering diverse embodiments, tasks, scenes, and visual appearances, and unify their state and action annotations through consistent end-effector representations and coordinate conventions.
This processing provides a common basis for learning how different robots act in space.
The resulting visual diversity also makes a single manually chosen alignment layer restrictive: a certain intermediate visual layer of VLA models suited to one domain data may not be equally suitable for another.
We therefore develop adaptive layer selection mechanism, using feature-dependent gates to aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision.
In addition, we adopt OmniVGGT (Peng et al., 2025) as the external 3D perception foundation to exploit partially available camera calibrations and depth annotations alongside RGB images.
We further introduce probabilistic state dropout during training to mitigate overfitting to demonstration trajectories and encourage the policy to make better use of visual cues, thereby improving generalization.
After continual pre-training, we retain spatial alignment during post-training to adapt the resulting foundation model to specific down-streaming tasks.
The teacher, alignment projector, and layer-selection gates are used only during training.
At deployment, the policy retains its original inference architecture without requiring the external perception model, alignment projector, or layer-selection gates.

Extensive evaluations across three public simulation benchmarks, one public real-world benchmark, and eight real-world deployment conditions are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our SLA.
On LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025), it achieves an overall success rate of 87.4% under diverse observation, language, and scene perturbations, outperforming the compared baselines.
On RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025a), training on clean demonstrations yields a 72.3% success rate in the Clean2Random setting and a 79.2% average across Clean2Clean and Clean2Random, demonstrating generalization beyond the training conditions.
On RoboCasa-Panda (Nasiriany et al., 2024), SLA achieves 68.4% success with only 50 downstream demonstrations per task, exceeding compared policies trained with 300–3,000 demonstrations per task.
On RoboDojo-Real (Chen et al., 2026b), a single policy adapted across three embodiments achieves 33.9% overall success, compared with 12.8% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, supporting its applicability to real robot manipulation.
Our eight deployment conditions further examine bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following.
SLA achieves the highest success rate among the compared methods in every condition, averaging 83.8% and improving over π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 24.0 percentage points.
Controlled data-scaling experiments further show that applying spatial alignment in both training stages outperforms either single-stage alternative at every tested data proportion.
Together, these results support developing spatial understanding during continual pre-training and stengthen it during downstream adaptation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce SLA, a robotic foundation model that implicitly enforces the integration of visual embeddings in VLAs with external spatial representations.

We introduce SLA, a robotic foundation model that implicitly enforces the integration of visual embeddings in VLAs with external spatial representations.

We extend SLA to continual pre-training on a carefully curated and unified corpus of public robot datasets, developing a spatially informed foundation model.

We apply SLA training principle during downstream post-training and demonstrate strong benchmark performance, together with bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following.

1. We introduce SLA, a robotic foundation model that implicitly enforces the integration of visual embeddings in VLAs with external spatial representations.

2. We extend SLA to continual pre-training on a carefully curated and unified corpus of public robot datasets, developing a spatially informed foundation model.

3. We apply SLA training principle during downstream post-training and demonstrate strong benchmark performance, together with bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following.

title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
authors: Sateesh Kumar,Arnav Balaji,Arpit Bahety,Skand Peri,Georgios Pavlakos,Roberto Martín-Martín
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

abstract:
Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint.
This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints.
Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented.
We present MoMaSplat, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions.
Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multi-view observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D.
MoMaSplat combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions.
We evaluate MoMaSplat on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MoMaSplat substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for large-scale real-world data collection.
More information at: https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/momasplat/
introduction:
Imitation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training visuomotor policies that perform complex manipulation tasks directly from image observations [1, 2].
However, these policies are notoriously sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint [3, 4, 5].
Even small deviations in camera pose can significantly degrade performance, since the policy learns a narrow visual distribution tied to the demonstrations used during training.

This sensitivity is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa).
Unlike tabletop manipulation setups, where demonstrations are often collected from a fixed robot camera pose, mobile manipulators rarely execute tasks from the exact same location at deployment time.
Navigation uncertainty, localization drift, obstacle avoidance, and imperfect planning routinely place the robot at different base poses relative to the workspace.
As a result, the robot observes the manipulation scene from viewpoints that may differ substantially from those seen during demonstration collection.
Robust deployment therefore requires visuomotor policies that generalize across a distribution of robot base poses rather than a single viewpoint.

A straightforward solution would be to collect demonstrations from many different robot locations.
However, large-scale real-world teleoperation is expensive and difficult to scale [6, 2, 7].
Recent work has therefore explored synthesizing additional demonstrations through novel-view synthesis (NVS), generating virtual observations from unseen viewpoints using real-world captures [8, 9, 10].
While promising, existing approaches assume a static scene and therefore fail during the most important part of manipulation: object interaction.
Since the manipulated object moves throughout the demonstration, prior NVS methods cannot consistently re-render the object from novel viewpoints during the post-contact interaction phase, restricting augmentation primarily to pre-contact motions or introducing geometrically inconsistent generations.

In this work, we present MoMaSplat, a demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions (Fig. 1).
Our key insight is that standard mobile-manipulation data collection naturally provides the multi-view observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D.
During navigation, the robot observes the scene from diverse viewpoints that enable scene reconstruction, while the manipulation demonstrations themselves provide object-centric observations that enable reconstructing the manipulated object and its motion.

Building on this observation, MoMaSplat separately reconstructs the static scene and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting [11] and feed-forward 3D foundation models [12].
Given a novel robot base pose, MoMaSplat re-renders the scene, manipulated object, and robot from the new viewpoint and retargets the original actions through kinematics-based transformations to generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations.

We evaluate MoMaSplat on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation.
Our experiments show that MoMaSplat substantially improves robustness to unseen deployment-time base poses, outperforming prior augmentation approaches across 1212 unseen base poses (33 rollouts per pose) per task as the robot moves farther away from the source demonstration locations.

Our contributions are threefold:

A novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete trajectories, including dynamic object interactions.

A geometry-consistent generation pipeline that separately reconstructs scenes and manipulated objects and retargets actions to unseen base poses.

Substantial improvements in robustness to deployment-time viewpoint variation across multiple real-world mobile manipulation tasks.

1. A novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete trajectories, including dynamic object interactions.

2. A geometry-consistent generation pipeline that separately reconstructs scenes and manipulated objects and retargets actions to unseen base poses.

3. Substantial improvements in robustness to deployment-time viewpoint variation across multiple real-world mobile manipulation tasks.

title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors - A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
authors: Sacha Jungerman,Kaustubh Sadekar,Avery Gump,Sriram Narayanan,Shantanu Gupta,Bhuyashi Deka,Srinivasa Narasimhan,Atul Ingle,Mohit Gupta
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.
introduction:
A robotics simulator presented with a scene will typically render a sharp, noise-free image. Yet, the same scene captured by a real conventional camera might show heavy motion blur from a long exposure; a real single-photon LiDAR aimed at a retroreflective object might report a phantom obstacle in front of it; a long-wave infrared (LWIR) thermal camera will show a lingering thermal footprint of a warm handprint on a desk or a radiator still glowing minutes after shutoff. These are not exotic edge cases — they are the operating conditions that decide whether a deployed robot succeeds or fails. However, they are largely absent from today’s general-purpose robotics simulators.

Modern simulation platforms have transformed how robots are trained, evaluated, and deployed: physics engines such as MuJoCo [93], Isaac Gym [54], and Genesis [3] model rigid-body dynamics with impressive fidelity, while rendering engines such as Unreal [22] and Blender [14] bring photorealistic digital twins of factories and cities within reach. However, these platforms share a critical blind spot: they do not faithfully simulate how agents actually see the world. Real-world agents act on what their sensors deliver, not on ground truth, and typically combine multiple complementary sensors (Table 1). Yet most simulation engines do not support the necessary breadth of sensors, or they model them only superficially: ideal cameras in a well-lit environment, LiDARs as noiseless range-finders, IMUs as perfect integrators, thermal cameras as static temperature textures. Such simplifications ignore the noise, motion blur, and modality-specific artifacts that dominate real measurements — from glare and pileup in single-photon LiDAR [31] to the geometry-, material-, and history-dependent emission that defines real thermal imagery.

Existing efforts address this gap only partially. Sensor-specific simulators, such as ESIM [71] and v2e [35] for event cameras, are highly specialized and cannot support cross-modality comparisons. Physically-based infrared generators such as MuSES [96] and DIRSIG [81] couple heat-transfer solvers to radiometric rendering, but target terrain-scale signature prediction driven by weather and atmospheric models, rather than the object-scale thermal phenomena central to embodied perception. General-purpose platforms such as CARLA [20], AirSim [82], Isaac Gym [54], and Habitat [77] expand sensor coverage but inherit the same idealizations. As a result, robot system architects cannot compare candidate sensor suites on common ground without expensive hardware prototyping.

Our guiding hypothesis is that a high-fidelity simulator must model not just world physics and geometry, but also perception itself — with realistic sensors that bridge photons to measurement. To this end, we present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded sensor simulation platform for robotics that aims to elevate sensor realism to a first-class concern, on par with scene and physics modeling (Figure 1). VisionSIM is built around the following key design goals:

Breadth across conventional and emerging sensors. VisionSIM simulates conventional and high-speed cameras, stereo rigs, passive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras, direct and indirect time-of-flight (dToF/iToF) LiDARs, event cameras, long-wave infrared (LWIR) thermal cameras, and inertial measurement units (Table 1). Candidate sensor suites can be evaluated on identical scenes and trajectories, enabling principled comparisons across a wide range of sensors.

High physical fidelity, including failure modes. VisionSIM emulates raw measurements for each modality (e.g., transient histograms, correlation taps, and asynchronous brightness changes). This naturally reproduces key failure modes: SPAD pileup and glare; iToF wrapping and motion artifacts; event refractory limits; and path-tracing-coupled dynamic thermal heat transport, capturing failure modes that, to our knowledge, lie beyond the reach of existing general-purpose simulators.

Fine-grained control over sensing parameters. VisionSIM exposes the physical parameters that govern each modality’s measurement process (Table 2): iToF correlation functions; event contrast thresholds; dead time and quantum efficiency for SPADs; microbolometer thermal time constants, and per-surface emissivity for thermal cameras; exposure, gain, and ISP parameters for conventional cameras. This parameterization lets a user not only sweep across sensor designs, but also match the simulator to a specific physical device — the basis for calibrated perceptual digital twins.

We demonstrate VisionSIM by constructing a digital twin of a real single-photon LiDAR, recovering some of its key parameters directly from captured data. This reduces the mean sim-to-real depth error and reproduces two failure modes not previously simulated at this fidelity: pileup-induced range walk, and point-cloud ghosting from retroreflective glare. We further show how VisionSIM can be used to augment existing datasets and to evaluate competing sensor suites (Sec. 5). These case studies focus on open-loop sensor fidelity; closed-loop validation is discussed in Section 8. Finally, we release an indoor dataset featuring synchronized raw outputs of all supported sensors and ground truth annotations (Table 3). To our knowledge, it is among the most comprehensive multi-modal datasets of its kind, supporting both training and benchmarking of sensor-fusion algorithms.

title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
authors: Chang Shi,Ann Majewicz Fey
abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor–critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03% vs. 0.63%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.
introduction:
Online 3D bin packing requires selecting and placing boxes as they arrive, without knowing the complete arrival sequence. In warehouse settings, a small processing buffer allows for limited reordering prior to placement (Fig. 1). The objective is to pack densely while keeping the stack stable, which depends on the box dimensions, physics, and the order, orientation, and location of placement.

Physical stability depends on more than the visible top surface. Supporting material properties and the arrangement of multiple supporting boxes can affect a placement’s outcome. One box collapse can leave the bin disorganized and hurt the long-term packing compactness. Therefore, there have been works trying to integrate physics-aware stability information into packing decision making.

Reinforcement learning (RL) packers usually handle stability with an action mask. Most masks are computed using geometric or physics-based rules on the height map or the stacking structure [1, 2]. Instead, [3] and [4] learn the stability mask through simulation outcomes together with a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy [5], but apply the masks as hard filters on the placement of a box the policy has already chosen. Stability therefore cannot influence which box to pack, leading to a policy that is not jointly optimal. Moreover, a placement is either allowed or forbidden, with no trade-off between its risk and the volume it adds. This motivates designing a more advanced joint policy in which stability awareness can directly affect selection among boxes, orientations, and placements in the long run.

We propose SHORE, which separates the prediction of the outcome of the current placement from the value of the subsequent packing, but intelligently fuses the stability information back to guide the long-term joint policy learning. A 3D U-Net reads bin occupancy and the oriented box properties to estimate whether the whole stack satisfies the stability test after the placement. A separate action-conditioned critic learns the return if the current placement holds, including its immediate reward and subsequent packing, from on-policy rollouts. The stability estimate modulates this value and provides a soft prior to the joint actions of the actor (Fig. 2). In this on-policy actor–critic method, the critic scores every valid (box, orientation, placement) triple, and the actor follows the exact expected gradient over all of them, so the stability estimate shapes which box is packed and how it is turned, not only where it goes. At inference, SHORE chooses each placement with one pass of the actor and of the stability network.

In short, our contributions are:

A physics-aware RL strategy that uses learned placement-stability probabilities as continuous weights on action values for policy improvement over joint box–orientation–placement actions, so that the packing agent can trade the risk of an unstable placement against the volume it adds.

A highly parallel, Isaac Gym-based bin packing environment that enables fast, large-scale on-policy RL training.

An empirical study of the efficiency of this method on a realistic box distribution, together with an initial real-robot deployment test.

3. An empirical study of the efficiency of this method on a realistic box distribution, together with an initial real-robot deployment test.
