title: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
authors: Aditya Iyer,Andy Ye,Akshay Narayan,Nora Ayanian
abstract:
Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to
estimate the motion of a robot team.
These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the
team’s estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift.
In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio
attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses.
Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an
interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a
Gaussian information matrix and vector pair.
RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map.
The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty.
We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations
across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose
estimates and covariances.
Across 10001000 simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation.
Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from 0.5420.542 m to 0.1400.140 m in a 50×5050\times 50 m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.
introduction:
To carry out tasks such as exploration, mapping, and environmental monitoring, robot teams rely on coordinated motion and shared observations. When global positioning is unavailable,
they can estimate motion through odometry and inter-robot measurements.
These observations constrain relative geometry, but the estimated team
can move away from its true location as a group. For example, translating every robot estimate by one meter leaves all pairwise distances unchanged.
This shared error matters when robots must reach mapped destinations or
report observations in world coordinates.

It is also important to precisely estimate uncertainty because the team can know its relative geometry while remaining uncertain about its position in the world. This ambiguity is called gauge freedom.
Gauge freedom describes indistinguishable coordinate frames, which in the presence of motion or noise leads to gauge drift. Gauge drift describes
the temporal growth of error or uncertainty in these shared-motion directions.
Teams construct a reference frame from a prior over their initial poses, but subsequent noisy observations determine how well the team remains localized.
For trajectories without a fixed point of reference, common translations and rotations maintain relative observations, but they do not provide useful information about global state.

A radio attenuation map aligned to the world frame can provide
a reference because received power depends on both link length
and the attenuation field.
For example, in Fig. 1, a common translation preserves separation and distance loss but changes link attenuation. Using a global attenuation map which captures knowledge of obstacles in the environment can help distinguish the team’s positions by using differences in the received power they observe.

We propose the Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI) interface which leverages this behavior.
The RPI is an interface between two components:
First, a radio module predicts received power from the current poses and attenuation map,
then determines the power mismatch and pose sensitivity as an information matrix and vector.
Second, a pose estimator uses this message to compute a correction and its uncertainty.

This paper describes three contributions:

We show that fixed weights on relative measurements add zero direct
information about common motion. We characterize which shared motions
the attenuation map and observed links can detect.

We propose the Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI) interface, which converts power residuals and pose sensitivity into an information matrix and vector for pose estimation.

We derive centroid covariance growth and a lower bound on mean-squared common-position error under stated motion and measurement assumptions. We evaluate agreement with joint estimation,
drift correction, and sensitivity to map error.

title: GPWM: Modeling the World as 3D Particle Motion
authors: Robert Ren,Matthew Bronars,He Zhu,Yikai Tang,Jianing Zhang,Sergey Zakharov,Pavel Tokmakov,Katerina Fragkiadaki
comment: . Robert Ren and Matthew Bronars contributed equally (ordered by coin flip). Project page:this https URL
abstract:
We introduce GPWM, a Generative Particle
World Model that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by
generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene
appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single
representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and
granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction.
GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines
flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical
trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate
GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse
geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments.
GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average.
Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains.
GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties,
object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables
contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint
actuator–object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained
actions, planning searches the model’s latent noise for interactions
that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model,
noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on
pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to
discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve
goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or
goal-specific policies.
introduction:
A general-purpose physical world model should predict how a 3D scene
evolves and how to act to bring it toward a desired state. This requires
modeling diverse objects and materials, maintaining coherent dynamics
over long horizons, and reasoning through physical contact.
Recent generative video world models capture rich and multimodal scene
evolution (NVIDIA, 2026; Wan et al., 2025; Bruce et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026),
but generate visual appearance rather than explicitly representing the
motion and interactions of physical objects in 3D.
Particle- and point-based models instead represent physical state
directly in 3D (Li et al., 2019; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Pfaff et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2025a; Duisterhof et al., 2026). However, existing learned 3D
dynamics models are typically limited by deterministic prediction,
short generation horizons, or specialization to particular materials
and interactions (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026).
We ask: can a generative model of 3D particle motion capture
diverse physical dynamics, predict over long horizons, and support
planning through contact?

We introduce GPWM, a generative world model that represents 3D
scenes as particles and rigid bodies and predicts their motion over
time (Figure 1). Deformable objects are modeled through
particle displacements and rigid bodies through body-level
transformations, providing a common representation for rigid,
deformable, cloth, and granular dynamics.
GPWM conditions on observed 3D scene history and, when available,
physical properties and future actuator motion. Actuators share the
same geometric representation as other scene components, allowing
their trajectories to either condition physical prediction or be
generated jointly with object motion for planning.

Learning generative particle dynamics at scale presents two challenges:
scenes may contain thousands of particles across interacting objects,
and prediction errors accumulate over long rollouts.
GPWM addresses the first with object-aware multi-resolution
tokenization and spatio-temporal attention in relative 3D coordinates.
To address the second, we combine flow matching with
diffusion forcing, independently varying noise levels across
future frames. This enables streaming generation, where
near-future states are progressively resolved and committed while
farther-future states remain uncertain and revisable, allowing
generation far beyond the training horizon.

We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a corpus of 25.5 million
simulated frames spanning rigid, elastic, elastoplastic, granular,
and cloth dynamics, with diverse geometries, physical properties,
interactions, and robot embodiments.
Unlike prior learned dynamics models trained for individual physical
domains (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a), we also train a single
Unified GPWM across heterogeneous physical regimes.
Across six domains, the best GPWM variant reduces prediction
error by 31% on average relative to the strongest applicable prior
baseline. Remarkably, the Unified model outperforms domain-specific
specialists on Dragging and Pick and Place, demonstrating that heterogeneous
physical dynamics can be learned within one set of weights.
GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical
properties, object counts, and long rollout horizons.

Beyond prediction, GPWM learns a generative prior over
physical interactions that enables contact-rich planning.
Conventional action-space planning searches actuator commands and
predicts their consequences, but can struggle to discover complex
contact sequences or exploit world-model errors through
out-of-distribution actions. By jointly generating actuator and
object trajectories, GPWM instead allows planning in its latent
noise space, biasing search toward learned interaction patterns.
We optimize this noise using either gradient-based latent noise
optimization (Eyring et al., 2024; Ben-Hamu et al., 2024; Karunratanakul et al., 2024) or gradient-free sampling, guided by
sparse rewards on desired object configurations.
Using the same world model, noise-space planning substantially
outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking.
The resulting actuator trajectories execute successfully in
simulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific
policies.

Our contributions are as follows.
(1) We introduce GPWM, a generative world model
that predicts the motion of particles and rigid bodies across
heterogeneous physical regimes, with streaming generation far
beyond its training horizon.
(2) We introduce ParticleWorlds, a 25.5M-frame corpus
spanning diverse physical dynamics, interactions, and robot embodiments.
(3) GPWM achieves state-of-the-art physical prediction
across diverse domains, generalizes to unseen geometries, physical
properties, object counts, and rollout horizons, and demonstrates
that a single Unified model can outperform domain-specific specialists.
(4) We demonstrate contact-rich planning through
generative interaction priors, showing that searching the learned
distribution of actuator–object trajectories is substantially more
effective than direct action-space optimization.

title: Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation
authors: Gabriel Parra,Kimia Khoshnami,Daniel S. Brown,Laura A. Hallock
comment: Accepted for presentation and publication in the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL). PMLR, 2026
abstract:
Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. Prescribing motions that elicit desired activity is challenging because muscle activity is hysteretic and stochastic, noninvasive measurement methods (e.g., surface electromyography, or sEMG) are noisy and sensor-location-dependent, and interventional datasets are costly to collect, inhibiting model development. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals’ muscle activations (as measured via sEMG) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder–decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <<8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. User-specific fine-tuning further reduces error using only minutes of additional data collection and training. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15%15\% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. To enable further development by scientific and user communities,
data and code have been open-sourced
as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK (simtk.org/projects/openrobotrehab).
introduction:
Robot-mediated therapy is a promising
treatment for
neuromotor injury (e.g., stroke), but existing systems (which largely rely on impedance-style error correction to desired kinematic trajectories) have not yet demonstrated meaningful improvement in rehabilitation outcomes over standard of care [14]. Neuroscientists posit that improving such outcomes requires systems to reinforce healthy neuromotor pathways — i.e., induce healthy patterns of underlying muscle activation, not just guide the user through desired kinematic motions [10, 13].

An ideal robotic rehabilitation system (of the type illustrated in Figure 1) would allow a new patient to arrive at a clinic, interact with the robot briefly to calibrate the system, then perform a set of therapy tasks that induce healthy activations for that individual. (Note that what constitutes “healthy” motion is an active area of investigation [19, 2]; in this work, we consider this to be a therapist- or expert-specified time series of muscle activations.) However, there do not yet exist models relating prescribed therapy activities (i.e., trajectories) to neuromotor activations of a given individual: even the healthy human neuromotor system exhibits complex (hysteretic and probabilistic) behavior, noninvasive measurement methods (e.g., surface electromyography, or sEMG) are noisy and dependent on sensor location, and large-scale data of patient populations are prohibitively expensive to collect, inhibiting both physics-based and data-driven model development.

In this work, we leverage the robust modeling capabilities of transformers [21] and flow matching [12] to construct a trajectory prescription model with the following properties:
(1) given a target sEMG-measured time series of muscle activations, predict the required target trajectory to induce these activations;
(2) require minimal per-user calibration accomplishable within a single therapy session (i.e., taking only a few minutes);
(3) once calibrated, predict trajectories in a sufficiently short time (i.e., a few seconds maximum) to enable a therapeutically meaningful number of repetitions and distinct motions within a session; and
(4) provide well-calibrated uncertainty modeling to flag out-of-distribution target muscle activations, supporting decisions about when prescribed trajectories should (and should not) be trusted.
Specifically, we present the following contributions:

Construction and training of a flow-matching-augmented, transformer-based trajectory prescription model mapping desired sEMG-measured muscle activations of the arm to the associated end-effector (hand) force target trajectory, quickly fine-tunable to new users.

Demonstration in an exemplar cohort of 16 healthy users performing 15 trajectory tracking tasks that our model achieves an average of <<8% trajectory prediction error on held-out users and tasks (with the bulk of that error attributable to the conservative, training-distribution-seeking behavior of the flow matching algorithm), and that user-specific calibration can substantially reduce that error within a few minutes’ data collection and training with quantifiable time–performance tradeoffs.

Deployment of the model during live rehabilitation tasks for 5 healthy users, demonstrating an average task-accumulated error between model-prescribed and sEMG-measured user neuromotor activations of 15%15\%.

The open-source release of all data and modeling code as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK (simtk.org/projects/openrobotrehab), enabling both additional insights on neuromotor behavior and further model augmentation and population-specific refinement by the wider rehabilitation and machine learning communities.

We present this work as a first-of-its-kind, proof-of-concept system: our preliminary cohort establishes the feasibility of activation-targeted trajectory prescription, laying the foundation for expansions toward numerous clinical applications (e.g., post-injury muscle-specific strength training, post-stroke muscle coordination training).

3. Deployment of the model during live rehabilitation tasks for 5 healthy users, demonstrating an average task-accumulated error between model-prescribed and sEMG-measured user neuromotor activations of 15%15\%.

4. title: Aligning Policy Encoders with a Shape Teacher
authors: Madelon Bernardy,Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani,David M Knigge,Riccardo Valperga,Artem Moskalev
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: 3D-aware representations can improve robotic manipulation by providing geometric information that is robust to changes in viewpoint, object position, and occlusion. However, using 3D inputs at deployment requires additional sensing and processing, making image-based policies more practical. We ask whether an image-based policy can acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment. We propose shape-teacher alignment, a training-time mechanism that uses a pretrained 3D shape representation as an alignment target for an image-based policy encoder. Specifically, we use Point-MAE features from individual objects as targets for corresponding image patches, transferring geometric structure to the policy without changing its deployment inputs or architecture. Geometric information is important for robotic manipulation, with 3D-aware policies demonstrating improved data efficiency and robustness to variations such as viewpoint changes, object displacement, and occlusion (Zhen et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Qu et al., 2025; Ze et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023). However, incorporating 3D observations into a robotic policy requires additional sensing and processing, including depth cameras, calibration, and depth estimation. These costs make purely image-based policies attractive in practice, but such policies can lack the geometric information needed for robust manipulation (Sun et al., 2025; Garcia et al., 2025). We therefore ask: can a 2D robotic policy acquire shape-aware representations during training without requiring 3D inputs at deployment?

Recent work on diffusion models has shown that pretrained representations can guide a target model through Representation Alignment (REPA). REPA (Yu et al., 2025) aligns intermediate representations with features from a frozen pretrained encoder, improving convergence and generation quality, and has since been applied to robotic policies using pretrained vision encoders as alignment targets (Li et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2026). A shape teacher can encourage the policy encoder to represent corresponding geometric structure across objects, while the policy itself remains image-based at deployment.

title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness
authors: Suhas S P,Samridhi Salwan,Arshan Ali Khan,Ujwal Pai Jakarbet,Savithramma R M,Ashwini B P
abstract: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM). For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index. At η=0.496\eta=0.496 remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30). After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal η50≈0.4956\eta_{50}\approx 0.4956 with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately [0.4955,0.4956][0.4955,0.4956]. One-factor-at-a-time ±10%\pm 10\% plant perturbations shift η50\eta_{50} by up to 0.05495 for thrust coefficient and 0.04974 for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass −10%-10\% and thrust-coefficient +10%+10\%. At fixed η=0.496\eta=0.496, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch.
introduction:
Quadrotors have little actuator redundancy: degradation of one motor changes the set of control effects available to the vehicle and can compromise landing safety. Rotor faults have therefore motivated fault-tolerant control (FTC), reduced-attitude recovery, control reconfiguration, and constrained control allocation [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Control allocation is attractive because it separates nominal motion control from the redistribution of actuator commands under saturation or failure [6, 7, 8].

This work asks a narrower question than general fault recovery: under the same partial single-motor LoE severity, does the best emergency allocator depend on which motor fails? We compare bounded WLS/PINV, finite-candidate QP-lite residual allocation, and an offline CEM-tuned QP-lite variant in CrazySim [9]. In the implemented supervisor, “fault geometry” is represented only by the known failed-motor index; no online geometry estimator or fault detector is evaluated.

A second question is whether a controller-selection conclusion remains meaningful when the simulated plant is perturbed. We therefore separate three stages: development-set allocator comparison, frozen-policy validation on new seeds, and an M2-focused plant-sensitivity study. The contributions are: (1) matched evidence that allocator ranking depends on failed-motor location, with a close M3 comparison explicitly retained; (2) frozen motor-conditioned routing evaluated on fresh seeds and in an integrated randomized-order supervisor; and (3) nominal-boundary, OFAT, failure-criterion, and paired-routing analyses that quantify how M2/PINV behavior changes under the tested plant perturbations.

title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
authors: Satvik Sharma,Hengyuan Hu,Mihika Kamat,Dorsa Sadigh,Jeannette Bohg
abstract:
Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra’s score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%.
Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.
introduction:
Recently, foundation models (FM) have begun controlling robots through several approaches: training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Zitkovich and others, 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025), integrating models into hierarchical control systems (Ichter et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Belkhale et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026b), and generating executable perception and control code, as in Code-as-Policies (CaP) (Liang et al., 2023), more recently inside coding-agent harnesses that write programs (Fu et al., 2026) or computation graphs (Chen et al., 2026a).
Frontier multimodal FMs now allow a fourth approach: the agent observes the world directly through pixels and controls robots itself with no learned policy or program in between. We refer to this setting as agentic robot control (ARC).

Evaluations of ARC disagree about how well it works. Commanding end-effector motions directly, the models in Berman et al. (2026) completed at most 5.5% of LIBERO tasks, or 32% of a ten-task subset with a cursor tool. Through a 3D visual interface, VIA (Hu et al., 2026a) reached 96.7% on three LIBERO-Goal tasks. On the 42 tasks of RoboDojo, GPT-6 Astra reached 22.5% (Zhang et al., 2026). Each study used its own tasks, models, and interface, so these results cannot be compared with one another. RoboARCade provides a common benchmark built for ARC that is not saturated: the VIA interface that nearly saturates LIBERO-Goal reaches 43.6% subtask success here.

RoboARCade brings together custom and preexisting tasks and assets in a unified codebase, spanning single-arm and bimanual manipulation, assembly, physical puzzles, and high-precision biolab-inspired procedures. Fig. 1 shows a subset of the task suite. For tasks adapted from prior work, we increase difficulty by broadening the range of initial conditions and improve visual fidelity through Blender rendering. All tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, and each is a self-contained data pack, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently.

Using this suite, we evaluate two families of frontier agents, Codex and Claude Code, and compare their performance and efficiency across two control interfaces. The first, multi-view RGBD, provides color and depth images from multiple cameras and sends end-effector commands directly to the controller. The second, from Visual Interface Agent (VIA) (Hu et al., 2026a), provides an interactive 3D virtual workspace in which agents can adjust a virtual target gripper using visual feedback before commanding the robot to move. The results reveal substantial differences across agents and interfaces: with VIA, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves a success rate of 14.0%, compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1 and 49.8% for GPT-6 Astra. For Fable, VIA improves success over multi-view RGBD by 6.8 percentage points but increases the average cost per trial by 67%. Even the strongest combination, Astra with VIA, succeeds on fewer than half of trials, leaving substantial room for improvement in both agents and control interfaces.
Scene understanding is rarely the obstacle: only 2 to 6% of attempted subtasks end there. Failures come instead from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely. Retries help with both: Astra’s subtask success rises from 34% on the first try to 50% after five or more. Agents also misjudge their own progress, incorrectly claiming success on 24% (Astra) to 39% (Claude Opus 5) of attempted subtasks.

We further evaluate in-context learning from successful rollouts and autonomous text-only prompt optimization on a subset of five tasks. In prompt optimization, agents revise their instructions using rollout feedback. GPT-6 Astra’s mean rubric score increases from 53.5% to 73.0% with in-context learning and 72.0% after two rounds of prompt optimization. Despite these gains, precision errors and incorrect claims of success persist.

title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
authors: Mateo Clémente,George Z. Xue,Amin Abyaneh,Liheng Ma,Rui Heng Yang,Tongtong Cao,Zhanguang Zhang,Yingxue Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: . Code:this https URL
abstract: World-action models commonly adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While the knowledge accumulated through large-scale pretraining is certainly useful, it remains unclear how much generation-oriented architectural choices affect control performance, and whether the trade-off required to access this pretraining is worth it. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, so that its architecture and capacity can be chosen for control. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, including contact-heavy pushing and long-horizon multistep manipulation, its average success is comparable to π0.5\pi_{0.5}, outperforming non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We also correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. These results establish a compact, efficient foundation for JEPA-based world-action modeling: without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies built on video and language generation models, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed specifically for control rather than inherited from generation.
introduction:
World-action models increasingly adapt pretrained video-generation transformers to robot control, inheriting useful visual and temporal priors along with the representation space, tokenization, and architecture of a model built for video synthesis (Yuan et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Vision-language-action policies take a similar route using language-generation transformers aligned with visual inputs (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). The success of these two types of architectures raises two practical questions: must robot policies necessarily inherit the architecture of a generative backbone to be competitive, and can a compact world-action transformer trained from scratch actually reach the performance of these policies?

Most world-action models (WAMs) are VAE-based because they build on pretrained video generators, yet better-suited latent spaces are available. Video VAEs retain accurate information but spend much of their capacity on pixel-level fidelity that control does not require. JEPA representations, in contrast, are developed and evaluated for downstream tasks such as video understanding, depth estimation, and segmentation, which are closer to the needs of embodied agents (Assran et al., 2025; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026). Previous work aligns VLMs or video-generation models to the JEPA space (Lin et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or learns a JEPA-style latent space jointly with the policy (Vujinovic & Kovacevic, 2025); to our knowledge, no prior work trains a compact world-action policy from scratch in a pretrained JEPA feature space.

We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a world-action model that learns future-feature prediction and action generation directly in the dense spatial and temporal feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 video encoder (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026). Its World DiT and Action DiT are initialized from scratch, allowing their architecture and capacity to be chosen independently of the visual encoder. Following Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026), actions attend to observed context but not to future tokens, so predictive supervision can shape the policy during training without the cost of generating the future at inference time.

Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves the strongest clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 results and the strongest LIBERO-Plus results with corrected instructions (Section 5.2), with about four times fewer deployed parameters than the next-best policies, while running up to 5×\times faster than Fast-WAM, whose design we follow (Figure 1, Tables 1 and 2). With the released instructions, it is second only to NowWAM, which is insensitive to the corrupted text (Table 14). It also outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 (Table 3). On real-robot tasks ranging from cube placement to contact-rich pushing and long-horizon manipulation, La-JEPA trained from scratch on the target demonstrations achieves the highest average success among the compared policies, comparable to the embodied-pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Table 5). Together, these results demonstrate leading benchmark performance, efficient inference, and competitive physical manipulation without requiring a generative backbone.

To understand which design choices enable this performance, we study the impact of the representation space, different targets for predictive supervision, and robustness mechanisms. We adopt a compact first approach, making the architecture viable even for a policy with 0.1B trainable parameters, before increasing policy capacity. Comparisons of JEPA features and VAE latents span both benchmarks and multiple model configurations, showing that JEPA features generally outperform VAE latents, with the clearest gains for out of distribution evaluations (Section 4.1, Appendix A.1). Action-only controls separately confirm the benefit of WAM-style future prediction, and studies of temporal encoding, dropout, augmentation, and encoder adaptation complete the recipe. These analyses support the central contribution: a compact, effective world-action policy, together with evidence to guide its design. As a secondary contribution, we show that the released LIBERO-Plus evaluator appends perturbation parameters to most instructions, so that most variants apply two perturbations at once. This corruption affects policies to very different degrees, from no change to 19 points, and obscures the robustness study that the benchmark is designed for; we therefore re-evaluate the openly available baselines with corrected instructions under a single “clean” protocol that isolates each perturbation as intended (Section 5.2).

title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zuo Gou,Chenhao Lu
comment: . Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Everything Beneath the Policy. Code, specification, and every experiment's protocol, logs and findings:this https URL
abstract:
Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the
trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many
faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire
protocol and ask what notices a fault in it.
introduction:
An RL run has a boundary between the code that steps the environment and
the trainer, which collects experience and updates the policy: the
agent–environment interface [1], drawn in software. In many
stacks nobody designs it; it falls where the trainer puts it. A Gymnasium environment [2] is an
object in the trainer’s process. RLlib [3],
SRL [4] and RLinf [5] run environments in
workers that install the framework and join its cluster. Robot learning
moves the boundary further: to simulators in other languages, machines
with no GPU stack, and robots reaching a policy over the
network [6, 7].

Many faults at this boundary are silent: they raise no error or
warning [8]. Under its SAME_STEP
autoreset mode, Gymnasium 1.3’s vector episode statistics drop the first
reward of every episode after an environment’s first, and count its length
one short, until 1.4 (Sec. IV). Training goes on. For environments on
another machine, our own evidence that the boundary was right was
that the policy still learned.

We test that evidence. PlugRL makes the boundary an explicit wire protocol
(Sec. II). The environment side sends observations, applies
the actions it gets back, and feeds back rewards and episode ends. A
written specification and conformance checkers say what each side must do,
and lockstep bridges let Stable-Baselines3 (SB3) [9],
CleanRL [10] and RLinf train through it. On one machine
a run through it is deterministic, so we can compare a run with an injected
fault against the same seed without it. We call a difference between what
the environment took and gave and what the trainer sent and received a
boundary fault. Our method is mutation testing as
RLMutation [11] applies it to deep RL, and the checks

title: Educational robotics beyond ROS: a custom library for direct transfer of Webots controllers in the Turtlebot3
authors: Jaime P. Pérez-Moro,Alejandro Romero,Hector Quintian,Francisco Bellas
abstract: Robot Operating System (ROS) is becoming a standard in robotics courses at higher education, but its installation, configuration and distributed programming model can introduce a significant entry barrier in the new landscape of AI-based master and degree studies, where many students do not have a strong informatics background. This paper presents an educational experience that enables students to program a TurtleBot3 Burger directly in Python, while preserving a direct transfer path from simulation to the physical robot. The approach is based on a custom library that mirrors the Webots API, allowing the same controller code to be executed in the simulator and on the real TurtleBot3 with minimal modification. The library provides access to the robot motors, wheel encoders, inertial sensors and LiDAR, and is complemented by scripts that automate deployment and execution on the physical platform. It was used in a master-level course on introductory autonomous vehicles, and initial student feedback suggests that the approach reduces the perceived complexity of ROS-related infrastructure and helps learners focus on algorithmic logic and real-world behaviour.
introduction:
The use of ROS [1] in technical subjects and courses related with autonomous robotics at higher education is becoming a standard [2][3]. Its open-access nature, hardware abstraction and huge community of contributors make ROS as the optimal choice for teachers that aim to provide students with the most solid and long-term training in robotics. In addition, the current offer of affordable and versatile real platforms for educational/research purposes is mainly ROS-compatible and even ROS-exclusive, like those from Unitree, Universal Robots, PAL or Clearpath Robotics.

Since the “explosion” of generative AI in 2022, the interest of students in titles related with Artificial Intelligence (AI) has notably increased and, consequently, the offer of new titles related with this area has raised [4]. Many of these new students and titles do not have or require the high technical background associated with ROS, although they need learning about autonomous robotics in a solid and sound way. There are notably relevant initiatives that aim to “smooth” the ROS learning curve, such as the web-based Unibotics framework [5][6], but the real situation in many of these new courses is that installing Linux or relying on virtual machines is complicated, mainly due to time constraints in the subjects, and the lack of support from the institutions.

With this background, the current paper describes a custom library developed at the University of Coruña (UDC), in Spain, together with the educational experience in which it was applied. The library was created for a technical master program named “Industrial Informatics and Robotics” [7]. This subject is a clear example of the situation presented above, as it is mainly technical, but the number of students attending it with limited programming and computer science background increases every year. In particular, the experience described here was carried out in the realm of a subject named “Introductory Autonomous Vehicles”, where students learn the fundamentals of this field, including topics like perception, mapping, localization and control.

The practical part of the subject implies programming the response of an autonomous robot, in simulation and in the real-world, requiring a minimum proficiency level as a computer scientist. The specific platform existing in the UDC for this subject is the TurtleBot3 Burger, a ROS-exclusive platform that is shared with other subjects in the same master. To provide this heterogeneous group of students with a sound and simple educational environment that allow them to practice the subject fundamentals without relying on ROS, we decided to develop a custom library so they can program it in a simpler way using the Webots simulation environment [8].

This work describes the implementation details of this library, how it was validated in the simulator and the real robot, and its application during academic year 2025/26 within the aforementioned subject.

title: H-TRIP: Exact Many-to-Many Distance Index for Multi-Robot Exploration
authors: Elif A. Özaslan,Tolga Özaslan
abstract:
Frontier-based exploration systems repeatedly evaluate geodesic travel costs between robot poses and candidate viewpoints, and tour-based planners consume the full pairwise distance matrix built from them.
Recomputing these matrices with one graph search per source scales with the explored map size, whereas distance caches that refresh only locally affected or newly created frontiers can retain stale costs between surviving pairs when newly discovered free space creates a global shortcut.
We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring for monotonically growing occupancy grids.
H-TRIP partitions the known map into a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports.
Each unknown-to-free revelation is decomposed into efficient rank-one min-plus edge insertions at the affected leaf, and only decreased port-to-port summaries are propagated along its ancestor chain.
A shared hierarchical lift evaluates the dense many-to-many matrix of shortest distances for all active query points on the occupancy map.
We prove that sequential insertions preserve exact shortest-path distances on the grid.
Benchmark experiments confirm exact agreement with reference searches on fully built maps and show that dense many-to-many queries at a few dozen viewpoints are up to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential k×k\timesBFS.
On exploration runs with sixteen robots, in-loop queries on the growing occupancy graph are 2.21×2.21\times–8.59×8.59\times faster than co-scheduled k×k\timesBFS on maps with side 256256, 512512, and 10241024 cells.
introduction:
Autonomous exploration is foundational in search and rescue, inspection, and reconnaissance.
Mobile robot teams iteratively map free space, extract candidate frontier viewpoints, and coordinate assignments using travel cost, information gain, or both [1].
Tour-based planners repeatedly evaluate pairwise travel costs among candidate goals using geodesic distance as their spatial backbone, which can be combined with planner-specific kinematic or utility terms [2, 3, 4].
These geodesics are shortest paths on the free-space graph Gτ=(Vτ,Eτ)G_{\tau}=(V_{\tau},E_{\tau}) of an occupancy representation or an exploration roadmap.
Under undirected traversal the geodesic distance matrix is symmetric, so filling D∈ℝ¯≥0k×kD\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{k\times k} among kk robot poses and candidate viewpoints with the k⁡(k−1)/2k(k-1)/2 distinct pairwise distances of GτG_{\tau} requires substantial computational effort as maps and candidate sets grow.

As sensors reveal free space, the traversable graph GτG_{\tau} grows monotonically.
Recomputing DD from scratch with one graph search per source scales with both kk and |Vτ||V_{\tau}|, and competes with the planning cycle.
Newly revealed free cells can complete a doorway or corridor that shortens the true geodesic between two persisting viewpoints, making a previously cached distance stale.
The challenge is to keep the geodesic distance matrix DD exact without recomputing shortest paths over the full graph after every occupancy-map update.
We therefore ask how a multi-robot system can maintain exact all-pairs geodesic distances among surviving viewpoints under online monotonic map growth while keeping many-to-many queries within a planning-cycle budget.

We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact hierarchical distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring [5, 6] that maintains pairwise geodesic distances as occupancy grows and answers many-to-many queries for assignment and tour planners on online occupancy grids.
H-TRIP organizes the workspace into a balanced spatial hierarchy over fixed leaf tiles whose boundary-port sets remain fixed throughout exploration.
Sensor measurements that reveal previously unknown cells as free insert local edges in GτG_{\tau}, including newly passable cross-tile seams, and only decreased boundary-distance summaries propagate upward along the affected ancestor chain.

H-TRIP builds this hierarchy so that many-to-many geodesic distances can be evaluated by lifting each of the kk viewpoints all at once onto the boundary ports of their ancestor tiles and resolving pairwise distances as tropical products against stored boundary metrics.
H-TRIP realizes its query advantage by amortizing each hierarchical lift across the entire k×kk\times k matrix.
An isolated pair lookup pays that lift without sharing it, so batched many-to-many evaluation is the regime that reuses the work.
Hence H-TRIP can serve as a metric backend for multi-robot assignment and tour planners that require geodesic distance.

In simulation, H-TRIP consistently preserved exact geodesic distances while reducing the cost of repeated many-to-many evaluation relative to conventional graph-search baselines.
The advantage was most pronounced when multiple robot poses and frontier viewpoints were queried together, allowing hierarchical computations to be shared across the complete distance matrix.

The main contributions of this paper are:
(i) an exact hierarchical distance index for monotonically growing occupancy grids based on fixed geometric interfaces and min-plus closure;
(ii) a localized insertion-only maintenance procedure based on rank-one min-plus updates, with exactness established by Lemma 1 and Theorem 1; and
(iii) a batched hierarchical query that recovers the complete k×kk\times k geodesic distance matrix, with exactness established by Theorem 2.

title: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model
authors: Zihao Zhang,Xinyu Zhang,Bing Zeng,Xingyu Chen,Zhenning Li,Bin Yu,Ziyuan Pu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) jointly model future traffic states and driving actions for end-to-end autonomous driving in intelligent transportation systems. However, their action learning remains dominated by expert-trajectory imitation, leaving unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained. To improve WAM robustness in safety-critical scenarios, we propose NegWAM, a safety post-training framework for unified WAMs that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories. NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene–trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1 % relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Zizizi-hao/NegWAM.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving systems typically learn driving policies from large-scale expert demonstrations and perform well in routine scenarios [1, 2]. However, hazardous behaviors and failure cases are scarce in real-world driving data, making it difficult for imitation learning to acquire explicit safety boundaries [3, 4]. World-action models (WAMs) introduce stronger priors over scene dynamics into end-to-end autonomous driving by predicting future world states and leveraging future representations to guide planning [5, 6, 7]. Yet their action branches are still trained primarily through flow matching on expert trajectories. This supervision tells the model what to imitate, but not which near-expert alternatives should be rejected as unsafe. Consequently, stronger world modeling alone does not establish explicit safety boundaries, motivating safety-oriented post-training for WAMs.

Post-training offers a natural avenue beyond these limitations, but a central challenge is constructing learning signals that faithfully encode desired driving behavior [8, 4]. Existing methods primarily rely on two sources of supervision. One line of work (Figure 1a) explores policies in closed-loop environments built with a simulator [9, 10] or a world model [11, 12], but is constrained by the sim-to-real gap, environment construction costs, and reconstruction artifacts [13, 12]. Another line (Figure 1b) scores candidate trajectories using rule-based evaluators or learned reward models, but the quality of its supervision is limited by handcrafted rules, privileged information, and evaluator bias [14, 15, 16]. These limitations underscore the need for additional sources of effective supervision for autonomous driving post-training.

Unsafe driving behaviors provide critical cues for delineating safety boundaries and are often easier to characterize than the full range of desirable driving behavior [17, 18]. Building on this insight, we propose NegWAM, a negative-aware safety post-training method that incorporates offline negative supervision into a unified WAM (Figure 1c). Specifically, near-expert negatives serve as repulsive anchors that mark locally unsafe regions in trajectory space and as scene-conditioned rider tokens that enable shared attention layers to learn scene–trajectory compatibility. Together with the original imitation objective, these mechanisms enable the WAM to learn not only how experts drive but also which behaviors should be avoided in the current scene.

Unlike prior hard-negative learning that primarily regularizes planner outputs [17], NegWAM post-trains both the single-rollout action flow and the shared world–action representation of a unified WAM. It mines near-expert trajectories that fail offline safety evaluation and jointly optimizes the original flow-matching objective with two hard-negative objectives. The evaluator is used only for offline mining, while the rider branch and compatibility head are removed at inference, adding no inference-time modules. On NAVSIM v2 [19, 20], NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1 % relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest, surpassing the strongest baseline score of 92.9 by 0.4 points and demonstrating stronger challenging-scenario performance without compromising routine driving. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM [21] further supports cross-benchmark transfer, with NegWAM achieving a higher HD-Score than DriveWAM (30.6 vs. 27.2).

In summary, our key contributions are as follows:

We revisit unified world–action models through safety post-training, showing that augmenting flow-matching imitation with near-expert negative supervision improves challenging-scenario performance without compromising routine driving.

We propose NegWAM, a near-expert negative safety post-training method for WAMs that jointly optimizes the original flow-matching objective and two complementary near-expert negative objectives without introducing additional inference-time overhead.

We introduce two complementary near-expert negative mechanisms. Repulsive anchors push predictions away from locally unsafe trajectories, while scene-conditioned rider tokens enable the unified WAM to determine whether a trajectory is compatible with the current scene.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on end-to-end autonomous driving, world–action models, and policy post-training. Section III introduces NegWAM, including its core components and training objective. Section IV evaluates its planning performance and zero-shot closed-loop generalization, with ablation studies and supporting analyses. Section V summarizes the main findings and discusses limitations and future directions.

1. We revisit unified world–action models through safety post-training, showing that augmenting flow-matching imitation with near-expert negative supervision improves challenging-scenario performance without compromising routine driving.

2. We propose NegWAM, a near-expert negative safety post-training method for WAMs that jointly optimizes the original flow-matching objective and two complementary near-expert negative objectives without introducing additional inference-time overhead.

3. We introduce two complementary near-expert negative mechanisms. Repulsive anchors push predictions away from locally unsafe trajectories, while scene-conditioned rider tokens enable the unified WAM to determine whether a trajectory is compatible with the current scene.

title: An Integrated Open-Source Stack for Vision-Based Autonomous Navigation of Wheeled Rovers
authors: Iaroslav Kolomiets,Iaroslav Sheipak,Mikhail Reppo,Vsevolod Egorov,Viktor Chertopolokhov,Isaac Chairez
comment: Accepted at RiTA 2026
abstract: Vision-based rover autonomy requires integrating perception, localization, planning and platform-specific control under limited sensing and computing resources. We present an open-source ROS 2 stack for following directional arrows, reaching a terminal cone and returning autonomously to the start. It connects YOLOv8n detection and geometric direction, range and bearing estimation with RGB-D SLAM, wheel–inertial state estimation, kinematics-aware planning, behavior-tree mission management and STM32 actuation. Standard interfaces separate reusable autonomy from the hardware layer; a proportional path-following plugin supports low-speed rover motion. Public resources include software, configuration, a labeled dataset, trained weights and evaluation logs. On 478 held-out images, the detector achieves mAP@0.5 of 0.720 under the Ultralytics evaluator and outperforms a classical OpenCV baseline under a shared evaluation protocol. The reported perception latency is 25 ms on a Jetson Orin NX. Three missions, one indoor and two outdoor, demonstrate marker-guided navigation and autonomous return without operator motion commands or reported collisions. Field results document integration failures and corrective choices; repeated instrumented trials remain necessary to quantify physical navigation errors and reliability.
introduction:
Autonomous ground vehicles are central to exploration, agriculture, logistics, inspection and search-and-rescue [10], and wheeled rovers balance mechanical simplicity, energy efficiency and terrain adaptability [1]. Their key capability is autonomous navigation [17], and cameras, being lightweight, inexpensive and semantically rich, make vision-based navigation attractive for low-cost research and educational platforms [2, 15].

Lighting, texture, sensor noise and on-board computing constraints complicate deployment, while reusable integration remains difficult [16]. ROS 2 provides middleware and interface conventions [7]; established components include OMPL [13], Nav2 [8], RTAB-Map [6], integrated vehicle planners [3], and AprilTag/ArUco fiducials [11, 4]. Our pipeline instead interprets uncoded arrows and cones, converts observations into map-frame goals and executes them on a non-holonomic rover under mission-level supervision [5].

The contributions of this work are:

An integrated open-source ROS 2 stack from perception to STM32 actuation, separating reusable autonomy from platform-specific control.

A YOLOv8n marker-perception pipeline with geometric direction, range and bearing estimation, public data and weights, and a classical OpenCV comparison.

Behavior-tree marker search, goal generation and return, integrated with kinematics-aware planning and proportional path following.

Three documented physical-rover missions, including integration failures, corrective choices and per-mission outcomes.

title: STEP: Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
authors: Youhao Lyu,Chenghao Sun,Zhenxuan Ding,Shuting Zhang,Ziyang Dong,Wenhao Cui
abstract: For perceptive humanoid locomotion, the relevance of terrain geometry depends on the robot’s body state and how both evolve under its actions. Existing work has advanced terrain-aware sensory fusion and cross-modal prediction, improving how visual and proprioceptive information is combined and related. However, feature aggregation alone does not specify which cross-modal relationships should be learned, while prediction between simultaneous observations does not explicitly constrain their action-dependent evolution. We present Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction (STEP), a one-stage framework that jointly supervises cross-modal relationships and action-dependent state evolution within a shared control representation. Multiple learned queries aggregate depth and proprioceptive tokens into a compact policy state. Bidirectional masked prediction uses each visible modality to predict latent features of the omitted modality, explicitly supervising terrain-body relationships. An action-conditioned predictor maps the current policy state and executed action to the next fused state, with an exponential-moving-average target defined directly in the policy representation space. Simulation comparisons show overall improvements in terrain traversal over evaluated fusion alternatives and ablations, while depth-dropout and delay experiments demonstrate the benefits of both predictive objectives under degraded visual input. Deployed on a 23-DoF Noetix E1 humanoid with onboard sensing, STEP succeeds in 98 of 100 hardware trials across stairs, a 40 cm platform, a 70 cm gap, stepping stones, and backward stair traversal without rearward terrain visibility.
introduction:
Traversing stairs, gaps, and discrete footholds requires a humanoid robot to coordinate its motion with the geometry of upcoming contacts [1, 2]. Depth observations preview the terrain, while proprioceptive history describes body motion. The relevance of a stair edge or landing surface depends on the robot’s approach velocity, configuration, and ongoing step [3, 4, 5]. For the tasks in Fig. 1, the controller must extract body–terrain information relevant to action selection and subsequent contacts while compressing heterogeneous observations into a compact state for repeated policy inference.

Proprioception-conditioned terrain aggregation selects terrain features using body-state information [6], while cross-modal supervision provides learning signals between visual and proprioceptive observations [7]. Predictive representation learning further connects latent-state evolution to control through auxiliary prediction or model-based planning [8, 9]. These approaches provide complementary starting points, but information access and predictive supervision serve different roles: aggregation determines how observations are read, whereas prediction constrains relationships across modalities or time. For a compact locomotion state, the design challenge is to coordinate efficient information extraction with supervision of both current body–terrain relationships and action-dependent change, so that the resulting representation supports closed-loop traversal.

How can a compact control state retain relevant terrain and body information, represent their relationships and subsequent evolution, and remain efficient to compute? Our working hypothesis is that joint aggregation through multiple learned queries can provide useful information-reading paths, while cross-modal and action-conditioned temporal prediction can jointly supervise the relationships represented in the policy state. We examine this hypothesis through performance–cost comparisons and fixed-architecture objective ablations, using terrain traversal to assess the control value of the learned representation.

We present Spatiotemporal Training with Explicit Prediction (STEP), a one-stage framework that jointly learns a multimodal control state and a humanoid locomotion policy. STEP uses multiple queries to read a shared proprioceptive–depth context and unifies prediction across modalities and time: bidirectional masked prediction supervises same-time body–terrain relationships, while action-conditioned prediction supervises their subsequent fused representation. Both objectives train the policy’s shared encoder jointly with proximal policy optimization (PPO) [10], while Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) [11] is used to prevent latent collapse. The temporal target is the next unprojected exponential-moving-average (EMA) fused state, and prediction heads and target encoders are omitted at deployment. Simulation system comparisons show overall traversal gains, while the aggregation comparison shows higher success with slightly lower inference latency than proprioception-queried cross-attention. Hardware trials demonstrate multi-terrain locomotion, including backward stair traversal without rearward terrain visibility.

Our main contributions are fourfold:

One-Stage Perceptive Locomotion Framework. We propose STEP, a framework that jointly learns a depth-based humanoid locomotion policy and its multimodal control representation in a single policy-training process, without separate representation pre-training. Predictive supervision is confined to training, preserving direct policy inference at deployment.

Multi-Query Multimodal Aggregation. We use multiple learned queries to jointly aggregate proprioceptive and depth tokens from a shared body–terrain context. Pooling the query outputs yields a compact policy state, enabling multiple context-dependent aggregation paths within a lightweight fusion module.

Spatiotemporal Multimodal Prediction. We formulate cross-modal and action-conditioned temporal prediction as complementary supervision of a shared policy encoder: bidirectional masked prediction supervises same-time body–terrain relationships, while one-step prediction targets their subsequent fused state in the unprojected EMA representation space. Together, these objectives connect relationships across modalities and time to the representation used for control.

Simulation and Real-World Validation. We evaluate STEP through simulation system comparisons, aggregation analyses, and fixed-architecture objective ablations under nominal and degraded vision. Repeated onboard hardware trials demonstrate sim-to-real transfer across stairs, platforms, gaps, and stepping stones, including backward stair traversal without rearward terrain visibility.

1. One-Stage Perceptive Locomotion Framework. We propose STEP, a framework that jointly learns a depth-based humanoid locomotion policy and its multimodal control representation in a single policy-training process, without separate representation pre-training. Predictive supervision is confined to training, preserving direct policy inference at deployment.

2. Multi-Query Multimodal Aggregation. We use multiple learned queries to jointly aggregate proprioceptive and depth tokens from a shared body–terrain context. Pooling the query outputs yields a compact policy state, enabling multiple context-dependent aggregation paths within a lightweight fusion module.

3. Spatiotemporal Multimodal Prediction. We formulate cross-modal and action-conditioned temporal prediction as complementary supervision of a shared policy encoder: bidirectional masked prediction supervises same-time body–terrain relationships, while one-step prediction targets their subsequent fused state in the unprojected EMA representation space. Together, these objectives connect relationships across modalities and time to the representation used for control.

4. Simulation and Real-World Validation. We evaluate STEP through simulation system comparisons, aggregation analyses, and fixed-architecture objective ablations under nominal and degraded vision. Repeated onboard hardware trials demonstrate sim-to-real transfer across stairs, platforms, gaps, and stepping stones, including backward stair traversal without rearward terrain visibility.

title: Leave It Better Than Found: Value-Guided Cooperation in Sequential Tasks
authors: Mario Gomez Andreu,Michael Amir,Antonio Marino,Tianxu An,Marco Hutter,Amanda Prorok
abstract:
We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot.
Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assuming that the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a kk-nearest neighbors (KNN)-based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal learning tool, but as an effective basis for ad hoc coordination. 
Website: https://proroklab.github.io/PAVE/
introduction:
As robotic systems achieve greater autonomy, heterogeneous agents, e.g., cleaners, delivery bots, and security systems, will increasingly operate in the same public and domestic spaces. Robots modify these spaces to achieve their goals, leaving subsequent actors with the environments that they left behind.
These workspace overlaps require spontaneous cooperation between independently developed systems. We formalize this challenge as sequential task continuation: a setting where an agent must proactively anticipate how its physical actions will alter the shared space and affect subsequent actors.

Currently, robot behaviors are typically designed in isolation by different parties to perform distinct tasks. When actors interact in the same shared workspace, we require methods and protocols that bridge these independent systems. For instance, delivery bots should not drop packages along common patrol routes, and cleaners should not rearrange the environment in such a way that areas become inaccessible to other robots. Because hand-crafted rules are too brittle to handle the infinite edge cases of open-world environments, learning-based coordination is required. Training a separate cooperative policy for every possible pairing of robots is unrealistic, as the possible combinations increase exponentially with the number of robot embodiments and tasks.

Instead, we turn to ad hoc coordination between agents that does not require joint training, as robots can easily share key components of their decision-making with other agents. Given the representation of other agents’ preferences, robots can adapt their behavior on the fly (ad hoc) to aid other robots in their tasks while still pursuing their own.
Existing frameworks in this domain, however, rely on restrictive assumptions. Zero-shot coordination [15] trains a single robust policy, but it does not allow online adaptation. Ad Hoc teamwork, first proposed in Stone et al. [31] and implemented in PLASTIC [1] and TEAMSTER [26], adapts online but assumes a single common payoff and infers teammate behavior from observation rather than direct communication. Both approaches assume that actors act simultaneously and not sequentially.

Our approach is different: agents pursue distinct tasks and exchange compact representations of their preferences. Rather than relying on task-specific learned communication channels [9, 18], we leverage a quantity that reinforcement-learning agents already learn: the value function, which maps states to expected return.
For sequential task continuation, the relevant part is the follower’s value over shared environment states. Sharing the value function tells the leader which handoff states are useful for the follower.
Our method, Policy Adaptation via Value Exchange (PAVE), uses this single exchange of the value function to coordinate with the following agent without joint training, adapting the leading agent’s policy online using a receding horizon planner.

We contribute:

The formalization of sequential task continuation with environment handoff.

PAVE: A method that combines value-function sharing with an online receding-horizon planner to coordinate two independently trained robots.

An uncertainty-based grounding using a kk-nearest-neighbors distribution filter to prevent the receiving agent from acting on unreliable value estimates.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning typically relies on joint training with shared critics, as in MAPPO [36], MADDPG [20], COMA [10], and QMIX [25]. These approaches do not scale to sequential task coordination as the robots act not simultaneously but sequentially in a shared environment. Cooperative Consecutive Policies [8] instead train distinct policies acting on a shared embodiment to solve long-horizon tasks, by optimizing each current policy with respect to the next agent’s Q-function to ensure an optimal hand-off. Although distinct from our method, it assumes a shared embodiment and joint training, and it inspires one of our baselines.
Dhakal et al. [5] propose a planner for rearrangement tasks that anticipates the effects of its actions on future tasks of the same agent. PAVE differs by reusing an existing value function, filtering out-of-distribution value estimates, and considering multiple agents instead of a single agent.

Other approaches similarly treat the environment as the medium of inter-agent influence. Stigmergy [14, 7, 24] is a natural process used by swarm animals such as ants to coordinate through pheromone deposits in the environment. Environment Co-Design [11, 12, 17] also considers adapting the environment to benefit the agents acting within it. PAVE defines a middle ground: agents communicate directly via their value functions, but enact that coordination indirectly. One agent manipulates the physical space via its task-constrained policy to favorably shape the state for the next agent, achieving continuation without requiring central design or shared training. For an extended discussion of the related literature, we refer the reader to Appendix B.
