title: Terrain-Indexed Motion Priors and Geometric Support for Extreme Humanoid Parkour
authors: Chenghao Sun,Youhao Lyu,Zizheng Li,Shuting Zhang,Ziyang Dong,Wenhao Cui
abstract:
We present a progressive imitation framework that learns terrain-appropriate
humanoid parkour skills and subsequently adapts their hand–knee support.
Human demonstrations provide traversal behaviors, but their contact patterns
need not suit a robot’s proportions or the available support surfaces.
Our framework changes the role of demonstrations across three stages:
privileged imitation produces physically executable robot references;
terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide skill acquisition; and
geometric support guidance with a reduced motion-prior weight enables
contact adaptation. Candidate-based precontact attraction and actual-contact
evaluation guide support without prescribing a contact sequence.
The deployed policy selects behaviors from onboard depth, proprioception,
and velocity commands without an external skill label.
On the Noetix E1, the policy achieves 96.34% hybrid success in simulation
and transfers without real-world policy fine-tuning, completing 29 of 30
individual obstacle trials and four of five hybrid courses.
Support-adaptation ablations show higher traversal success for the complete
adaptation stage on the tested terrains, while qualitative observations
show changes in contact placement. These results support acquiring skills
from demonstrations before relaxing their influence to accommodate
robot-specific support configurations.
introduction:
Humanoid parkour extends mobility beyond conventional walking through
whole-body obstacle traversal. These maneuvers require
coordinating whole-body contacts as the robot mounts, crosses, and leaves
an obstacle. Terrain geometry determines both the appropriate motion and
available support. Human demonstrations provide examples of
such coordination, but differences in body proportions, actuation, and
available support surfaces make direct reproduction an incomplete solution.

Learning-based control has enabled robust perceptive quadrupedal locomotion
in natural environments [1] and diverse dynamic
bipedal skills [2].
Perceptive control has advanced humanoid obstacle traversal through visual
reinforcement learning and the use of human motion
information [3, 4, 5].
Adversarial motion priors (AMP) provide behavioral guidance alongside task
rewards [6], while multiple and terrain-conditioned priors organize
this guidance across skills and
environments [7, 8, 9, 10].
However, acquiring an executable skill does not alone determine
where it is appropriate or how its contacts should adapt. A demonstrated
contact pattern may be unsuitable for the robot or a different support layout.
We therefore ask: How can demonstrations guide the acquisition
of terrain-appropriate traversal skills while leaving the robot freedom to
adapt its support configuration?

Three connected difficulties arise: mapped motions may violate robot
physics; executable references may be inappropriate for the encountered
terrain; and demonstrated contacts may restrict alternative support
configurations. Addressing physical executability therefore does not eliminate
the need for terrain-dependent guidance or subsequent contact adaptation. Our design
principle is to use imitation as a scaffold for skill acquisition and
subsequently relax the motion prior while increasing geometric support guidance.
The aim is
to preserve what the skill accomplishes while allowing its physical
realization to change.

We propose a progressive physics-grounded imitation framework connecting
reference preparation, terrain-dependent skill learning, and support adaptation.
Privileged mimic training first prepares robot reference rollouts from human
motions. Terrain-organized reference pools then supervise adversarial motion
priors with a shared representation and separate terrain-specific heads,
guiding a single traversal policy. Support adaptation adds geometric hand–knee
candidates, precontact guidance, and actual-contact rewards, increasing support
weight while gradually reducing AMP weight to half its initial value to allow
robot-specific contact configurations rather than a prescribed sequence.
Terrain labels, reference discrimination, and support geometry are
confined to training. At deployment, the policy uses onboard depth, proprioceptive history,
and velocity commands without a separate skill command. The policy achieves 96.34% hybrid traversal success in simulation. Our evaluation examines terrain-organized supervision and support adaptation.

The main contributions are:

A progressive imitation framework that uses terrain-indexed motion
priors for skill acquisition and then relaxes them for support adaptation.

Geometric hand–knee support guidance combining precontact attraction
and actual-contact evaluation without prescribing a contact sequence.

Simulation comparisons and onboard hardware trials evaluating
single-policy traversal, support adaptation, and transfer to the tested
terrain-height shifts.

1. A progressive imitation framework that uses terrain-indexed motion
priors for skill acquisition and then relaxes them for support adaptation.

2. Geometric hand–knee support guidance combining precontact attraction
and actual-contact evaluation without prescribing a contact sequence.

3. Simulation comparisons and onboard hardware trials evaluating
single-policy traversal, support adaptation, and transfer to the tested
terrain-height shifts.

title: HITCH: Teaching a Vision-Language Model to Operate a Humanoid through a Whole-Body Harness
authors: Qingzhou Lu,Chenxin Liu,Xinming Wang,Liu Cao,Yanjiang Guo,Mengdi Xu,Jianyu Chen
comment: Project Page:this https URL
abstract:
Enabling vision-language models (VLMs) to control humanoid robots requires both reliable whole-body interfaces and
knowledge of how to use the body that carries over across tasks. We present HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command
Humanoids), a harness in which perception returns the 3D position of any point the VLM selects in its image, and
execution turns commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking, and gaze into whole-body motion with a learned tracker.
We find that both measuring the scene and executing commands accurately raise task success. We then fine-tune a VLM on trajectories in which
teacher policies solve five base tasks through HITCH, so that it learns how to operate the humanoid. Without
task-specific trajectories, the fine-tuned model completes 51% of SIMPLE episodes and 42.5% of HumanoidArena episodes,
and adding five trajectories per SIMPLE task raises its SIMPLE success to 95%. On a real G1, it carries a box and walks
to a goal without real training data.
introduction:
General-purpose humanoid robots should carry out everyday loco-manipulation tasks from language instructions, for
example, walking to a table, crouching to pick up a cup, and placing it in a basket on another table. Each of these
steps requires the legs, torso, and arms to act together while the head camera keeps the target in view, and every
motion must match the geometry of a scene the robot has never seen.

A common approach trains vision-language-action (VLA)
models [1, 2] or world action
models [3] that map observations and instructions directly to whole-body actions.
These models produce fluent motion, but they usually need many demonstrations of each task, and their performance
can drop when only a few are available [4]. For a humanoid, each demonstration requires
whole-body teleoperation or motion planning, which makes every new task expensive to add.

Agents built on foundation models offer another route, but on a humanoid they lack two things. Prompted language
models and vision-language models (VLMs) already solve many tabletop tasks without task-specific
training [5, 6, 7]. The first thing they lack on a humanoid is an
interface to the whole body. Existing humanoid agents mostly select skills from a library or command
task-space controllers [8, 9], which leave the posture of the legs and torso to the
controller. A task may require the agent to set this posture itself, and the interface must execute each command accurately, since the agent observes again only after a
command finishes. The second is skill in operating a humanoid body. Pretraining contains few examples of humanoid
motion: a model may understand 3D space well yet know little about how far a humanoid can reach, or when it must step
or crouch to bring its hands to a target. RAX acquires such knowledge through online exploration of each new task,
with success that grows with the exploration budget [10]. Yet much of this knowledge is shared
across tasks and could be learned once.

We first build HITCH (Harness Interfaces To Command Humanoids), a harness through which a VLM observes and
controls the robot. Its perception interface lets the
model measure the scene: it selects a point in the image and receives the 3D position of that point from depth, so it
does not have to guess distances from the image alone. Its execution interface exposes commands for each body part,
such as pelvis height, torso orientation, hand waypoints, walking, and gaze. A planner converts them into whole-body
references, which a learned tracker executes on a Unitree G1. We train this tracker further on the planner’s
references. Given the same commands, it executes them more accurately than baseline trackers, and more tasks succeed
with it.

With this harness, the VLM only has to choose the next call, but nothing in the harness tells it how to choose. We therefore fine-tune Qwen3.8-27B on trajectories in which teacher
policies use the same interfaces to solve five base tasks: tabletop pick-and-place, carrying objects between pieces
of furniture, navigation, opening drawers and cabinet doors, and opening room doors. From these trajectories, the
model learns skills for operating a humanoid through the harness, such as where to stand, how low to crouch, how far
to lean, and what to measure before acting.

We find that these skills carry over to new tasks in simulated
benchmarks [4, 11], and to real scenes on a G1 without real training data. On the SIMPLE humanoid benchmark, the model
trained on the base tasks completes about half of the episodes without task-specific trajectories, and adding
five trajectories per task raises its success to 95%. Compared with training on the task trajectories
alone, training on the base tasks as well raises success at every number of trajectories we tried. Without its perception interface, the model trained on the base tasks solves only
2.8% of SIMPLE’s episodes. On a real G1, the model completes 13 of 20 carrying and 6 of 10 navigation episodes.

Our contributions are:

a harness for humanoid agents with two interfaces: perception, which measures the scene on demand, and
execution, which turns body-part commands into accurate whole-body motion;

teacher policies that solve five humanoid base tasks through these interfaces, acting only on what the agent
observes, and a VLM fine-tuned on their trajectories that carries over to new tasks;

experiments on two humanoid benchmarks and a real G1, covering transfer to new tasks, learning from a few
trajectories per task, transfer to real scenes, and ablations of perception and execution.

1. a harness for humanoid agents with two interfaces: perception, which measures the scene on demand, and
execution, which turns body-part commands into accurate whole-body motion;

2. teacher policies that solve five humanoid base tasks through these interfaces, acting only on what the agent
observes, and a VLM fine-tuned on their trajectories that carries over to new tasks;

3. experiments on two humanoid benchmarks and a real G1, covering transfer to new tasks, learning from a few
trajectories per task, transfer to real scenes, and ablations of perception and execution.

title: Symmetry-Aware Surrogate-Assisted Testing of UAVs
authors: Anas Shrinah,Chris Bennett,Kerstin Eder
abstract:
We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by transforming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordinate frame.
This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training.
The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios.
We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions.
Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data.
This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance.
However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization.
To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.
introduction:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly employed in
applications that require autonomous navigation in complex
environments, such as indoor facilities [1],
urban areas [2], and disaster
sites [3].
In such environments, failures in obstacle avoidance can lead to collisions, making the safety and reliability of autonomous navigation systems a critical concern.

To address these concerns, verification and validation methods, such as simulation-based testing, play an important role in establishing confidence in the trustworthiness of these systems.
Simulation-based testing uses high-fidelity simulators to evaluate autonomous UAVs under a diverse range of environmental conditions while reducing the time, cost, and safety risks associated with physical flight testing.
However, the input space makes exhaustive testing impractical. Search-based testing offers a systematic approach to this challenge by guiding test generation towards scenarios that are more likely to reveal system failures [4].
This process, however, requires evaluating numerous candidate scenarios, making the computational cost of high-fidelity simulations a significant bottleneck.

Surrogate-assisted testing offers an approach to mitigating this bottleneck by using computationally inexpensive surrogate models to estimate test outcomes without executing the high-fidelity simulator [5].
These models learn an approximation of the relationship between test inputs and simulation outcomes using data from previously executed high-fidelity simulations. Since evaluating a surrogate model is generally much less expensive than executing a high-fidelity simulation, a large number of candidate test scenarios can be assessed before selecting a smaller subset for simulation.

In UAV obstacle-avoidance testing, test scenarios can be constructed by placing obstacles along a flight mission, with the objective of identifying configurations that cause the UAV to approach obstacles closely or exhibit unsafe behaviour.
A flight mission may consist of multiple segments with different positions and orientations, each requiring its own obstacle configurations. Developing an accurate surrogate model for such scenarios requires training data representative of the configurations encountered across these segments.
However, obtaining sufficient training data through high-fidelity simulations can be prohibitively expensive, especially when separate training data must be collected for different flight segments or missions.

An opportunity to address this challenge arises from the geometric symmetries between flight segments. Obstacle configurations associated with different flight segments may have identical relative geometries despite differing in their global positions and orientations.
Such geometrically equivalent configurations can be represented relative to a reference flight segment in a canonical coordinate frame, which we refer to as the canonical flight frame.

In this work, we investigate a surrogate-assisted test-generation approach that exploits these geometric symmetries to reuse a neural-network surrogate across different flight missions.
During training, the surrogate is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles for a reference flight mission. This reference flight mission defines the canonical flight frame.
During test generation, candidate obstacle configurations for a target flight mission are transformed into the canonical flight frame and evaluated using the trained surrogate.
Promising configurations are then transformed back into the target mission’s coordinate system and evaluated using the high-fidelity simulator.

Geometric equivalence does not necessarily imply equivalent UAV behaviour. The response of an autonomous UAV may also depend on factors such as its incoming velocity, heading, controller state, preceding flight segments, and the surrounding environment. Consequently, the extent to which a surrogate trained in a canonical frame can provide accurate predictions for different missions must be established empirically.

This work investigates the efficiency and effectiveness of canonical
surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing, as well as its
limitations. Specifically, we address the following research questions:

RQ1: How does surrogate prediction accuracy vary across different flight missions?

RQ2: To what extent does an NN-based surrogate improve the efficiency of test generation?

RQ3: How does filtering based on a canonical surrogate affect test-suite diversity?

To answer these questions and evaluate our approach, we apply it to efficiently create effective test cases for PX4-Avoidance, a vision-based autonomous obstacle avoidance system developed on top of PX4-Autopilot [6].
We benchmark our approach against the test case generators that participated in the UAV Testing Competition 2024, 2025 and 2026 versions [7, 8, 9, 10, 11].

By addressing these research questions, this work makes the following
main contributions:

A neural network surrogate model that approximates the PX-4 obstacle avoidance system and estimates the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and an obstacle.

An extensive empirical evaluation comparing the efficiency and effectiveness of the surrogate-guided test-case generator with those of state-of-the-art test-case generators.

The limitations of canonical surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing.

A dataset of simulation results for over 2500 different obstacle configurations for a flight mission, which can be used to develop other types of surrogate models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work and Section III introduces the UAV case study. Section IV describes the symmetry-aware testing approach, while Section V reports the empirical evaluation. Section VI discusses the findings, assumptions, and limitations. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper and outlines future work.

1. RQ1: How does surrogate prediction accuracy vary across different flight missions?

2. RQ2: To what extent does an NN-based surrogate improve the efficiency of test generation?

3. RQ3: How does filtering based on a canonical surrogate affect test-suite diversity?

1. A neural network surrogate model that approximates the PX-4 obstacle avoidance system and estimates the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and an obstacle.

2. An extensive empirical evaluation comparing the efficiency and effectiveness of the surrogate-guided test-case generator with those of state-of-the-art test-case generators.

3. The limitations of canonical surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing.

4. A dataset of simulation results for over 2500 different obstacle configurations for a flight mission, which can be used to develop other types of surrogate models.

title: A Unified Fractal Impedance Control Framework
authors: Adnan Takriti,Mahmoud Sadeq,Quentin Rouxel,Daniele Cafolla,Michael Mistry,Carlo Tiseo
abstract: Physical human–robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.
introduction:
Deploying robots in real-world settings requires the ability to interact
safely with unstructured surroundings. Under these conditions, the
environmental state is notoriously difficult to track and often impossible
to model accurately. Over the past four decades, interaction control has
evolved to manage both expected and unexpected physical contacts, ensuring
safe human-robot and robot-environment
interactions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
Until recently, these systems were largely confined to research
laboratories and highly specialised industrial contexts, where structured
environments and expert operators ensured proper deployment. However, there
is currently a strong push to introduce robots into unstructured domains
where operators may lack deep technical expertise. Consequently, learning
by demonstration (LbD) and, more recently, generative and agentic AI have
gained traction to bridge the skill gap in robot programming. Despite their
potential, the lack of robustness and explainability in these methods
raises significant safety concerns regarding their deployment near humans.
Furthermore, the extensive data and computational requirements of these
approaches raise critical questions regarding their environmental
sustainability and ethics.

Enhancing interaction control beyond the state-of-the-art to provide hard
safety guarantees and increased closed-loop dexterity is crucial prior to
integrating learning methods. This foundational improvement mitigates
safety risks, reduces reliance on data-driven approaches, and increases
sustainability by lowering computational overhead. At the foundation of
interaction control lie port-Hamiltonian controllers (i.e., impedance and
admittance control). Both approach the robot as an equivalent
mass-spring-damper system, acting as reciprocal formulations to each
other [1, 7]. Admittance control generates a flow command
from an effort error, while impedance control generates an effort command
from a flow error. These approaches carry opposite limitations: impedance
control excels at regulating position, whereas admittance control regulates
interaction force. Biological interaction control in humans and animals
naturally inspires robotic counterparts due to their ability to
effortlessly trade off between these skills during physical
interaction [8, 9, 10]. While variable
impedance control has been proposed to mimic this biological adaptability,
the stability challenges associated with these controllers have severely
limited their application in complex interactions and high-dimensional
systems [11, 12].

Fractal Impedance Control (FIC) [3] was introduced to
overcome these fundamental limitations. The controller relies on an
algorithmic formulation of a Liénard equation, which describes non-linear
systems such as Van der Pol oscillators [13]. The system generated by the FIC
acts as a critically damped, asymptotically stable attractor around the
desired state, defined algorithmically from an effort profile [3, 14].
Consequently, it enables the generation of asymptotically stable, passive
controllers that can be safely superposed and tuned online. FIC has
successfully demonstrated the capability to introduce an outer admittance
loop on top of a non-linear impedance controller, deployed within
biomimetic architectures for robust interaction in challenging dynamic
environments [4, 15]. Its intrinsically passive behaviour also yields excellent
performance despite significant feedback delays and low control
bandwidths, making it exceptionally well-suited for teleoperation
applications[3, 16, 4, 17].

This manuscript presents the integration of these theoretical advancements
into a unified library to support the development of FIC-based controllers
for manipulation and teleoperation. Notably, the library includes a robotic
implementation of the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), the most
advanced FIC architecture developed to model human motor control [18]. H-PMP can
autonomously trade off admittance and impedance behaviours without requiring
a rigid state machine or model-based interaction optimisation [18]. Furthermore,
the library is fully integrated with standard robotics infrastructure,
including MuJoCo for simulation, the Pinocchio library for inverse
kinematics optimisation, and ROS2. To streamline deployment, we introduce
FIC Studio—a user-friendly, modular Graphical User Interface (GUI) that
centralises these functionalities, featuring drag-and-drop controller
tuning and Python live scripting for high-level control integration. Fig. 1 shows the arm in two of the experiments for the evaluation of the interaction performance.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows:
Section II introduces related work.
Section III provides an overview of the FIC Suite functionalities.
Section IV describes the FIC library and the robotic
implementation of H-PMP. Section V presents an evaluation
comparing the proposed control architecture against an earlier
implementation of the Task-Space FIC. Finally,
Section VI draws the conclusions.

title: Time-Indexed Skill Success Models for Latency-Aware Skill Selection and Timing in Dynamic Manipulation
authors: Mohsen Omidi,Maria Chiara Leva,Brian Vaughan
comment: : 9-page letter with 4 figures and 2 tables, followed by of supplementary material (14 tables, 6 figures). Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
abstract:
Robots that manipulate moving objects act on observations that are outdated when the chosen skill starts, and
the best skill can change within a few hundred milliseconds. Skill competence models, however, predict success for a
launch at the moment of observation. We propose time-indexed skill success
models, which predict whole-task success when a skill is launched after a given delay. Trained on rollouts branched
at a grid of launch delays, they let a receding-horizon planner select both the skill and its launch time under fixed
or random latency. In a MuJoCo study in which a UR5e captures a sliding puck with three skills, the planner exceeded
a static competence model by 2.8 to 6.2 percentage points at 100 to 300 ms of latency, including when that model
was evaluated on point or sampled forecasts of the launch state. Across five complete runs (three training seeds and
two distribution shifts), all 80 paired 95% intervals against four baselines excluded zero. On delayed launches,
the time-indexed model was calibrated (expected calibration error 0.009 against 0.239), and pausing the world during
latency overstated success by up to 23 points. On a real UR5e that captures a rolling ball after 0.2 s of injected
latency, a static model trained in a hardware-matched simulator predicted 99% success on a prespecified subset of 35
delayed launches that it rated at least 0.8. Of these, 63% succeeded (95% interval 46 to 77%), and the
time-indexed model predicted 56%. In this single-skill, predictable regime, a matched physics-based forecast was
also well calibrated.
introduction:
Robots act on information that is already old. Between the exposure of a camera frame and the
first motion of a skill, the system transfers the image, estimates the state, runs inference and sends the command.
For current vision-language-action policies, this end-to-end latency is about 100 to 300 ms
[1, 2, 3]. When the object is at rest, the delay costs only time, but when
it moves, the robot acts in a world that differs from the one it observed. For example, a puck sliding at
0.5 m/s travels 5 cm in 100 ms, and an interception that was feasible at the moment of observation may no longer
be feasible when the skill starts.

Skill-based and task-and-motion planners select skills with learned competence models, such as initiation
classifiers, affordance values and success discriminators, which map the current state to the probability that a
skill succeeds [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. These
models estimate the success of a skill that starts immediately, which is not possible under latency. The planner
needs the probability that the task succeeds if skill kk starts after a delay τ\tau, which
includes the unavoidable latency and any extra wait that the planner chooses. Waiting is a real option in dynamic
tasks. A puck that is too fast to grasp may become graspable once friction has slowed it down, while an interception
that is possible now may soon expire (see Fig. 1).

The standard remedy for delay is prediction, as in delay-compensated control [9] and in robot
policies that condition on the state rolled forward to execution time [10, 11]. At the skill
level, the equivalent is to evaluate a static competence model on a forecast of the launch state. We show that this is
exact only in expectation over the forecast distribution and that the error of a point forecast grows with the
forecast spread relative to the tolerance of the skill. With several skills, even sampled forecasts recovered only
part of the loss in our experiments.

In this letter, we therefore learn skill competence as a function of the launch delay. A time-indexed skill
success model Gk​(z,τ)G_{k}(z,\tau) predicts the probability that the whole task succeeds when skill kk is launched τ\tau
seconds after the observation of the decision state zz. The letter makes three contributions. First, we formulate skill
competence as a function of the decision state and the launch delay, and relate it to static models evaluated on
forecasts, which shows when a forecast is sufficient (Section III). Second, we introduce branched
rollouts that give exact training labels for delayed launches, and a receding-horizon planner that selects the skill
and its launch time under fixed or random latency (Section IV). Third, we compare the approach with
static, forecast-based and rule-based planners in a simulation whose clock keeps running during latency, with
replication over seeds and distribution shifts, a calibration analysis and a frozen-clock comparison
(Sections V and VI), and we test the predicted calibration gap on a real UR5e
(Section VII). Unlike delay-aware continuous policies, the approach works at the level of skill
selection and decides which skill to launch and when from an estimate of whole-task success.

title: AffordJEV: Affordance Grounding by Confirming Candidate Regions
authors: Jincheng Li,Yutian Zhang,Jianyu Zhang,Xinshun Wang,Mengyuan Liu
abstract:
Affordance grounding asks which visible part of an object performs a requested operation, a basic capability for
embodied manipulation and human–robot interaction. Most existing methods follow a System Two paradigm: a
multimodal language model first writes a chain of thought and then turns its conclusion into a box or points for a
segmenter. This incurs considerable inference cost, gives the semantic decision little direct control over the
extent of the final region, and makes mistakes hard to correct. Yet locating an affordance is essentially a
perceptual judgment that need not be argued out in words. We therefore propose AffordJEV, in which frozen segmenters
propose candidate regions and a System One model decides directly which of them perform the operation, generating
no text and reading each decision from a single forward pass. Our contributions are twofold. (1) An inference
framework that confirms candidate regions level by level, from object to part to sub-part, with evidence passed
between the levels in both directions so that the levels correct one another. (2) A System One model trained for
this framework: existing System One models are built for general-purpose decisions, judge one candidate per
request and are ill-suited to the framework’s region questions, so ours learns directly from the requests the
framework itself produces and judges all candidates of a level at once. Trained only on InstructPart and evaluated
with definition-aligned operation words, AffordJEV outperforms chain-of-thought methods in domain and in zero-shot transfer to UMD and IIT-AFF, is better overall
than existing System One models run in the same framework, and needs fewer judge requests. To our knowledge,
AffordJEV is the first approach to bring System One models to affordance grounding.
introduction:
A robot asked to cut with a knife needs the blade, not merely a correctly recognized knife. Affordance grounding connects an object and an intended operation to the visible surface that performs it. The output must be spatially precise, but the difficulty is mostly semantic: a handle, a working surface, and the support under an object are all clean segments, and only one of them serves the requested operation.

A popular recipe is to let a multimodal language model reason about the request before answering. Affordance-R1 [42] and VisionReasoner [26] write a reasoning trace, decode a box or points, and hand them to a segmenter. This is a System Two procedure in the sense of Kahneman [17]: slow, sequential, and general. Yet grounding an affordance rarely calls for deliberation. People do not need to think in words to find the handle of a mug; they look at the mug and then at its parts. This suggests a System One alternative in which segmenters propose regions and a judge scores them directly, reading its decision from a single forward pass instead of decoding text. The alternative is already competitive: placed in our region pipeline without any fine-tuning, the released Valen-4B judge [40] reaches 75.0% gIoU on UMD [29], against 63.9% for Affordance-R1 under aligned operation words (Tabs. 2 and 1).

Such a pipeline must still decide what to ask the judge. One question over every region of an image is fragile:
the queried part is small, regions of other objects compete with it, and a wrong object is never corrected. People
narrow down instead, and they revise: if no part of the chosen object fits the operation, the object was probably
wrong. Our first contribution turns this into an inference framework. The judge confirms the object, selects its
parts and refines them with sub-parts, and its verdicts pass between the levels: weak part evidence under an unsure
object reopens the object decision, and sub-part verdicts trim an accepted part or rescue a rejected one. Every step
asks a question of the same form — which of these regions answer the query — so one judge serves all levels.

Within this framework, what limits accuracy is not the candidates but the interface through which they are judged.
On the regions our frozen segmenters propose, a judge that accepted exactly the candidates lying mostly inside the
ground truth would reach 77.677.6 gIoU on InstructPart; the released Valen-4B extracts 51.551.5 from the same regions,
and the strongest System Two model reaches 59.559.5. The judges used for this are general-purpose decision models built
for arbitrary multiple-choice questions: they see one candidate per request, learn its identity from a marker
painted into the image, pool the whole context into a single vector in which a small part is diluted, and score
through a head trained from scratch on millions of unrelated decisions. None of these choices follows from the task.

Our second contribution is a judge built for the framework’s questions. Each candidate becomes one token, pooled
from the vision encoder’s own output over its mask and given its geometry, so the judge reads the pixels a candidate
covers instead of a drawn marker. All candidates of a level share one sequence and one forward pass, and a small set
block lets them see one another, because the framework outputs the union of what it accepts. The score is the
projection of the readout state on the model’s own Yes−-No embeddings, which adds no parameters
and lets the judge be trained from the raw Qwen3.5-4B weights [33]: before any training it already
separates parts at AUROC 0.6180.618. We train it on the candidates the frozen segmenters produce on the training photos,
at every level the framework asks about, with each candidate’s purity as the target that acceptance at 0.50.5 needs.

Comparing judges fairly required care. We retrained Valen and JevAny with their own native heads and losses on our
object and part groups, from the same raw weights and with matched optimisation settings. We also found that the
same operation word names different regions in different datasets — InstructPart marks a vessel’s body for
grasp, UMD and IIT-AFF a tool’s handle — so a judge that fits the training convention better is penalised
for it on transfer. We therefore report a frozen definition-aligned protocol alongside the original words.

Our contributions are:

An inference framework that grounds affordances by confirming candidate regions level by level — object,
part, sub-part — with evidence passed between the levels in both directions, so that one judge answering one form
of question serves the whole hierarchy. Removing evidence passing lowers in-domain gIoU from 70.470.4 to 65.765.7.

title: TactileLab: Sim-to-Real Dexterous Robot Manipulation with Efficient Shear-Sensitive Tactile Simulation
authors: Yijiong Lin,Wenhao He,Toby Jack,Max Yang,Haoran Li,Nathan F. Lepora
abstract:
Robotic simulators that represent shear within tactile sensing are becoming increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation. However, simulating contact shear with high-fidelity deformable or soft-body simulation is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large-scale reinforcement learning. Here we introduce TactileLab, a scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework built on IsaacLab, with a particular focus on a new optical-flow-based tactile representation termed simulated tactile flow. Instead of relying on soft-body physics to model shear deformation, TactileLab uses rigid-body simulation to efficiently estimate dense tangential motion at the contact interface, producing tactile flow fields that encode shear-relevant contact dynamics. This flow field complements geometric features from a contact depth field. We further introduce a novel policy architecture for jointly processing long-horizon proprioceptive signals and rich tactile observations. Across multiple contact-rich tasks, policies trained using simulated tactile flow learn efficiently at scale and exhibit emergent contact-aware behaviours. To facilitate sim-to-real policy deployment, we then propose a novel real-to-sim tactile translation method that maps real tactile image streams to simulated tactile flow and depth fields, together with a new tactile data collection method, and validate it across diverse tactile sensor designs. Using this pipeline, we demonstrate real-world deployment on tasks encompassing dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation. Overall, TactileLab provides an end-to-end sim-to-real framework for scalable tactile policy learning, enabling diverse shear-sensitive manipulation across heterogeneous tactile robotic systems.
Project webpage: https://yijionglin.github.io/tactilelab/
introduction:
Tactile sensing provides local, contact-grounded feedback that is essential for fine manipulation tasks. This is the case when a robot must finely regulate interaction forces such as to maintain contact or respond to small changes at the contact interface. For such tasks, vision-based tactile sensors are attractive because they provide high-resolution and highly-sensitive spatial observations. However, scalable simulation methods still struggle to represent tangential interaction efficiently, which is needed for tasks that depend on shear forces.

Most existing tactile simulators fall into two categories: 1) soft-body simulators can model compliant contact with high fidelity [1, 2, 3], but can be too slow for large-scale reinforcement learning; 2) rigid-body simulators are fast and scalable, but usually provide only depth-like signals [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. As a result, they are well suited for normal-contact reasoning but less effective for tasks in which shear, slip, or tangential motion matters. This limitation is important for manipulation problems such as in-contact trajectory following, insertion, and in-hand object manipulation in the presence of external perturbations. Depth-only observations cannot fully capture contact dynamics over time: similar depth signals may correspond to different contact states and future outcomes, making the task partially observable and harder for policies to learn. Because of this, recent tactile simulators have modelled distributed normal and shear feedback by relying on geometry-dependent contact formulations and object-specific preprocessing [9, 10]. Here we introduce a new way to instead calculate dense shear cues directly from rigid-body simulation without those assumptions, using a novel optical-flow-based tactile representation that we term simulated tactile flow.

This new flow representation allows us to address the gap of efficient shear-sensitive tactile simulation and robot learning, by introducing TactileLab: a complete sim-to-real framework that augments rigid-body tactile sensing with a dense tangential displacement field. Rather than explicitly simulating elastomer deformation, the framework represents contact using two complementary components: normal-contact depth and a tangential-displacement vector field. This combination gives a compact and sim-to-real transferable tactile observation that is efficient to compute, maps onto various tactile sensor designs, and is suitable for large-scale reinforcement learning.

Our main contributions are as follows:

1. A scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework for contact-rich manipulation:
TactileLab is built on top of IsaacLab [11] and supports GPU-parallel simulation for efficient reinforcement learning. It provides multiple tactile sensing modalities, including contact forces, contact positions, contact depth images, and simulated tactile flow, allowing researchers to study both low-dimensional and high-dimensional tactile feedback within a unified framework.

2. A novel simulated tactile modality for shear-relevant contact interaction:
We introduce simulated tactile flow, an optical-flow-inspired tactile modality that represents dense tangential motion at the contact interface. Together with contact depth, simulated tactile flow provides complementary high-dimensional tactile observations of normal contact geometry and tangential contact motion, enabling policies to exploit shear-relevant cues without explicit soft-body simulation.

3. A diverse suite of tactile robotic manipulation environments:
TactileLab provides a set of contact-rich robotic environments for single-arm, dual-arm, and dexterous in-hand manipulation. These show the scalability and generality of TactileLab for policy learning with high-dimensional contact-depth and tactile flow observations. We conduct detailed simulation studies on two representative tasks: dual-arm object following and dexterous in-hand object manipulation.

4. A new sample-efficient policy architecture for fusing proprioceptive history and tactile observations:
We propose PETS-Net (Positional-Encoding Temporal-Spatial Network) for encoding long-horizon low-dimensional proprioceptive histories and fusing them with high-dimensional tactile observations. Experimental results show that PETS-Net learns more efficiently than baseline policy architectures, demonstrating the benefit of jointly encoding temporal robot-state histories and spatial tactile features for contact-rich manipulation.

5. A new real-to-sim tactile transfer method for multimodal tactile observations:
Building on a previous static transfer method for single tactile images, we propose separate real-to-sim translators for contact depth and tactile flow. Specifically, the tactile-flow translator takes real tactile image streams as input and predicts simulated tactile flow, extending real-to-sim transfer from static contact-depth reconstruction to dynamic tangential-motion representations. We further validate the real-to-sim pipeline across diverse tactile sensor designs, demonstrating its applicability beyond a single sensor configuration.

6. Real-world deployment of TactileLab-trained policies:
Using the proposed multimodal tactile simulation and real-to-sim transfer pipeline, we demonstrate successful real-world deployment of policies trained in TactileLab on two representative contact-rich manipulation tasks: dual-arm object following and dexterous in-hand object manipulation. These results demonstrate the applicability of the TactileLab framework across distinct robotic embodiments and manipulation settings.

TactileLab will be released as an open-source framework to lower the barrier to entry to tactile robot learning, enable reproducible research, and accelerate progress in tactile robotics.

title: Learning Robotic World Models with Semantic and Visual Feedback
authors: Hao Wu,Yuqi Li,Yizhou Zhao,Kun Wang,Xiao Luo,Yu Cheng,Bo An,Yingli Tian,Laszlo A. Jeni,Ming-Hsuan Yang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

abstract: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.
introduction:
Robot world models predict how scenes evolve under actions, enabling robots to assess potential outcomes before execution [1, 2, 3, 4]. As learnable internal simulators, they support planning, policy evaluation, and long-horizon reasoning [5, 6, 7, 8]. Unlike generic video generation, which primarily emphasizes visual quality, robot world models must capture action-induced state changes, object contacts, and interactions to provide reliable guidance for manipulation decisions [9, 10]. Visual observations describe the current scene, action sequences specify the execution process, and natural-language instructions provide task goals; together, they form the multimodal context for understanding and predicting robot interactions. Prediction quality therefore depends not only on visual fidelity, but also on how accurately the model captures physical evolution under the given actions and its relationship to the task goal [11, 12].

However, evaluating predicted futures remains a central challenge in training robot world models. Existing methods typically use maximum-likelihood, reconstruction, or perceptual objectives [10, 13, 14, 15]. These objectives provide effective visual supervision, but visual similarity alone does not fully capture task-relevant changes. For example, a prediction that preserves scene appearance may still miss action-induced object displacement or changes in contact. Conversely, multimodal semantic evaluation assesses visible task progress using instructions and scene context, yet may be insufficiently sensitive to local structural distortions and fine-grained appearance errors. As Figure 1 illustrates, visual fidelity and task semantics provide complementary perspectives on prediction quality. Aligning robot world models therefore calls for both forms of feedback: constraining visual detail while assessing whether predicted state transitions are plausible under the given actions and task conditions.

Prior work explores reward-based post-training for robotic world models [16]. RLVR-World rewards action-conditioned forecasts using visual prediction metrics [10]. RoboAlign-R1 [17] distills a vision–language judge into a lightweight reward model that scores individual generated videos. Such semantic feedback motivates a broader question: how should alternative futures be constructed and evaluated to provide informative learning signals? Absolute video scores require calibration across scenes and tasks, whereas futures generated under shared observations, actions, and instructions can be compared directly for visible task progress. However, nearly identical candidates provide little basis for comparison, and semantic preferences alone may overlook local visual errors. Effective comparative learning must therefore address both candidate construction and feedback design. We investigate how diverse candidate futures and complementary semantic and visual feedback jointly shape the learning of robotic world models.

We propose RoboImagine, a framework for learning autoregressive robotic world models by comparing candidate futures with semantic and visual feedback. Conditioned on visual observations, actions, and task instructions, grouped diverse beam search (GDBS) [18] constructs alternative trajectories under shared inputs. A frozen multimodal evaluator, mJev (hereafter Jev) [19], compares candidate videos for visible task progress using the instruction and initial observation; evaluating both presentation orders mitigates position bias. Pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback [20] complements these preferences by constraining fine-grained prediction errors. The two signals are standardized across candidates and combined into group-relative advantages for policy optimization [21]. Each branch retains fixed initial context and a dynamic anchor together with its own rolling state–action history. This bounded history supports continued generation, while replaying the recorded history keeps policy scoring consistent with the conditions under which each candidate is generated.

We evaluate separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, and conduct controlled studies of post-training, candidate search, feedback composition, and memory. On RT-1, comparative post-training improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning from the same initialization for the same number of updates, at a higher computational cost. Visual-only feedback achieves the strongest visual metrics in the reward ablation, whereas combined feedback yields a higher external multimodal evaluation mean while retaining comparable visual fidelity. Long-horizon evaluations further assess the benefits of rolling history and the associated inference costs. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

❶Learning robot world models by comparing imagined futures. We introduce RoboImagine, which couples GDBS with comparative post-training under shared observations, actions, and instructions. Bounded branch-specific histories support autoregressive rollouts and are replayed during policy scoring to preserve conditioning consistency.

❷Complementary semantic preference and visual consistency feedback. A frozen multimodal judge evaluates pairwise task progress among candidates with bidirectional comparisons to mitigate order bias, while pixel- and perceptual-level consistency feedback constrains fine-grained visual errors. Group-wise standardization and relative advantages translate both signals into policy updates without backpropagating through the evaluator or the video decoder.

❸Evaluation of prediction quality and learning mechanisms. Experiments on three manipulation datasets assess visual prediction and task-level consistency. Controlled RT-1 comparisons isolate the effects of additional supervised training, feedback composition, and candidate search, while long-horizon and window-size studies characterize the quality and inference cost of bounded memory.

title: A Sequential Framework for Urban Drone Delivery: Network Design, Vehicle Sizing, and Energy and Cost Assessment
authors: Hong-Su Nam,Seokhwan Lee,Jungwoo Cho,Hak-Tae Lee
abstract: A sequential engineering framework is presented for urban drone delivery, linking hub location, route planning, mission-specific vehicle sizing, and energy and operating cost assessment. Aggregate origin–destination demand is assumed known a priori. For each hub configuration, the maximum required link distance is minimized, and feasible routes that return to their departure hubs are generated. Route frequencies are determined using mixed-integer linear programming to satisfy delivery demand. The resulting range requirement guides motor–propeller selection and battery sizing to minimize vehicle takeoff mass. Flight distances and frequencies, cruise performance, and vehicle dimensions are combined to estimate monthly energy consumption, fleet size, hub area, staffing, and operating cost. The framework is applied to district-level Seoul delivery data. Increasing the number of hubs from one to four reduces the required range from 30.6 to 21.9 km and vehicle takeoff mass from 8.12 to 6.12 kg. Despite a 21.5% increase in total flight distance, monthly flight energy consumption decreases by 13.1%, from 15.2 to 13.2 MWh. Battery replacement is the largest vehicle-related operating expense, while operating cost per delivery increases from USD 1.18 to USD 2.20 because of higher rent and labor costs at the hubs. Among the designs evaluated, range-matched vehicles achieve the lowest operating cost in the two- and four-hub networks; a longer-range vehicle is least costly in the three-hub network. Sensitivity analyses further examine the effects of delivery demand and operating assumptions. The results demonstrate that reductions in vehicle mass and energy consumption do not necessarily lead to lower system operating cost.
introduction:
E-commerce and on-demand delivery have increased interest in fast and flexible last-mile transportation. Drones can operate independently of the road network and have been studied in terms of efficiency, accessibility, and sustainability[1, 2, 3]. However, the feasibility and cost of urban drone delivery depend on numerous technical and operational factors. These include vehicle range and energy consumption, hub locations, fleet size, and facility and staffing costs. Furthermore, these factors are not independent, and changes in one may affect several others.

Quadrotor drones are considered in this study because their vertical takeoff and landing capabilities and ability to hover are advantageous for urban delivery. However, their relatively low cruise efficiency compared with fixed-wing aircraft limits their flight range. Consequently, the distances between delivery hubs and service locations become important factors in vehicle design, as longer required ranges generally lead to larger batteries and heavier vehicles.

For example, increasing the number of hubs may reduce the required flight range and allow lighter vehicles, but it may also increase facility and staffing costs while changing fleet requirements. Such competing effects motivate an integrated assessment of network design, vehicle sizing, energy consumption, and operating costs.

Drone routing research addresses cooperation between transportation modes and vehicle energy constraints. Murray and Chu[4] formulated a drone-assisted delivery routing problem, and Agatz et al.[5] investigated optimization approaches for the traveling salesman problem with a drone. Dorling et al.[6] incorporated energy consumption dependent on battery and payload mass, together with drone reuse, into route planning. Other studies have addressed cost minimization in truck–drone cooperation[7] and extensions of operating range using public transportation networks[8, 9, 10]. These studies demonstrate the importance of linking feasible routes and energy use when evaluating delivery plans.

Facility and network studies relate flight range and base locations to service coverage and routing. Hong et al.[11] considered the coverage of recharging facilities under range restrictions, whereas Pinto and Lagorio[12] addressed point-to-point drone delivery networks with intermediate charging stations. Liu[13] evaluated a battery-constrained depot network through optimization and simulation. Studies of facility coverage and capacity[14] and delivery routing with parcel lockers[15] also connect transportation infrastructure with route planning. These contributions provide a basis for evaluating networks in which facility location and vehicle range constraints interact.

Research on urban-scale operations has expanded to corridor and route-network design[16, 17, 18], risk-aware unmanned aerial vehicle traffic networks[19], urban airspace availability assessment [20, 21] and very-low-level traffic-density estimation[22]. Online demand planning[23], consumer delivery preferences[24], third-party ground-risk assessment[25], and barriers to urban air mobility adoption[26] further highlight the role of demand, safety, and institutional conditions.

Doole et al.[22] estimated drone-based food-delivery costs of 0.40–2.51 EUR per meal order across scenarios that included annualized investment and operating costs. Bao et al.[27] estimated 4.17 EUR per parcel in a 200-customer-node scenario using a five-year total-cost-of-ownership model that included vehicle and battery acquisition, labor, and infrastructure costs. Differences in service units, operating assumptions, and cost coverage limit direct comparisons of these estimates. Moreover, the effects of network-dependent range requirements on component level vehicle design, and their subsequent implications for energy consumption, fleet requirements, and hub operating costs, have received comparatively limited attention.

This paper presents a sequential engineering framework for assessing how network design affects vehicle sizing, energy use, and operating cost in urban drone delivery. Building on the framework introduced by Nam and Lee at the AIAA AVIATION 2026 Forum [28], the present study details how hub locations determine the range required for route planning and vehicle sizing. The resulting flight plan and vehicle performance are then used to estimate fleet size, hub staffing, energy consumption, and operating cost. Vehicle sizing and performance evaluation are based on the approaches of Jeong[29], Pollet et al.[30], and Nam et al.[31].

The sizing estimates are compared with commercial drone specifications. Ground-delivery data from Seoul, Republic of Korea, provide a case study to demonstrate the framework and examine whether the cost rankings of hub configurations change with demand and operating assumptions.

The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows:

A closely linked framework is established to integrate network design, flight-route optimization, component-based vehicle sizing, and energy consumption and operating cost assessment. The sequential procedure explicitly accounts for the interdependencies among these stages.

The framework is applied to Seoul using actual ground delivery data. Increasing the number of hubs from one to four reduces vehicle mass and total flight energy consumption despite an increase in total flight distance, but increases operating cost per delivery from USD 1.18 to USD 2.20. Comparisons across vehicle designs show that minimum-mass designs do not necessarily minimize operating cost because vehicle range also affects flight frequency and staffing requirements.

The effects of delivery demand, operating hours, component lifetimes, hub area, and staffing are examined to assess the robustness of operating cost comparisons. The one-hub configuration remains the least costly across the evaluated parameter ranges, although the relative cost rankings of multiple-hub configurations can change.

Section II introduces the delivery system and the framework. Section III presents hub location and flight-route planning, and Section IV describes vehicle sizing and performance evaluation. Section V uses their outputs to calculate energy consumption, fleet size, hub space, staffing, and operating costs. Section VI presents the Seoul baseline, comparisons across vehicle designs, propulsion selection, and sensitivity results. Section VII concludes the paper.

title: Flexible Piezoelectric Tactile Sensing System for Intelligent Object Recognition
authors: Razan Khalifeh,Mohamad Yaacoub,Christian Gianoglio,Moustafa Saleh,Maurizio Valle,Yahya Abbass
abstract:
By providing direct information about the physical properties of objects (e.g., texture and shape), tactile sensing often outperforms vision-based solutions in enabling safe, efficient grasping to enhance robot-object interaction. Numerous approaches to object recognition have been proposed; however, reliable recognition during the early stage of grasping under strict real-time constraints remains a significant challenge.
In this study, we propose a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system designed for early-stage and real-time object recognition in robotic grasping. The system was experimentally validated using six representative daily-life objects. Tactile signals acquired during the robot grasping of objects were leveraged to develop and compare three recognition approaches: (i) feature- based learning using Support Vector Machines (SVM), (ii) raw signal learning using 1D Convolutional Neural Networks (1D-CNN) and Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (C- RNN), and (iii) a spatio-temporal heatmap representation processed with a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (2D-CNN). Moreover, a comprehensive quantitative analysis was conducted to evaluate the influence of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition performance and real-time feasibility.
Results demonstrated that increasing the number of sensing elements substantially enhances the recognition performance of all approaches. For the best-performing approach, specifically the spatio-temporal heatmap representation combined with the 2D-CNN, the F1-score improved from 0.9796 (16 sensors) to 0.9846 (24 sensors), reaching 0.9903 when all 32 sensors were included. The optimal configuration (32 sensors, 100 ms temporal window, corresponding to 50 tactile samples) was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of ≈\approx 101 ms from contact onset, with an energy consumption of 63.8 µJ per inference. These results underscore the effectiveness of the proposed distributed flexible tactile sensing system for fast, embedded, and early-stage object recognition, highlighting its strong potential for real-time robotic manipulation applications.
introduction:
Tactile perception in robotics plays a crucial role in sensing the environment and enabling effective interaction with objects. Many robotic systems demand the ability to perceive reaction forces, detect contact, manipulate objects, and safely interact with the environment [1]. This is especially true in emerging domains like bio-inspired soft robotics, where robotic sensing systems are engineered from materials that mimic the soft human skin [2]. However, to fully mimic the sensing capability of human skin, it is essential to develop a sensing system that can detect various physical quantities and process tactile information in real-time [3].

Although several approaches have been developed for object recognition [11], most of them rely on vision [12]. However, vision sensors may encounter difficulties in data collection, such as when handling transparent objects, and properties of objects including stiffness, hardness, and texture, which cannot be effectively perceived using vision sensors [13]. In contrast to vision sensors, tactile sensors overcome these limitations and acquire information through direct physical contact with the object; their lower data dimensionality compared to visual sensors makes them more suitable for real-time processing in embedded systems [14]. To obtain meaningful tactile information of grasped objects, the sensor design must align with the specific requirements [15]. For instance, object exploration demands sensors with a wide dynamic range, high sensitivity, and fast response time [16]. Recently, in [17], artificial sensing systems were developed. These systems are based on flexible sensors and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies for force measurement, grasp stability analysis, and tactile-based object recognition, highlighting the importance of combining sensing technologies and AI methods to achieve breakthroughs in tactile intelligence. Among numerous tactile sensing technologies, piezoresistive, capacitive, and piezoelectric sensors have been intensively developed [18]. These tactile sensing technologies are commonly used in robotic manipulation, prosthetic, and human-robot interaction applications for tasks including object recognition, force estimation, and slippage detection [18].
However, in most of these sensing technologies, the sensor response is often complex (e.g., noisy, non-linear, or multidimensional), making it difficult to extract meaningful information using conventional methods such as handcrafted features or thresholding. To address this, signal processing techniques, such as filtering, wavelet transforms, and principal component analysis (PCA), have been employed to denoise signals, extract relevant features, and enhance data quality [19, 20].

Machine learning (ML) has become an essential factor in enhancing the functionality of artificial sensing system by improving data processing and pattern recognition [21].
When tactile signals are extracted and processed using signal processing techniques, ML methods become essential to interpret pattern recognition in real time. These advanced techniques help in interpreting complex tactile signals collected from different sensors, making tactile sensors more efficient and effective in robotic and prosthetic applications [22].
Thus, these techniques serve as a preprocessing step before applying ML and deep learning (DL) algorithms, which have been widely used to improve object recognition[23, 24].
ML and DL algorithms such as support vector machine (SVM), convolutional neural network (CNN), and long short term memory (LSTM) are commonly used to analyze and classify tactile data. This enables robots equipped with tactile sensing system to perform tasks (i.e, object recognition), mimicking the perception of human skin [21].

Methodologies combining tactile sensors and learning methods have been widely applied in the literature. As an example, Drimus et al.[4] developed a tactile sensor array based on flexible piezoresistive rubber. The sensor consists of an 8×\times8 array of distributed taxels, providing a spatial resolution of approximately 2.5 mm per taxel.
Two sensors were mounted on the fingers of a robotic gripper to demonstrate the system’s ability to distinguish between rigid and deformable objects through squeezing. The study also examined the impact of the number of sensors on the recognition performance, revealing a proportional relationship between object recognition and the number of sensors. To classify 10 rigid and deformable objects, a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) algorithm was implemented.
A piezoresistive tactile sensor with a spatial resolution of 27.6 taxels/cm2 was introduced in [5]. The sensor has 1400 tactels producing pressure images during contact with objects.
Integrated into a robotic arm, the sensor captured pressure images to facilitate the recognition of 22 different objects. Several convolutional neural network (CNN) based models were used for object classification. Moreover, authors in [6] presented a 16×\times16 piezoresistive tactile sensor array for object recognition for humanoid robot hand with a spatial resolution of 3.5 mm. The sensor captures tactile images when the robot hand touches objects. Several DL algorithms were implemented to recognize 20 objects.

Capacitive technology is widely used among sensing transducers and has been extensively applied in robotic applications [1]. For example, authors in [7] proposed a flexible capacitive sensor for recognizing objects during grasping. The sensors were mounted on the five fingers of a robotic hand to grasp five different objects. A Support Vector Machine (SVM) and CNN algorithms were implemented to classify the objects. In [8], a 4×\times4 flexible capacitive tactile sensor array with a spatial resolution of 2 mm was presented. Each array consists of 16 sensors, and four arrays were mounted on a robotic hand with two fingers (two arrays per finger). The proposed system was evaluated for tactile-based material recognition, considering three materials for an easier classification task and five material classes for a more challenging scenario. Several dimensionality reduction techniques, including Multidimensional Scaling (MDS), PCA, and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), were applied and subsequently fed into two ML models, including SVM and k-NN.
Experimental results demonstrated that the best-performing pipeline (MDS + SVM) performs better in the three-material task than in the five-material classification.

Piezoelectric sensors are widely used due to their unique properties [25]. Many studies have used piezoelectric materials as tactile sensors [26, 9]. In [9], a signle bionic tactile sensor was fabricated from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) piezoelectric film for recognizing object properties, including surface softness and texture roughness. The sensor was mounted on the fingertip of a robotic manipulator and used to collect tactile signals when touching and sliding over object surfaces. Eight time-domain features were extracted and fed into neural network classifiers.
Chung et al. [10] developed a tactile sensing module comprising two PVDF films one functioning as an actuator and the other as a sensor mounted at a single contact point on a robotic hand. During grasping, the actuator excites the object with a frequency-swept signal, and the resulting vibration response is measured to compute a frequency-response-based feature vector of 1000 frequency-domain components, which is directly fed into a fully connected neural network (i.e, MLP) classifier to recognize 17 objects.

Table I provides an overview of the most relevant existing works in the literature on tactile-based object recognition.

Despite notable progress, most of the existing sensing systems exhibit at least one limitation, including rigidity, which prevents integration into soft grippers, bulk hardware requirements, and a high computational cost due to the processing of high-resolution tactile images [5, 6]. Moreover, the presented studies do not report hardware deployment and end-to-end system latency, both of which are critical for real-time robotic manipulation tasks such as object handling.

For real-time applications, time segmentation allows the system to analyze streaming data efficiently and make timely predictions [27]. Moreover, object recognition at the early stage of robot grasping is important, as it allows the robot to assess the object’s properties at the moment of contact, enabling the optimization of the manipulation strategy. Therefore, selecting an appropriate window size is crucial to ensure that object recognition is fast enough for real-time interaction and precise enough to support reliable and safe interaction with objects.
While multiple studies in the literature address object recognition in robotic applications, they neglect the systematic evaluation of the number of tactile sensors required to attain high recognition performance. Similarly, the choice of window size WW for real-time applications is rarely analyzed, despite its direct impact on system responsiveness, accuracy, and computational efficiency. A segmentation technique is needed, enabling a tactile system to capture local temporal features.
In addition, for accurate object recognition, robotic grippers must integrate multi-point electronic skin (e-skin). Given the increasing demand for tactile sensors that are flexible, sensitive, and suitable for real-time object recognition, it is essential to integrate advanced materials with efficient signal processing and learning algorithms.

In this study, we present a flexible piezoelectric sensing system for recognizing daily-life objects at the early stage of grasping. The piezoelectric system combines flexible sensing arrays and multichannel embedded electronics. Two arrays, each of 16 sensors, were used to develop soft, customizable, and wearable sensing caps that can be mounted on robotic end-effectors. We describe the integration process and present the electrical characterization of the sensor arrays. To demonstrate the system’s effectiveness, a representative dataset was collected by recording the sensors’ response while grasping 6 daily-life objects. The dataset was used for processing and recognizing patterns in tactile information, through the development of ML and DL methods for object recognition.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as
follows:

We present a customizable, soft, and flexible piezoelectric sensing arrays with a wide frequency bandwidth and high sensitivity. The system was mounted on the TIAGo grippers, to grasp daily-life objects.

We present a customizable, soft, and flexible piezoelectric sensing arrays with a wide frequency bandwidth and high sensitivity. The system was mounted on the TIAGo grippers, to grasp daily-life objects.

We propose approaches to assess the capability of the proposed sensing system in enabling object recognition at the early stages of grasping.

We present a signal preprocessing framework to process tactile data as sequential input. Within this framework, a feature extraction method was implemented, and a systematic evaluation was conducted to assess the effect number of sensor needed for accurate recognition.

We assessed the impact of signal time segmentation to enable the system to capture local temporal features.
Based on this, a real-time recognition system is also introduced to demonstrate the capability of the system in performing object recognition at the earliest stage of grasping.
