title: Wedge-Jamming Mechanism for String Configuration
authors: Taro Tako,Takanori Jin,Hiroshi Kaminaga,Taisuke Kobayashi
comment: conference
abstract:
Variable stiffness mechanisms that achieve both flexibility and rigidity are important technologies for robotic systems.
Recently, wire-based jamming mechanisms have attracted significant attention.
In the wire-based jamming mechanisms, modules are chained by a wire, and the overall stiffness is controlled by changing the friction between the modules through wire tension.
These mechanisms have been widely studied due to their simple structure and controllability.
However, conventional wire-based jamming mechanisms mainly focus on holding torque along the joint axis, and the resistance against disturbances in other directions has not been sufficiently explored.
In this study, we propose a wedge-jamming mechanism that introduces wedge-shaped contact surfaces into the modules of wire-based jamming structures.
By changing the wedge angle, the holding characteristics against disturbances in different directions can be adjusted.
Experimental results show that an out-wedge configuration improves resistance to vertical disturbances, while an in-wedge configuration enhances resistance to torsional disturbances.
These results demonstrate that the anisotropic holding performance of wire-based jamming mechanisms depend on wedge geometry.
introduction:
In humans, force transmission is achieved through the musculoskeletal system, consisting of muscles, tendons, and the skeletal structure.
This system enables a balance between flexibility and stiffness, which are inherently conflicting properties.
Flexibility allows safe interaction with external forces and impacts, whereas stiffness is essential for efficient force transmission and accurate positioning[1].

Replicating this balance in robotic systems requires mechanisms capable of adapting their stiffness according to task demands.
Therefore, variable stiffness mechanisms play a crucial role in robotic systems[2].

Among various variable stiffness mechanisms, wire-based linear structures have attracted attention due to their simple mechanical design and high controllability.
Such mechanisms have been widely applied to robotic hands and grippers[3][4][5].
In these systems, multiple modules are chained by a wire.
By changing the wire tension, the frictional forces between adjacent modules are modified, resulting in variable stiffness characteristics accordingly.

However, the holding performance of wire-based variable stiffness mechanisms remains limited, particularly under high external loads.
To address this issue, this study proposes a novel module design based on a wedge-shaped structure for variable stiffness mechanisms using linear configurations.
The proposed design enhances holding performance by effectively increasing frictional forces under load.
The effectiveness of the proposed mechanism is evaluated through analytical modeling and experimental validation.

title: Dual-Arm Tabletop Rearrangement with Movable Stacking and Gap-Aware Push Transfers
authors: Mohammadreza Firoozalizadeh,Zakiye Rostamirad,Arman Barghi,Ahmad Kalhor,Mohammadreza Nayeri,Mehdi Tale Masouleh
abstract: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.
introduction:
The ability of an autonomous agent to physically interact with its environment and modify object configurations is central to embodied AI [1]. Object rearrangement is a canonical task in this area because it couples perception, planning, and contact-rich manipulation under geometric constraints. In tabletop settings, the problem becomes especially challenging in cluttered scenes, where limited free space and overlap between start and goal poses often require intermediate buffers and multi-step relocations [2, 3].

Object rearrangement in clutter is inherently combinatorial because resolving occlusions among multiple objects requires reasoning over action sequences rather than single-step feasibility [2]. Search-based planners have therefore been widely studied for cluttered manipulation [3]. Among them, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) balances exploration and exploitation [5] and has shown strong performance on large discrete rearrangement action spaces [6, 7].

Extending rearrangement planning to dual-arm systems introduces an additional coordination challenge. Although two manipulators can improve efficiency through parallelism, they also create tighter coupling in shared workspaces: an action useful for one arm may obstruct the other, and naive coordination can cause deadlocks when free space is scarce [8]. These interactions become more severe in dense layouts, where each relocation affects later action feasibility.

Many dual-arm methods rely on heuristic coordination, dependency reasoning, or task-and-motion planning frameworks [7, 9, 10]. In many of them, as illustrated in Fig. 2, inter-arm exchange is handled through a fixed handoff configuration, restricting where objects can cross the shared boundary and often forcing both manipulators to meet at a specific location within overlapping reach. This coupling can reduce transfer flexibility, especially in cluttered scenes. As summarized in Table I, representative prior frameworks differ not only in robot setting and planning backbone, but also in coordination style, transfer mechanism, and the assumptions underlying rearrangement execution. To relax this limitation, asynchronous planning and execution have also been explored in related multi-robot manipulation settings [11]. Although such approaches are not developed specifically for tabletop rearrangement, they highlight the potential benefit of reducing strict synchronization between agents. These designs increase flexibility, but in tightly constrained rearrangement transfer, decisions remain strongly coupled with buffering and placement.

Non-prehensile manipulation, particularly pushing, has long been used to extend reachability and enable object motion in cluttered environments [12, 13]. In the present setting, pushing can facilitate cross-boundary object exchange without requiring a synchronous grasp-and-release handoff between the two manipulators. However, in many frameworks the shared boundary is still treated as a predetermined transfer interface rather than as a region whose crossing location can be selected online.

Beyond choosing where and how objects cross the shared boundary, non-monotone rearrangement also requires effective management of intermediate buffers. Most dual-arm planners model buffers as static planar table locations [9], which is restrictive in densely cluttered scenes. Prior work has shown that stacking can compact objects, free workspace, and serve as temporary buffering during rearrangement [14, 15]. Recent work further shows that temporary stacks can remain movable rather than acting only as strictly static structures [4]. In the present setting, this is valuable because multiple objects can occupy a smaller footprint, improving local space utilization and creating better conditions for inter-arm transfer.

In fixed handoff formulations, inter-arm exchange requires both arms to meet at a designated transfer configuration, which tightly couples the timing of the two manipulators. In contrast, a push-based transfer strategy relaxes this synchronization requirement by allowing one arm to push an object across the shared boundary while the other arm continues its local operation and retrieves the object later, as depicted in Fig. 3. The challenge is therefore not only to choose a transfer primitive, but also to integrate transfer selection with buffering and dual-arm coordination under clutter.

Building on these observations, this paper presents a dual-arm tabletop rearrangement framework that combines Gap-Aware Push Transfer for cross-boundary exchange with movable stacking, as showed in Fig. 1. Instead of restricting inter-arm transfer to a fixed aerial handoff pose, the proposed method searches the shared boundary for collision-free transfer gaps, places the object near a selected crossing point, and pushes it into the receiving workspace. This design reduces synchronous coupling between the two manipulators. In addition, a joint MCTS planner coordinates both arms while jointly reasoning about buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the quality of the generated plan. Compared with a fixed single-location handoff baseline, the proposed framework achieves better performance, particularly in denser scenes.

The proposed framework is detailed in Section II, including the problem formulation, Gap-Aware Push Transfer, the MCTS-based planner, and the experimental setup. The benchmark evaluation and discussion are presented in Section III, and the conclusion is given in Section IV.

title: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human-Humanoid Social Interaction
authors: Nikita Kuzmin,Georgii Demianchuk,Mariya Lezina,Yara Mahmoud,Iana Zhura,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.
introduction:
As humanoid robots enter human environments, they must participate in social rituals like handshakes, hugs, and fist bumps (Fig. 1). Unlike object manipulation, these interactions involve an active human partner whose intent must be inferred, requiring the robot to meet a moving target while ensuring safe, comfortable contact (Block et al., 2021; Block et al., 2023).

Existing approaches address this only partially: learned whole-body policies rely on explicit operator commands (Huang et al., 2026), compliance controllers typically use fixed settings (Lu et al., 2025), and vision-language pipelines infer intent with high latency, lacking physical execution (Bao et al., 2025). While end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can generate contact-rich motions, they risk unsafe false activations when human intent is uncertain.

To address this, we propose a four-component pipeline: (1) RGB-based intent recognition to gate and prompt the VLA, (2) VLA-based whole-body motion generation, (3) task-specific compliance adaptation, and (4) an independent voice-triggered safe stop.

This work investigates the following research questions:

RQ1: Which VLA model best performs contact-rich HRI actions
after fine-tuning on the same dataset?

RQ2: Does the preferred arm compliance depend on the type
of social interaction?

RQ3: Does intent gating improve the selection of the correct interaction, and can ongoing contact be safely interrupted?

Our main contributions are:

A comparative evaluation of four fine-tuned VLA models (Being-H0.5, GR00T, RLDX-1, UnifoLM-VLA-0) on social touch tasks .

An intent-gated VLA pipeline with task-conditioned compliance and voice-triggered safe stopping, validated via ablation and user studies.

title: Not Losing Your Way: Mitigating Visual-Inertial Odometry Drift through On-Demand Visual Feature Creation
authors: Simone D'Angelo,Gianmarco Corrado,Federico Esposito,Vincenzo Scognamiglio,Fabio Ruggiero
comment: . Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)
abstract: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) can degrade during aerial inspection in repetitive or poorly textured environments. We propose an active environment-modification framework for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) relying on cameras and an inertial measurement unit only, without prior maps or additional localization sensors. Inspired by the fairy tale of Tom Thumb, the UAV creates visual features on demand by releasing ground markers or marking walls through physical contact. An information-based indicator triggers interventions using temporal confirmation and hysteresis. Evaluation includes three simulated environments and a 900900-run factorial campaign. Lower cruise speed and active marking are associated with reduced divergence, while accuracy among non-divergent runs depends on speed–strategy interactions. Corridor experiments, with five runs per configuration, use OptiTrack for flight control while VIO-based marking decisions remain active online. The combined framework reduces the reported position root mean square error by approximately 35%35\% relative to baseline VIO, supporting active feature creation for drift mitigation.
introduction:
Aerial inspection in global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments can require unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to traverse tunnels and corridors with repetitive structures, shafts and tanks with uniform walls, or indoor spaces dominated by weakly textured surfaces. Such inspection routes may necessarily cross extended regions with insufficient distinctive visual features.

We consider localization using only onboard cameras and an inertial measurement unit (IMU), without prior maps or external positioning infrastructure. Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) and other complementary sensors are outside this setup. Although multi-modal sensor fusion [1, 2, 3] and deep learning-based feature extraction [4] have advanced localization, additional sensing changes the hardware configuration, while image processing remains limited by the available visual information. Without usable visual constraints, visual-inertial odometry (VIO) relies on inertial propagation and cannot guarantee reliable localization through prolonged visual deprivation. Perception-aware motion helps only when informative viewpoints remain accessible along the inspection route.

These challenges are particularly relevant to underground inspection, where tunnels, mines, and damaged structures can combine limited visual distinctiveness with airborne dust affecting both cameras and LiDARs [5, 6]. Geometric degeneracy can also challenge LiDAR-inertial odometry in tunnels, while dust and poor lighting impair VIO [5]. Propeller downwash can further reduce visibility by resuspending dust[6]. Here, we specifically address insufficient visual texture under visibility and illumination conditions that still allow newly introduced features to be observed.

Inspired by Tom Thumb’s trail of pebbles, our UAV introduces persistent visual features by depositing ground markers or marking accessible walls through physical contact (Fig. 1). These features provide additional visual constraints to support estimation and limit further drift accumulation.

We propose an integrated framework that couples online VIO quality monitoring with on-demand feature creation. Motivated by the information-based analysis of estimation degeneracy in [7], we construct an operational degradation indicator from the extended Kalman filter (EKF) information matrix and use temporal confirmation and hysteresis to trigger interventions. The robot selects a marking action according to the available surfaces and enabled mechanisms, and monitors the subsequent estimation response.

Hence, our contribution is the integration of degradation monitoring, physical feature creation, and navigation within a camera-and-IMU localization framework for aerial inspection in visually degraded environments.

title: PhySA: Decoupling Aesthetic and Physical Rewards for Humanoid Locomotion
authors: Yunwan Fu,Sicheng He,Jiageng Mao,Yue Wang
comment: . Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on R2RL: Roadmap to Sample-Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Humanoid locomotion policies trained without an explicit smoothness objective tend to produce jerky, high-energy gaits that stress actuators. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer an appealing reward source: given a rendered rollout, a VLM returns an aesthetic quality score on [0,10][0,10] without task-specific feature engineering. We find, however, that aesthetic preference and physical smoothness point in opposite directions: across four production VLMs, clips with higher joint acceleration receive higher aesthetic scores (mean Pearson r=+0.66r{=}{+}0.66). We study PhySA (Physical Smoothness and Aesthetics), which keeps the two on separate, independently removable reward channels: a sparse, asynchronous VLM score and a phase-triggered correction channel that adjusts physical penalty weights from simulator state. Ablations attribute the smoothness gain to the correction channel. On MuJoCo Humanoid-v5 at 2.6M steps, PhySA lowers joint acceleration by 2626 to 32%32\% relative to vanilla PPO, Text2Reward, and Eureka (three seeds), at the cost of shorter episodes. In a single extended run it lowers joint acceleration by 59.5%59.5\% relative to Prompt2Policy, while a three-seed replication shows a smaller, non-significant reduction (7.2%7.2\%). The gain does not transfer to IsaacLab or the Unitree G1, even after rescaling the smoothness term.
introduction:
Smooth motion is a practical requirement for deploying humanoid robots on hardware. High joint velocity accelerates actuator wear, increases energy draw, and produces trajectories that low-level servo controllers struggle to track faithfully [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Yet locomotion policies trained without an explicit smoothness objective consistently learn jerky, high-energy gaits. Encoding smoothness alongside forward progress in a single reward requires careful weight balancing: a large smoothness coefficient tends to destabilize early training, while a small one leaves joint acceleration ‖𝐪¨‖2\|\ddot{\mathbf{q}}\|_{2} uncontrolled.

Vision-language models (VLMs) trained on human motion video offer an appealing alternative reward source: given a rendered rollout, a VLM returns a continuous aesthetic quality score on [0,10][0,10] without task-specific feature engineering [6, 7, 8, 9]. Prompt2Policy [10] and related work [11] demonstrate this in practice by querying a VLM at every training update and incorporating the score directly into the per-step reward. LLM-synthesized reward functions [12, 13] take a different route: reward code is written once from a natural-language description, avoiding in-loop queries, but the resulting structure is fixed and cannot respond to failure modes that only emerge during training. Smoothness-specific regularizers [14, 15] encode the objective directly but require per-robot weight tuning and can destabilize early training if applied too aggressively.

One might hope that a VLM aesthetic score could serve as a jerk proxy, sidestepping hand-crafted penalties altogether. The data say otherwise. Across four production VLMs, jerkier, more energetic motion consistently scored higher; these models appear to read large joint excursions as confident locomotion and smooth, low-amplitude motion as stiff or hesitant. Using the aesthetic score as a smoothness signal would therefore push the policy toward higher joint acceleration, not lower. VLMs can, in principle, judge gait qualities such as knee flexion timing and swing symmetry that per-step losses do not encode, so the aesthetic signal may still be worth keeping, but not as a proxy for smoothness. Keeping aesthetic scoring and physical smoothness on separate channels lets each be measured and adjusted without disturbing the other.

We propose PhySA (Physical Smoothness and Aesthetics), a reward engineering framework for humanoid locomotion built around two separate channels: an asynchronous VLM aesthetic scorer and a phase-triggered physical correction module. The channels share no reward terms, so each can be ablated or tuned without touching the other. In a single extended training run on MuJoCo Humanoid-v5 [16, 17], PhySA reduces joint acceleration ‖𝐪¨‖2\|\ddot{\mathbf{q}}\|_{2} by 59.5%59.5\% relative to Prompt2Policy [10], with 43%43\% lower mechanical power and 57%57\% longer episodes; a three-seed from-scratch replication shows a smaller, non-significant reduction (7.2%7.2\%, p=0.45p{=}0.45). Against vanilla PPO, Text2Reward, and Eureka at 2.6M steps (three seeds), PhySA lowers joint acceleration by 2626 to 32%32\% while producing shorter episodes. The VLM channel in isolation raises joint acceleration by 136%136\%, and ablations attribute the smoothness gain to the correction channel. The smoothness gain does not carry over to IsaacLab or the Unitree G1, even after rescaling the smoothness term; a timestep experiment within MuJoCo points to the numerical integration scheme [18, 19, 20] as a major source of this gap.

Our main contributions are:

A finding that VLM aesthetic scores and joint-acceleration roughness are positively correlated across four production VLMs (mean Pearson r=+0.66r{=}{+}0.66), so a VLM aesthetic score should not be used as a proxy for physical smoothness.

PhySA, a reward design in which an asynchronous VLM aesthetic scorer and a phase-triggered physical correction module operate on two separate reward channels, each removable without affecting the other; ablations show the smoothness gain comes from the correction channel, and a timestep experiment points to physics integration as the main obstacle to cross-simulator transfer.

title: Energy-Aware Open-Vocabulary Detection Scheduling for Low-Power Robotic Autonomy
authors: Abdul Basit,Muhammad Shafique
comment: accepted for publication in ICARCV 2026
abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.
introduction:
Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets mobile robots ground run-time object queries, such as “find the bottle near the doorway,” in their camera stream instead of searching only fixed trained labels. This capability is enabled by vision-language models and open-vocabulary detection/grounding systems, including CLIP [1], OWL-ViT [2], GLIP [3], Grounding DINO [4], Detic [5], and YOLO-World [6]. In robotics, similar representations support language-grounded maps, open-vocabulary scene graphs, and object-centric navigation [7, 8, 9, 10].

The deployment problem is that OVD is expensive on embedded robots. A low-power robot must share a small battery across the embedded GPU, RGB-D camera, LiDAR, wireless stack, controller, and drive base. Mean Jetson input power is therefore a practical Jetson-side power-draw metric, especially for robots that keep monitoring or waiting after a target event. A fixed high detector rate gives fast response but wastes power during idle motion, map revisits, or low-information views. A fixed low-rate or quantized detector saves power but can delay target acceptance or miss short visual opportunities. The right operating point changes during the mission.

This motivates mission-level perception scheduling: each inference should be worth its energy at the current robot state. We ask whether an embedded robot can reduce Jetson input power for OVD while maintaining mission completion by scheduling detector rate from robot state. Our hypothesis is that low-value frames can be sampled sparsely, while candidate-target phases need high-rate response. A stationary frame in a stable map has lower marginal value than a frame near a plausible target; once a target appears, aggressive throttling is risky.

Existing work covers pieces of the problem but not the full intersection. OVD papers emphasize zero-shot recognition, language-grounded navigation emphasizes semantic goal reaching, and adaptive video analytics emphasizes throughput or resource budgets for passive streams. Our focus is more targeted: deciding when an embedded robot should spend OVD compute during search. As summarized in Table I, prior works generally do not combine OVD, robot-state-aware adaptation, Jetson input-power/energy accounting, and task-level metrics such as success rate and time-to-detect (TTD).

We present an energy-aware OVD scheduler that treats detector invocations as mission-level computational resources. The scheduler uses odometry, map changes, and detector confidence to adaptively switch among low-, mid-, and high-power operating modes. We evaluate YOLO-World-S on a Jetson Orin Nano mobile robot against fixed-rate 8 Hz, 5 Hz, and 2 Hz baselines across bottle and cup search tasks. Fig. 1 illustrates the overall runtime flow.

Our main contributions are:

We formulate energy-aware OVD as a mission-level scheduling problem that trades Jetson input power and detector invocation rate against search success and TTD, rather than only reducing per-frame inference cost.

We design a finite-state runtime that switches OVD rate from robot-native signals with explicit thresholds and hysteresis, including a low-power configuration for low-value frames.

We implement the scheduler with YOLO-World-S on an AgileX LIMO equipped with a Jetson Orin Nano and compare it against fixed-rate high-, medium-, and low-rate baselines.

We report a real-robot evaluation with 40 navigation trials across two queried objects and a separate stationary microbenchmark that isolates perception power.

We show empirically that lower mean power does not necessarily imply lower mission-window Jetson input energy, because slower or less reliable perception can increase navigation time.

The main finding is that lower instantaneous detector power is only one part of the robot objective. The scheduler reduces mean Jetson input power relative to the high-rate baseline and shows slightly higher aggregate success in the evaluation logs, but mission-window Jetson input energy still depends strongly on runtime. We therefore report power, energy, success, TTD, and time-domain traces rather than optimizing energy in isolation.

2. We design a finite-state runtime that switches OVD rate from robot-native signals with explicit thresholds and hysteresis, including a low-power configuration for low-value frames.

3. We implement the scheduler with YOLO-World-S on an AgileX LIMO equipped with a Jetson Orin Nano and compare it against fixed-rate high-, medium-, and low-rate baselines.

4. We report a real-robot evaluation with 40 navigation trials across two queried objects and a separate stationary microbenchmark that isolates perception power.

5. We show empirically that lower mean power does not necessarily imply lower mission-window Jetson input energy, because slower or less reliable perception can increase navigation time.

title: GraspBench: Execution-Aware Cross-Robot Evaluation of 6-DoF Grasp Generation in MuJoCo
authors: Abdul Basit,Bibek Poudel,Muhammad Shafique
comment: accepted for publication in ICARCV 2026
abstract: Modern 6-DoF grasp generators are often evaluated using grasp scores, dataset-level metrics, or single-robot demonstrations, yet proposal quality alone does not determine whether a grasp is executable by a particular robot. We present GraspBench, a controlled MuJoCo protocol for evaluating complete grasp-generation pipelines after robot-specific inverse-kinematics filtering, motion planning, and fixed approach-close-lift execution. GraspBench evaluates six configured pipelines across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects, and a structured tabletop pose grid, yielding 540 scenarios per method and 3,240 method-scenario evaluations in total. Missing outputs are conservatively counted as failures, and success follows the binary lift criterion produced by each method’s execution runner. GraspGen achieves the highest overall success rate (73.1%), followed by EconomicGrasp (63.5%), while robot- and object-conditioned analyses reveal substantial variation across embodiments and object geometries. GPG produces the largest native candidate sets but achieves 44.3% success, indicating that proposal volume alone does not guarantee robot-executable grasps. Cluster-aware paired intervals support the principal method differences while not estimating repeated-execution uncertainty. The results characterize complete configured pipelines on fixed scenarios rather than intrinsic model quality or stochastic repeatability, showing that grasping performance depends jointly on the generator, robot embodiment, scene, and execution protocol.
introduction:
Reliable robotic grasping remains a central requirement for practical manipulation. Recent 6-DoF grasp generators can produce dense or diverse candidate grasps from point clouds, and large-scale datasets have accelerated progress in grasp prediction [1, 2]. Yet a high-scoring grasp proposal is not necessarily executable by a specific robot. The final outcome depends on how the predicted grasp distribution interacts with object geometry, workspace placement, robot kinematics, approach feasibility, collision constraints, and the execution controller. A well-ranked proposal may be unreachable for one arm, feasible for another, or invalid during approach and lift.

This issue becomes sharper across robot embodiments. Differences in reach, joint limits, wrist geometry, and gripper placement can change which candidates survive feasibility filtering. Aggregate success can therefore hide structured failures: a method may perform well on box-like shapes but degrade on thin or concave geometries, succeed near the table center but fail near workspace boundaries, or generate many candidates that downstream constraints discard. These observations motivate evaluating grasp generation as part of an execution pipeline rather than as pose prediction alone.

Existing grasp resources provide indispensable scale and standardization. GraspNet-1Billion offers dense RGB-D grasp annotations and benchmark metrics [1]; ACRONYM provides millions of simulated grasps over thousands of objects [2]; and Dex-Net demonstrated the value of synthetic grasp analysis for robust manipulation policies [3]. In parallel, grasp generators such as GPG, the geometric candidate generator associated with GPD [4], Contact-GraspNet [5], AnyGrasp [6], EconomicGrasp [7], GraspGen [8], and HGGD [9] have advanced geometric, contact-based, dense, budget-aware, generative, and heatmap-guided grasp proposal mechanisms. These works address important parts of the grasping problem, but dataset-level annotations and method-specific demonstrations do not fully answer a complementary question: how do different generators behave when their outputs are routed through a common scenario-indexed feasibility and simulated-execution structure? Unlike dataset-level grasp benchmarks that evaluate pose annotations or generator outputs independently of a fixed execution stack, GraspBench fixes the robot, object, workspace, and execution protocol so that generated grasps can be compared under robot-conditioned feasibility constraints.

We study this question through four research questions:

How much do 6-DoF grasp-generator rankings change across robot embodiments?

Which object, workspace, and pose conditions expose failures hidden by aggregate success?

How do method-native candidate-set sizes relate descriptively to simulated execution success?

How does failure-aware accounting affect denominator consistency and reported aggregate performance when methods fail to return outputs?

GraspBench evaluates a shared robot-object-workspace-pose grid, enabling paired comparisons across AUBO i5, Franka, KUKA iiwa, and PiPER; five diagnostic objects; workspace positions; and object pitch. For each scenario, a generator proposes grasps, robot-specific filtering selects the highest-ranked feasible candidate, the motion planner produces the robot trajectory, and MuJoCo executes a fixed approach-close-lift sequence scored by its recorded binary lift outcome.

The evaluated pipelines span dense perception (AnyGrasp), contact-based prediction (Contact-GraspNet), geometric sampling (GPG), budget-aware generation (EconomicGrasp), generative modeling (GraspGen), and heatmap-guided detection (HGGD). We evaluate execution consequences under scenario-aligned downstream stages, not training recipes or implementation efficiency.

Conservative scenario-level accounting counts missing outputs as failures instead of removing them. This prevents missing scenarios or repeated rows from changing the common denominator. Normalized records retain available candidate counts, scores, condition identities, and failure labels for reproducible scenario-level analysis.

Three observations emerge. First, method gaps and rankings depend on robot embodiment and object geometry. Second, native proposal volume has no apparent monotonic relation with execution success, although differing budgets preclude a causal candidate-count comparison. Third, missing and explicit no-grasp outputs are execution-relevant outcomes; counting them as failures provides a conservative common denominator rather than excluding absent records.

The main contributions of this paper are:

Execution protocol: a controlled MuJoCo benchmark protocol for evaluating 6-DoF grasp generators across multiple robot embodiments under a scenario-aligned IK-filtered execution pipeline.

Scenario diagnostics: a structured robot-object-workspace-pose grid and paired scenario-level analysis that reveal robot-, object-, workspace-, and pose-conditioned failure patterns.

Failure-aware study: a conservative evaluation of six configured grasp-generation pipelines showing that aggregate and condition-specific execution outcomes can diverge.

The study is intentionally limited to controlled, single-object simulation. Its five geometries are diagnostic rather than representative of broad object diversity, and the opaque glass model does not test transparent-object perception. GraspBench therefore complements, rather than replaces, cluttered-scene benchmarks, candidate-level Success@K analysis, repeated stochastic trials, and real-robot validation.

1. How much do 6-DoF grasp-generator rankings change across robot embodiments?

title: Real-Time Event-Based LED Tracking and Pose Estimation with PWM-Encoded Markers
authors: Junkai Niu,Sheng Zhong,Delei Kong,Xin Wang,Kaizhen Sun,Yusen Zhang,Mingzhen Gan,Yi Zhou
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
abstract:
Event cameras are neuromorphic vision sensors with pixels that independently and asynchronously respond to brightness changes at microsecond resolution, supporting state estimation under rapid motion, motion blur, and high dynamic range (HDR) illumination.
This also enables capture of high-frequency blinking patterns from light-emitting diodes (LEDs).
Based on this, we propose a real-time event-based framework for LED tracking and six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) relative pose estimation using pulse-width modulation (PWM)-encoded LED markers.
Multiple LEDs share a common blinking frequency and encode identities through distinct PWM duty cycles, reducing frequency-resource requirements and computational cost.
Our dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework combines low-rate LED detection with high-rate raw-event updates, maintaining robust LED identity association and accurate pixel-level tracking under rapid motion.
LED identities and positions establish reliable 2D-3D correspondences for real-time metric 6-DoF relative pose estimation.
Extensive evaluations on a self-collected dataset demonstrate robustness under large motion flow and transient image-plane LED overlap.
Furthermore, we develop a coordinated robotic platform comprising a quadrotor and a Mecanum-wheeled mobile robot, demonstrating the proposed framework’s potential for closed-loop drone guidance through hovering and target-following experiments under time-varying HDR illumination, with onboard deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.
The dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research.
introduction:
Robust and low-latency estimation of the 6-DoF relative pose between rigid bodies is important for robotic manipulation, multi-robot coordination, autonomous landing, and augmented reality [1, 2, 3, 4].
Conventional solutions often rely on radio-frequency links, motion-capture infrastructure, or frame-based fiducial markers such as AprilTag [5] and ArUco [6], whose performance can degrade when communication or external infrastructure is unavailable, or when rapid motion and challenging illumination cause motion blur and intermittent observations.
Active LED markers provide a compact and controllable alternative [7, 8].
Given a known geometric configuration of LEDs, their position measurements can be used to recover the metric relative pose of the marker [9].
Marker identity can be encoded either spatially, through the geometric arrangement of multiple LEDs, or temporally, through their blinking patterns. Compared with spatial coding, temporal coding allows individual LEDs to carry identification information independently, thereby reducing the dependence on complex spatial layouts.
Reliable decoding of such temporal patterns requires accurate sensing of rapid ON-OFF transitions.
Event cameras are particularly well suited to this task, as they asynchronously capture pixel-wise intensity changes with microsecond-scale temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and low latency [10, 11, 4], enabling robust perception under high-speed motion and challenging illumination [12, 13, 14, 15].
For active LEDs, the precise timestamps and polarities of the resulting events directly capture the temporal structure of their blinking signals, supporting event-based LED detection and identification.

Despite these advantages, existing event-based LED identification methods face limitations in achieving robust multi-marker association under asynchronous event streams.
Existing active-marker systems commonly associate LEDs through event counts, inter-event intervals, or distinct blinking frequencies [8, 9, 16].
Assigning a separate frequency to each marker, however, becomes increasingly restrictive as the marker count grows: within a fixed frequency range, increasing the number of markers reduces the spacing between assigned frequencies and can require longer observation intervals for reliable identification [17].
Pulse-interval encodes avoid allocating a distinct frequency to each marker by encoding identities through sequences of unequal transition intervals [18].
This motivates a coding scheme that distinguishes multiple LEDs while retaining a common fixed blinking period for detection.
Moreover, many pipelines accumulate events into fixed-duration windows or pseudo-frames.
When tracking updates rely on these accumulated detections, the detection interval limits the update rate of position measurements.

These limitations reveal two key challenges: developing a coding scheme that reduces the required frequency resources for reliable multi-marker identification, and designing an asynchronous tracking strategy that combines detection robustness with event-level temporal precision.
We address these challenges with an event-based relative-pose framework based on PWM-encoded LED markers.
As demonstrated in Fig. Real-Time Event-Based LED Tracking and Pose Estimation with PWM-Encoded Markers, all markers share a common blinking frequency while encoding their identities through duty cycles, thereby reducing the frequency range that needs to be covered by the detector.
Inspired by event-wise blob tracking [13], we adopt a dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework fram that combines periodic detection corrections with high-rate updates from associated raw events.
Finally, the recovered marker identities establish 2D-3D correspondences for accurate perspective-nn-point (PnP) pose estimation.

The primary contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A PWM marker encoding and identification method for event cameras, where multiple LEDs can share the same blinking frequency and be distinguished by their PWM duty cycles, reducing the required frequency resources and consequently lowering the computational cost of marker identification (Sec. III-B).

A dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework that combines low-rate LED detections with high-rate updates from associated raw event data for robust marker tracking.
By integrating both measurements into a unified state estimation framework, the proposed method achieves accurate and responsive tracking under scenarios with large optical flow (Sec. III-C).

A real-time 6-DoF relative pose estimation framework based on the identification and tracking of PWM-encoded LED markers, which can be used for drone guidance in time-variant HDR environments.
Extensive experiments on a self-collected dataset and drone flight experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and practical performance, and the dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research (Sec. III-D).

Outline:
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Sec. II reviews active LED coding and identification, as well as event-based marker tracking and pose estimation.
Sec. III introduces the proposed PWM detection, asynchronous tracking, and pose-estimation pipeline.
Sec. IV presents the experimental evaluation, followed by the conclusion in Sec. V.

1. A PWM marker encoding and identification method for event cameras, where multiple LEDs can share the same blinking frequency and be distinguished by their PWM duty cycles, reducing the required frequency resources and consequently lowering the computational cost of marker identification (Sec. III-B).

2. A dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework that combines low-rate LED detections with high-rate updates from associated raw event data for robust marker tracking.
By integrating both measurements into a unified state estimation framework, the proposed method achieves accurate and responsive tracking under scenarios with large optical flow (Sec. III-C).

3. A real-time 6-DoF relative pose estimation framework based on the identification and tracking of PWM-encoded LED markers, which can be used for drone guidance in time-variant HDR environments.
Extensive experiments on a self-collected dataset and drone flight experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and practical performance, and the dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research (Sec. III-D).

title: Data-Driven Configuration of Protective Separation Zones in Collaborative Robot Cells from Operator Occupancy
authors: Aulon Bajrami,Theo Jacobs,Werner Kraus
comment: . Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE Stuttgart Conference on Automotive Production (SCAP). \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE
abstract:
The protective separation zone of a collaborative robot cell is commonly
dimensioned for a worst case that disregards where the operator is actually
present during the task. This paper presents a camera-based, data-driven method
that configures this zone from observed operator occupancy. Operator positions
accumulated over several production shifts are aggregated into an occupancy
heatmap, from which a protective field is derived that trades off the achievable
robot velocity against the required safety distance, following the speed and
separation monitoring principle of ISO/TS 15066. The resulting configuration is
advisory, that is, reviewed within the risk assessment rather than applied
autonomously to the robot controller. The method, which builds on a pose-based
perception pipeline with activity recognition, was evaluated in two operational
cells at two industrial partners, where the protective field could be reduced by approximately 17% and
a productivity increase of 9% was measured. However, adoption proved to depend
on more than the demonstrated gain alone.
introduction:
Collaborative robots promise to combine the repeatability of automation with the
flexibility of the human operator, and they have consequently attracted
considerable attention as a means of automating tasks that resist full
automation, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises
[1, 2, 3]. Realising this promise
in production, however, requires the shared workspace to be kept safe without
sacrificing the very productivity that motivates the deployment
[4, 5]. The present work is concerned
with this tension in cells that implement speed and separation monitoring in the
sense of ISO/TS 15066 [6].

The contribution of this work is twofold. First, a data-driven method for
configuring the protective separation zone of a collaborative cell is presented:
operator positions observed over time are aggregated into an occupancy heatmap,
from which an optimised size of the protective field is derived that trades off
the achievable robot velocity against the required safety distance, following the
speed and separation monitoring principle of ISO/TS 15066. The result is
advisory, that is, it is provided as a proposal reviewed within the risk
assessment before adoption rather than applied autonomously to the robot
controller. Second, the perception pipeline from which the occupancy is obtained
is described, comprising pose-based person tracking and an activity recognition
step that distinguishes interaction with the cell from unrelated traffic. Unlike prior fluency and safety approaches that
are validated in simulation or in the laboratory under idealised perception
(e.g., [7]), the proposed approach was developed and evaluated
together with industrial partners in a real production setting, where occupancy
estimation and activity recognition must contend with the occlusions, layouts
and operator behaviour encountered on the shop floor.

title: Whole-Body Elasto-Geometrical Calibration of Wheeled Humanoid Robots Using a Shared-Waist Dual-Chain Model
authors: Pengxin Zha,Yi Lu,Haojun Ma,Jun Zhu,Minghao Qiu,Xiaoyan Wang,Wei Shan,Maoqing Yao
abstract: Wheeled humanoid robots carry both arms on one actuated waist, usually without torque sensors, so the accuracy of both end-effectors depends on a single waist model. After a first stage that estimates the tracker and target extrinsics, we identify the waist and both arms in one problem from the target positions on both flanges, measured by an optical tracker. The kinematic model is complete, with waist-base, parallel-axis, and branch parameters; arm compliances are driven by measured torques and waist compliances by gravity torques of the robot’s mass model; and Gaussian priors with evidence-maximizing scales stabilize the estimate. Independent and sequential single-chain calibration are restrictions of this problem, and its waist information is the sum of the single-chain Schur complements. On two robots with different waists, each without and with a payload, calibration reduces the mean errors on held-out poses from 11.3–31.1 mm to 0.50–1.11 mm. For every training-set size from 20 poses to all, the method has 17–63% lower mean errors than adaptations of two published whole-body calibration methods, mainly through the waist compliance. Independent calibration yields two waist models; using either for both arms raises the other arm’s error to up to 3.21 mm.
introduction:
Humanoid robots are moving from research laboratories into industrial work [1]. Wheeled humanoids replace the legs with a mobile base and carry both arms on an actuated waist. In dual-arm tasks, both end-effectors must be accurate in one common base frame, and both depend on the same waist: an error in the waist model moves both hands at once, while geometric deviations along each chain accumulate at the end-effectors [2, 3]. Harmonic drives add compliance, so joint deflections under load add to the geometric errors [2, 4]. The waist joints carry the upper body and both arms, but on wheeled humanoids they usually have no torque sensors.

Industrial manipulators are calibrated with external instruments such as laser trackers [5]; the identifiable parameters [6] of a linearized error model of the serial chain are then estimated from the measurements [7]. Elasto-geometrical calibration adds joint compliances driven by the joint loads [4, 8, 7]; without joint torque sensors, the loads follow from a gravity model of the links, which can be identified from the same calibration poses [8] or together with the kinematic parameters [7, 9], and the pose of a joint axis also varies with the posture of the axes that follow it [10]. Systems of two manipulators are calibrated with a holistic error model of the link parameters and of the base, camera, and marker transforms [11], or with one arm as the measuring instrument of the other [12]; on an industrial dual-arm robot, calibrating the cameras first and then the kinematics was more effective than calibrating all parameters simultaneously [13]. The two arms of a humanoid, however, share the waist joints, which raises the question of how the shared parameters are identified.

Early humanoid calibration relied on onboard sensors: head-mounted stereo cameras for the upper body [14], self-touch with artificial skin to close a kinematic chain [15], and link orientation sensors with both feet flat on the floor for the joint offsets [16]; Tanguy et al. [17] calibrated the geometric parameters of the whole kinematic tree online. In simulation on iCub, calibrating a chain together with other chains that share joints with it improved the optimization results and the observability [18]. Tenhumberg and Bäuml [19] modeled the upper body of Agile Justin with joint and transversal elasticities under its own weight, and identified its Denavit–Hartenberg parameters and elasticities by least squares with priors from the end-effector positions of both arms, measured by an external tracking system, which reduced the mean position error from 21 to 3.1 mm.

Two recent works calibrate the whole body of a humanoid and evaluate it by cross-validation. Bonnet et al. [2] calibrated the bipedal TALOS with motion capture and its joint torque sensors: the head–trunk and both arms were identified in one least-squares problem that shares the trunk parameters, elasticities were driven by the measured torques, and identifiable parameters were selected by a QR decomposition on simulated configurations; the cross-validated marker error was 2.2 mm RMS. Nguyen et al. [3] calibrated TALOS without external instruments, from contacts of the gripper with a single plane: two foot-to-hand chains, whose four identifiable torso parameters are common, are identified geometrically with a parameterization in the Unified Robot Description Format (URDF), and the cross-validated plane-contact error dropped by a factor of 2.3 relative to the manufacturer’s model. Neither work reports how much the shared parameters gain over identifying the chains independently or one after the other, and neither addresses a wheeled robot whose waist carries no torque sensors.

This article studies these questions on wheeled humanoids calibrated in production with an optical tracker. Its contributions are as follows.

A shared-waist dual-chain elasto-geometrical calibration for wheeled humanoids with a general waist (any number of revolute or prismatic joints): two stages separate the tracker and target extrinsics from the body model; waist-base, parallel-axis [20], and branch parameters complete the modified Denavit–Hartenberg (MDH) model; waist compliances about and perpendicular to the joint axes are driven by the gravity torques of the mass model of the robot description; and Gaussian priors, whose scales maximize the evidence of the training data, stabilize the estimate. The identification runs in the production calibration software of the robots.

An identifiability analysis in which independent and sequential single-chain calibration are row and column restrictions of the same system, and the dual-chain waist information is exactly the sum of the two single-chain Schur complements.

Experiments on two robots with different waists, each without load and with a payload, that compare the dual-chain formulation with independent and sequential calibration and with adaptations of [2, 3] on held-out poses, for training sets from 20 poses to all, and that quantify the contribution of each part of the model.

The identification runs in the production calibration software of the robots.

title: Unified Overview of Safety Certificate Functions: Techniques from Hamilton--Jacobi Reachability and Control Barrier Functions
authors: Hao Wang,Max Cohen,Zeyuan Feng,Donggeon David Oh,Oswin So,Songyuan Zhang,Javier Borquez,Chuchu Fan,Jaime Fernández Fisac,Haimin Hu,Jason J. Choi,Somil Bansal
abstract: Safety is a central concern in modern autonomous systems. Safety certificates—functions whose existence guarantees that a system meets its safety specification—have long been used as a principled tool for rigorously reasoning about safety. Methods for synthesizing such certificates are scattered across research areas, with little guidance on when to use a particular approach. This tutorial provides a holistic treatment of safety certificate synthesis centered on two widely used families: Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis and control barrier functions (CBFs). For each family of methods, we first introduce its general formulation, along with classical and learning-based tools for certificate synthesis. Next, we introduce two benchmark problems consisting of vehicle systems of differing complexity to assess the certificate quality of different synthesis methods and their effectiveness in safety-critical control. We use these benchmarks to compare various methods and provide practical guidance for selecting an approach.
introduction:
As autonomous systems increase in complexity and capability, safety remains a central concern in their design and deployment. These systems are often safety-critical, operating in close proximity to people or other systems, where unsafe behavior can cause physical harm or other serious consequences. Establishing that such a system is safe requires careful and principled mathematical reasoning.

A popular framework for rigorously establishing safety properties is the safety certificate: a function whose existence certifies that a dynamical system satisfies, or can be controlled to satisfy a desired safety specification. This perspective closely parallels Lyapunov theory for stability and inherits from it the underlying philosophy of function-based certification and corresponding synthesis techniques [1]. For control systems, a safety certificate provides a condition for determining whether a candidate controller renders the system compliant with the desired safety specification. Establishing safety can therefore be reduced to finding a valid certificate, which subsequently serves as a constructive basis for designing a safety-critical controller.

Methods for synthesizing safety certificates have been developed using various approaches, each with its own formalism and terminology.
This makes it difficult to discern what these methods have in common, how they differ, and which one best fits a given problem. A holistic treatment of their foundations, their synthesis, and the trade-offs among them would make these methods far more accessible to the broader research community.

In this tutorial, we address this gap for the two most widely used families of certification methods: Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [2] and control barrier functions (CBFs) [3, 4]. We start by outlining the theoretical formulation of each method and how it yields a safety certificate. We then compare the two methods through two benchmark problems, and provide general guidance for selecting an approach based on the properties of the system at hand.
This tutorial complements existing tutorials and surveys on HJ reachability and CBFs [4, 2], as well as on safety filters that build on these methods [5, 6, 7].
First, rather than surveying these methods in isolation, we frame them around a common goal: the construction of safety certificates and how they can be used for safety filtering.
Second, we provide an overview of various certification synthesis methods for each of the two families, including more recent developments in learning-based methods.
Third, we contribute a set of case studies, built around two vehicle systems of differing complexity, that serves as a benchmark for assessing both the quality of synthesized certificates and their effectiveness in safety-critical control. Our goal is not to provide an exhaustive treatment of each featured technique, but rather to present a concise summary of its core principles from a unified safety-certificate perspective. The tutorial is therefore intended primarily for researchers who have some prior exposure to one or more of these methods and seek a broader understanding of how they relate, what their respective strengths and limitations are, and how to select an appropriate approach for certifying and enforcing safety in a given control system.

Our key findings are detailed in Sec. VII and summarized in Fig. 1. We note that the choice of synthesis method is largely determined by two properties of the problem: whether a closed-form dynamics model is available, and the dimension of the state. For low-dimensional systems with closed-form dynamics, classical methods apply. Numerical HJ reachability [8, 9] recovers the closest approximation to the maximal safe set, whereas CBFs [10, 3] admit analytical constructions under special structures of the dynamics [11, 12] at negligible computational cost, though control bounds complicate their design. Decomposition [13] and reduced-order [14, 15] techniques extend both families to higher dimensions, at the cost of additional design effort. When the state dimension is high, learning-based methods require less manual tuning and are preferable. Neural CBFs [16, 17, 18] are computationally efficient but rely on a nominal controller. PINN-based reachability [19, 20] targets the exact safety value function, given continuous-time dynamics and an effective sampling scheme. RL-based reachability [21, 22] is the natural choice when the system is accessible only as a black box.

The tutorial is organized as follows. Secs. II and III build up from the notion of safety to safety certificates, and then to the theory underlying CBFs and HJ reachability analysis, in the continuous-time and discrete-time settings, respectively. Sec. IV and Sec. V then present classical and learning-based synthesis tools, and Sec. VI reports the two case studies with a discussion of the results. Finally, Sec. VII offers a practical guide to selecting a synthesis tool, and Sec. VIII concludes with limitations and directions for future work.

title: Semantics-to-Contact: A Stagewise Framework for Robust Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Guanren Qiao,Ruixiang Ouyang,Sheng Xu,Yueci Deng,Yunxin Tai,Kui Jia,Guiliang Liu
comment: NeurIPS 2026
abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise control under complex contact dynamics while remaining robust to diverse visual conditions. However, real-world reinforcement learning often overfits to the visual appearance of training scenes. We propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise framework for visually robust contact-rich manipulation. The insight is to decompose the problem into two stages: semantic focusing and contact refinement. In the first stage, a vision-language model localizes task-relevant regions across visually diverse scenes, providing coarse spatial guidance and reducing the burden of exploration. In the second stage, a real-world human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning policy learns fine-grained contact behaviors within the localized region using force feedback. To further improve visual robustness, we introduce an object-centric visual augmentation strategy that randomizes background appearance while preserving the robot and task-relevant objects. Experiments on six contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks exhibit that S2C consistently improves success rates over strong baselines and maintains reliable performance under significant visual and positional variations. These results demonstrate that stagewise semantic focusing and contact refinement provide a practical path toward visually robust real-world contact-rich manipulation. Our demos can be seen in https://edem-ai.github.io/S2C/.
introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation is a key capability for enabling robots to operate in real-world applications [26], such as insertion [28], alignment [55, 49], and pressing [25, 55], which often require robots to perform fine-grained adjustments under multimodal force signals and frequently changing contact states. In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated strong adaptability in such tasks [27, 17, 33, 30], particularly learning contact policies through human-in-the-loop (HIL) interaction with the real-world environment [25, 26]. However, real-world reinforcement learning (RWRL) still faces a fundamental challenge: visual observations are highly susceptible to variations in background textures and lighting conditions, making policies learned in one scenario difficult to generalize to new real-world environments.

Existing methods often rely on domain randomization in simulation to improve visual robustness. By randomly varying background textures, lighting conditions, and environmental parameters, policies can learn representations that are more robust to visual perturbations across a large number of virtual environments [48, 51, 38]. However, constructing a high-fidelity simulation environment for contact-rich manipulation is challenging [54]. Contact-rich manipulation tasks often exhibit a large sim-to-real gap [16]. For example, in industrial assembly, tight insertion tasks may involve clearances smaller than 0.1 mm, leading to complex contact dynamics that are difficult to accurately model in simulation. Therefore, a natural question arises:
Can we learn visually robust contact policies directly on real robots without relying on complex simulation environments?

To address the above challenges, we propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise framework for visually robust contact-rich manipulation. We argue that a robot is a complex system in which perception, planning, and control are tightly coupled. Therefore, visual generalization cannot be achieved by optimizing a single module alone; instead, it requires a stagewise, system-level design [41]. The key idea is to decompose the task into two complementary stages: semantic focusing and contact refinement. In the first stage, a vision-language model (VLM) uses RGB-D observations and language instructions to identify task-relevant regions and guide the robot toward a semantic neighborhood. This stage provides coarse spatial grounding [24] across diverse scenes and prevents the RL policy from blindly exploring a large spatial range. In the second stage, human-in-the-loop real-world residual RL learns fine-grained contact behaviors within the localized region using proprioceptive and force feedback. This decomposition is particularly suitable for contact-rich manipulation: once the robot has been guided close to the target, it typically only needs to perform subtle pose adjustments to finish tasks successfully according to local force feedback.

To further enhance visual robustness, we introduce an Object-centric visual augmentation strategy during real-world training. Specifically, we extract task-relevant foreground regions from wrist-camera images and apply random perturbations to the background [5, 38], including changes in color and texture. The augmented images are then directly fed into the RWRL policy for training. In this way, the policy is encouraged to focus on manipulable objects and contact-relevant regions, rather than overfitting to the visual background of a specific experimental setup. At the control level, we adopt residual RL [28, 17, 2, 1] to improve the efficiency of real-world policy learning. Instead of learning a complete action policy from scratch, residual RL learns local corrections on top of an existing policy, thereby reducing the exploration space and improving learning efficiency.

We evaluate our method on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks and test its robustness under diverse visual and spatial variations. Experimental results show that, compared with strong baselines, S2C maintains a high success rate under both positional shifts and visual disturbances, while other methods almost fail to complete the task under visual disturbances. In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise real-world reinforcement learning framework that decomposes visually robust contact-rich manipulation into semantic focusing and contact refinement.

We introduce a simulation-free visual robustness strategy that combines VLM-guided semantic localization with an object-centric visual augmentation strategy, enabling RWRL policies to better generalize across background textures and lighting conditions.

We conduct many experiments and provide a number of videos to identify the robustness and scalability boundaries of S2C. The results illustrate that S2C achieves strong performance under most robust settings.

1. We propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise real-world reinforcement learning framework that decomposes visually robust contact-rich manipulation into semantic focusing and contact refinement.

2. We introduce a simulation-free visual robustness strategy that combines VLM-guided semantic localization with an object-centric visual augmentation strategy, enabling RWRL policies to better generalize across background textures and lighting conditions.

3. We conduct many experiments and provide a number of videos to identify the robustness and scalability boundaries of S2C. The results illustrate that S2C achieves strong performance under most robust settings.

title: Embodied RAG++: Retrieval-Augmented Generation From What Exists to What Works in Embodied Scenes
authors: Fan Yang,Tatsuya Kikuzuki,Jun Liang,Jun Liu,Wenkai Li,Ryosuke Kawamura,Ananya Hazarika,Prajit KrisshnaKumar,Shaunak Mehta,Yuushi Toyoda
comment: accepted to SII 2027
abstract: To serve a request in a human environment, a robot system must find an object that satisfies a functional requirement and a robot that can feasibly reach it. Scene graphs record which objects exist and where, but they often omit capabilities documented only in product manuals. Retrieval-augmented generation methods can read such manuals, yet they rarely reason jointly over object capabilities, physical instances, robot states, and dynamic connectivity. We introduce E2W-Bench, the Exists-to-Works Benchmark, which links dynamic hybrid scene graphs with real product manuals to evaluate capability-grounded robot–object assignment under availability, mobility, vertical-reach, and connector constraints. We also present Embodied RAG++, a spatially grounded retrieval framework that scopes retrieval to the manuals linked to candidate objects, caches extracted capabilities per product model, and resolves robot–object feasibility through deterministic spatial reasoning. On E2W-Bench, Embodied RAG++ reaches a pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, compared with at most 0.30 and 0.55 for the baselines, while requiring the shortest preprocessing time among the retrieval-based methods and tying for the lowest total token count.
introduction:
Robots operating in human environments need more than knowledge of which objects exist and where they are located. To serve a request, a system has to find which physical object can satisfy the user’s functional requirement and which available robot can feasibly reach it. Consider a request to heat a 27 L food container to 240°C. A scene graph may contain several microwave ovens, but the required cavity capacity and convection temperature are specified only in their product manuals. Even after identifying a suitable appliance, the system has to check whether an available robot can reach it under the current mobility and connectivity conditions. If an elevator becomes unavailable, for example, a wheeled robot may be unable to access another floor, whereas a legged robot may use the stairs. Resolving such a request therefore requires combining capabilities documented in manuals with the current state of the objects, robots, and connectors in the scene.

Existing work addresses parts of this problem but not their combination. 3D scene graphs [1, 2], open-vocabulary maps [3], and hierarchical planners [4] model spatial layouts and navigation paths, while benchmarks such as ScanRefer [5] and SQA3D [6] evaluate visual language grounding. These representations capture what exists and where, but not the non-visual functional attributes stored in external documentation. Graph-structured retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [7] frameworks such as GraphRAG [8], RAPTOR [9], and HippoRAG [10], for their part, retrieve document knowledge but return textual answers that are not tied to physical instances and ignore reachability, robot availability, and changing scene state. EmbodiedRAG [11] introduces spatial retrieval over observational memory, but its knowledge is limited to what the agent has perceived, not to external manuals. In addition, processing multi-page manuals anew for every query and every physical instance repeats the same work whenever several instances share a product model.

We introduce E2W-Bench (Exists-to-Works Benchmark), a benchmark for capability-grounded robot–object assignment over dynamic hybrid scene graphs. E2W-Bench connects physical object instances with product manuals and unifies robots, spatial connectors, and dynamic environmental states within a single graph. Each query has a machine-verified unique ground-truth pair, so a single exact-match check evaluates document reasoning and spatial allocation together.

We also propose Embodied RAG++, a spatially grounded retrieval framework that couples document-grounded capability inference with deterministic feasibility verification (Fig. 1). Embodied RAG++ uses the scene graph’s object-to-manual links to restrict retrieval to the manuals of candidate objects. It resolves reachability, mobility, and connectivity constraints with deterministic spatial reasoning, which requires no large language model (LLM) calls. To avoid reprocessing the same manuals, Embodied RAG++ stores extracted facts in Capability Cards, memory units keyed by product model that grow incrementally as queries request new fields. Every physical instance of a model and every later query that needs the same field reuses the card.

Our contributions are as follows:

E2W-Bench, which links dynamic hybrid scene graphs to real product manuals and gives every query a machine-verified unique ground-truth pair (§III).

Embodied RAG++, which combines manual-scoped, aspect-split retrieval, model-level Capability Cards, availability filtering, and deterministic spatial reasoning (§IV).

An evaluation with three LLM backbones and four baselines, in which Embodied RAG++ reaches a pair accuracy of 0.90 with Qwen2.5-32B and 1.00 with Llama3.3-70B, compared with at most 0.30 and 0.55 for the baselines, with the shortest preprocessing time among the retrieval-based methods and the lowest total token count, tied with EmbodiedRAG (§V).
